“Say, ‘I find nothing in what has been revealed to me forbidden to anyone who eats it, unless it be carrion or blood poured forth.’”

Since blood that is not poured forth is excused, despite being blood, it is clear that He, glorified be He, has distinguished between blood that flows and other blood. Thus, during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Muslims would put meat into broth and eat it while streaks of blood were clearly visible in the cooking pots, as ‘Ā’ishah reported. Were this not the case, they would have extracted the blood from the veins, as the Jews do.

Allah Most High has forbidden animals that die of themselves or are killed by something other than a sharp, wounding implement. Thus, He forbade animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, or by being gored. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also forbade game killed by the broad side of an unfeathered hunting shaft, saying, “It has been killed by a blow,” but not game killed by its point. The distinction between the two is simply whether the blood is shed. This indicates that the cause of impurity is the blood’s being retained and trapped within the animal.

If, however, the blood is shed in an unclean manner, by invoking a name other than Allah’s over the animal, the uncleanness here arises from another cause. Prohibition may therefore result either from the presence of blood or from invalid slaughter, as with slaughter performed by a Magian or an apostate, or slaughter performed somewhere other than the proper place.

Since this is so, bones, horns, nails, cloven hooves, and similar parts contain no blood that is poured forth, so there is no basis for regarding them as impure. This is the view of the majority of the early generations. Al-Zuhrī said, “The best members of this community used to comb their hair with combs made from elephant bones.”

Moreover,

---

## Page 10506

a well-known hadith concerning ivory has been reported, but it is open to criticism that need not be discussed here, since we do not need to rely on it as evidence. It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said regarding Maymūnah’s sheep:

“Why did you not take its hide and make use of it?” They replied, “It died without being slaughtered.” He said, “Only eating it has been forbidden.”

Sahīh al-Bukhārī contains no mention of tanning, nor did most of al-Zuhrī’s students mention it when narrating from him. Ibn ʿUyaynah, however, did mention it, and Muslim included his narration in his Sahīh. Imam Ahmad criticized this addition, indicating that Ibn ʿUyaynah had erred in it. He also mentioned that al-Zuhrī and others permitted the use of hides from animals that had died without lawful slaughter, even without tanning, on the basis of this hadith. Accordingly, this text implies that using them after tanning is permissible with even greater reason.

Yet even if it is argued that Allah subsequently forbade the use of hides until they were tanned, or that tanning does not purify them, this does not entail prohibiting bones and similar parts. The hide is a part of the dead animal containing blood, like its other parts. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, treated its tanning as its lawful slaughter, because tanning dries out its moisture. This indicates that moisture is what causes the impurity. Bone, however, contains no flowing moisture, and whatever moisture it contains dries up. Moreover, bone lasts and remains preserved longer than hide, so it has an even stronger claim to purity.

The scholars have disagreed concerning tanning: does it render the hide pure?

---

## Page 10507

Mālik and Ahmad, according to the well-known position reported from each, held that tanning does not render the hide pure. The position of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and the majority is that it does. Ahmad subsequently adopted this view, as al-Tirmidhī reported from him through Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī.

The hadith of Ibn ʿUkaym indicates that “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade them to make use of the hide or sinews of an animal that had died without lawful slaughter,” after previously allowing them to do so. This prohibition, however, may concern hides before tanning, whose use he had previously permitted. For the authentic hadith narrated by al-Zuhrī makes clear that he had permitted the use of hides from animals that had died without lawful slaughter before tanning. Thus, he may initially have allowed them to do this, then prohibited it when he forbade using such hides before tanning. For this reason, some lexicographers state that ihāb denotes an untanned hide. This also explains why sinews are mentioned alongside it, since sinews are not tanned.

Section

Regarding the milk and rennet of an animal that has died without lawful slaughter, scholars hold two well-known views:

The first is that they are pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and others, and one of the two views reported from Ahmad.

---

## Page 10508

The second is that they are impure. This is the position of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, and the other view reported from Ahmad.

This disagreement underlies their disagreement concerning cheese made by the Magians. Animals slaughtered by the Magians are unlawful to eat according to the overwhelming majority of earlier and later scholars. Indeed, it has been said that the Companions unanimously agreed on this. Thus, when the Magians make cheese—and cheese is made with rennet—these two views apply to it.

The stronger view is that their cheese is lawful, and that the rennet and milk of an animal that has died without lawful slaughter are pure. This is because, when the Companions conquered Iraq, they ate cheese made by the Magians, and this practice was open and widespread among them. Reports that some of them disapproved of it are questionable, for they were transmitted by certain people of the Hijāz, and that transmission is open to question. The people of Iraq were better informed about this, since the Magians lived in their lands, not in the Hijāz.

Further evidence for this is that Salmān al-Fārisī served as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb’s deputy over al-Madā’in and used to call the Persians to Islam. It is reliably reported that he was asked about certain kinds of clarified butter, cheese and furs. He replied:

“What is lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book, and what is unlawful is what Allah has forbidden in His Book. Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.”

Abū Dāwūd also narrated this as a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is well known that the question was not about cheese made by Muslims or the People of the Book, for this is a matter

---

## Page 10509

that is clear. Rather, the question concerned cheese made by the Magians. This shows that Salmān used to rule that it was lawful. If this has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then the dispute is settled by the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Moreover, neither the milk nor the rennet itself died. Those who deemed them impure did so only because they were contained in an impure vessel, making them liquid in an impure vessel. The ruling that they are impure thus rests on two premises: that the liquid came into contact with an impure vessel, and that such contact renders it impure.

The first response is: We do not concede that a liquid becomes impure through contact with impurity. It has already been shown that the Sunnah indicates its purity, not its impurity.

The second response is: Contact within the body has no legal effect, as Allah Most High says:

“We give you to drink, from what is in their bellies, pure milk from between digested matter and blood, palatable to those who drink it.”

This is why it is permissible to carry a small child during prayer despite what is in the child’s belly. And Allah knows best.

## Page 10510

Chapter: Cleansing After Relieving Oneself

He, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about someone who claimed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Face west, not east.”

Others claimed that he said:

“Face east, not west.”

He replied:

Both hadiths are fabrications. However, it is reported from him in the Sahīh that he said:

“Do not face the qiblah when defecating or urinating; rather, face east or west.”

It is also reported from him in the Sunan collections that he said:

“What lies between east and west is the qiblah.”

He was addressing the people of Medina and those similarly situated, such as the people of Greater Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, and Iraq. As for the people of Egypt, their qiblah lies between east and south, toward the point where the sun rises in winter. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 10511

He was also asked about cleansing after relieving oneself:

“Does a man need to stand up, walk about, clear his throat, and cleanse himself with stones or other materials every little while as he goes to and fro, thinking that something has come out of him? Did the early generations, may Allah be pleased with them, do this? Or is it an innovation, or something permissible?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

Clearing one’s throat after urinating, walking about, jumping upwards, climbing stairs, hanging from a rope, checking the penis by making urine flow, and similar practices—all these are innovations. They are neither obligatory nor recommended according to the leading Muslim scholars. Indeed, according to the correct view, tugging at the penis is also an innovation; the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe it. Likewise, squeezing out urine is an innovation that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe.

The hadith narrated concerning this is weak and has no basis. Urine flows naturally, and when urination is finished, it stops naturally. It is as has been said:

“Like an udder: leave it alone and it rests; milk it and it flows.”

---

## Page 10512

And whenever a person opens the tip of his penis, some urine may come out; if he left it alone, none would come out. He may imagine that something has come out, but this is an obsessive misgiving. Someone troubled by this may feel a cool sensation when something touches the tip of the penis and think that something has come out, although nothing has.

Urine may remain held at the end of the urethra without dripping. If a person squeezes the penis, the private parts, or the opening with a stone, a finger, or something else, moisture comes out. This too is an innovation. The scholars agree that this retained urine need not be expelled, whether with a stone, a finger, or anything else. Indeed, whenever he expels it, more replaces it, since it continually seeps through.

Cleansing with stones is sufficient; there is no need to wash the penis with water. It is recommended for someone who has cleansed himself after relieving himself to sprinkle water over his private parts, so that if he feels moisture, he can say, “This is from that water.”

As for someone with urinary incontinence—meaning that urine flows involuntarily and does not stop—he should use a protective pad to contain it. If the urine stops long enough for him to purify himself and pray, he does so; otherwise, he prays even while urine is flowing, like a woman with non-menstrual bleeding, who performs ablution for each prayer. And Allah knows best.

## Page 10513

Chapter: The Siwāk

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Is it preferable to use the siwāk with the left hand rather than the right, or the reverse? Is it permissible to rebuke someone who uses it with the left hand? Which is better?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. It is preferable to use the siwāk with the left hand. Imam Ahmad explicitly stated this in the report transmitted by Ibn Mansūr al-Kawsaj, who recorded it from him in his Masā’il (Questions). We know of no imam who disagreed with this.

This is because using the siwāk falls under the removal of offensive matter, like expelling water from the nose, blowing the nose, and similar acts of removing offensive matter. These are done with the left hand, just as removing impurities—by cleansing oneself with stones and the like—is done with the left hand. Whether obligatory or recommended, the removal of offensive matter is done with the left hand.

Actions are of two kinds: those involving both limbs, and those specific to one of them. The principles of Islamic law have established that actions in which

---

## Page 10514

both the right and left sides are involved should begin with the right when they are of an honorable nature, such as ablution, ritual bathing, beginning with the right side when using the siwāk or plucking the armpit hair, dressing, putting on shoes, combing the hair, entering the mosque or the home, leaving the lavatory, and similar actions.

The left takes precedence in the opposite cases, such as entering the lavatory, removing shoes, and leaving the mosque. As for actions performed with only one hand, those of an honorable nature are done with the right, such as eating, drinking, shaking hands, handing over and receiving books, and similar actions. Those of the opposite nature are done with the left, such as cleansing oneself with stones, touching the penis, expelling water from the nose, blowing the nose, and similar actions.

If it is argued:

“Using the siwāk is an act of worship in its own right, prescribed when rising for prayer even if no dirt is present; and an act of worship in its own right is performed with the right hand.”

The response is:

Neither premise is conceded. Using the siwāk was prescribed precisely to remove what is inside the mouth, and scholars agree upon this rationale. This is why it is prescribed following things that cause changes in the mouth, such as sleep and loss of consciousness, and before acts of worship for which purification is prescribed, such as prayer and recitation. Since the mouth is liable to such changes, using the siwāk is prescribed when

---

## Page 10515

rising for prayer, just as someone performing ablution is prescribed to wash his hand before beginning, since the hand is used to pour the water.

Scholars have differed over whether washing the hand is recommended when it is known to be clean. There are two well-known opinions. Those who recommend it—as is the well-known position in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—do so in view of what occurs occasionally—indeed, usually—and to replace doubt with certainty. The same may be said of using the siwāk, if it is considered recommended when rising for prayer even when the mouth is clean, although the purpose of washing the hand before rinsing the mouth is cleanliness. This explains the objection to the first premise.

As for the second premise: assuming that using the siwāk is an act of worship in its own right, what evidence establishes that performing it with the right hand is recommended?

There is no evidence for this premise. Rather, it may be said that acts of worship are performed in the manner appropriate to them, and precedence is given within them to whatever is appropriate.

Furthermore, consider the statement, “It is an act of worship in its own right.” If this means that it is a purely devotional act whose rationale cannot be understood, that is incorrect, for Muslims agree that using the siwāk has an intelligible rationale; it is not like casting pebbles at the pillars during Hajj.

If, however, it means that this act requires an intention, as ritual purification does, and that it is prescribed even when cleanliness is certain, and the like, then, if this description is conceded, nothing in it requires the act to be performed with the right hand, since there is no evidence for that. For the fact that it is performed with an intention or prescribed even when cleanliness is certain

---

## Page 10516

does not preclude its being a means of honoring the right hand in particular; indeed, this is possible even with that description. Do you not see that circumambulating the House is among the noblest acts of worship intended in their own right? It is recommended to remain close to the House while doing so. Nevertheless, the left side is nearer the House, because in this circular movement the right side relies upon the left. Since the honor here belongs to the outer side, that position is assigned to the right. Nor has it been transmitted that, because circumambulation is intended in its own right, the right side should be placed nearer the House. Rather, honoring the right side here means keeping it on the outside. Likewise, using the left hand to expel water from the nose honors and safeguards the right hand. The same applies to using the siwāk.

Further, if it is said that using the siwāk is fundamentally a means of removing offensive matter, and if it is said that it is prescribed, and that switching from the right hand to the left in performing it better honors the right hand even apart from that, this does not preclude removing offensive matter from being an established and intended purpose of it. This is comparable to cleansing oneself with three stones according to those who require it, such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad: they require the third stone even when cleanliness has already been achieved with fewer. The same applies to washing impurities three or seven times wherever this is obligatory: those who require it prescribe it even when the impurity has already been removed with fewer washings. Likewise, washing each limb three times during ablution is recommended even if the limb becomes clean with fewer washings. Yet there is no doubt that removing impurity is an intended purpose of cleansing oneself with water or stones after relieving oneself.

---

## Page 10517

Likewise, removing offensive matter from the mouth is unquestionably an intended purpose of using the siwāk, even though its use is prescribed in the absence of such matter to ensure that the intended purpose is achieved. This does not prevent it from being done with the left hand, just as the third stone used in cleansing oneself after relieving oneself is applied with the left hand, as is the seventh washing of a vessel licked by a dog. The same applies to similar acts whose original purpose is to remove offensive matter, even if it is said that they are prescribed in its absence to fulfil their purpose completely, replace doubt with certainty, and treat exceptional cases according to the prevailing rule.

Moreover, the underlying wisdom may be difficult to discern, so the ruling is tied to its presumed indication. Someone may suppose that the offensive matter has disappeared entirely without being certain, and certainty in this regard may be difficult to attain. The presumed indication is therefore made a substitute for the underlying wisdom. Thus, using the siwāk is prescribed when rising to pray, regardless of whether any change has occurred, because worship consists in the occurrence of change. If this explanation is advanced, it is of the kind found in scholarly opinions.

None of this removes this type of act from the category of removing offensive matter, even if it is an act of worship intended in its own right, for which an intention is prescribed. Accordingly, it should be performed with the left hand, like expelling water from the nose, cleansing oneself with stones after relieving oneself, and directly rubbing or otherwise cleaning the area licked by a dog. Pouring water, by contrast, belongs to the category of honorable acts. Hence, a person performing ablution draws water into the nose with the right hand and expels it with the left; a person cleansing himself after relieving himself pours water with the right hand and rubs with the left.

Likewise, a person taking a ritual bath or performing ablution with water puts his right hand into the vessel and pours water with it onto his left, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did, even though

---

## Page 10518

the left hand is used to touch the private parts during the ritual bath. Likewise, someone washing an area affected by impurity pours water with the right hand and, if direct contact with the area is needed, uses the left. The evidence of Islamic law and its underlying principles amply supports this. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:
“When should circumcision be performed?”

He replied:
Circumcision may be performed whenever one wishes. However, as a boy approaches puberty, he should be circumcised, as was the practice of the Arabs, so that he reaches puberty already circumcised.

As for circumcision on the seventh day, there are two opinions, both transmitted from Ahmad. One holds that it is not disliked, because Abraham circumcised Isaac on the seventh day. The other holds that it is disliked because it is a Jewish practice, and imitating them is disliked. This is Mālik’s position. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:
“Is it permissible for a sane adult Muslim to fast and pray while he is uncircumcised and has not been purified? What is the ruling concerning someone who forgoes circumcision?”

He replied:
If there is no fear that circumcision will harm him, he must be circumcised, for

---

## Page 10519

it is a strongly enjoined practice for Muslims, as the imams unanimously agree. It is obligatory according to al-Shāfiʿī and, according to the well-known position reported from him, Ahmad. Abraham, the close friend of Allah—peace be upon him—was circumcised after the age of eighty. Trustworthy physicians should be consulted to assess the risk of harm. If circumcision would harm him in summer, he should postpone it until autumn. And Allah knows best.

He was asked about women:
“Should a woman be circumcised or not?”

He replied:
Praise be to Allah. Yes, she should be circumcised. Her circumcision consists of cutting off the upper part of the skin that resembles a rooster’s comb. The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to the woman who performed circumcision:

“Cut only a little, and do not cut excessively, for that makes the face more radiant and makes her more pleasing to her husband.”

This means: do not cut excessively. The purpose of male circumcision is to cleanse him of the impurity trapped beneath the foreskin, whereas the purpose of female circumcision is to moderate her sexual desire. For if she is uncircumcised, she is sexually excitable and has intense desire.

Hence the insult, “You son of an uncircumcised woman!” For an uncircumcised woman is more drawn to men. This is why forms of sexual immorality are found among Tatar and Frankish women that are not found among Muslim women. If the circumcision is excessive, sexual desire is weakened, and the man’s aim is not fully realized. When the cutting is done without excess, the intended purpose is achieved in moderation. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 10520

He was asked:
“If a boy dies uncircumcised, should he be circumcised after death?”

He replied:
No one is to be circumcised after death.

He was asked:
“How long may a man wait before shaving his pubic hair?”

He replied:
Anas—may Allah be pleased with him—reported:
“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—set them a time limit for shaving the pubic hair, plucking the underarm hair, and similar practices: they were not to leave these unattended for more than forty days.”

This is recorded in al-Sahīh. And Allah knows best.

What do the esteemed scholars—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning people who have their heads shaved by shaykhs and at graves that

---

## Page 10521

they venerate, regarding this as an act of devotion and worship: is this Sunnah or a religious innovation? Is shaving the head in general Sunnah or a religious innovation? Please give us your ruling, may you be rewarded.

Shaykh al-Islām replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Shaving the head is of four kinds.

The first is shaving it during Hajj and ‘umrah. This is something Allah and His Messenger have commanded, and its prescription is established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslim community. Allah Most High says:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety, with your heads shaved or your hair shortened, without fear.”

Mass-transmitted reports establish that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—shaved his head during his Hajj and ‘umrah pilgrimages. Likewise, some of his Companions shaved their heads, while others shortened their hair. Shaving is better than shortening, which is why he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“O Allah, forgive those who have shaved their heads.”
They said, “O Messenger of Allah, and those who have shortened their hair?”
He said, “O Allah, forgive those who have shaved their heads.”
They said, “O Messenger of Allah, and those who have shortened their hair?”
He said, “O Allah, forgive those who have shaved their heads.”
They said, “O Messenger of Allah, and those who have shortened their hair?”
He said, “And those who have shortened their hair.”

During the Farewell Pilgrimage, he instructed the Companions who had not brought sacrificial animals with them to shorten their hair for ‘umrah after circumambulating the House and going between al-Safā and al-Marwah, and then to shave their heads after completing Hajj. Thus, he combined for them shortening the hair first and shaving it afterward.

---

## Page 10522

The second kind is shaving the head out of necessity, such as for medical treatment. This too is permissible according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. Allah has permitted a person in ihrām, who is ordinarily forbidden to shave his head, to do so if he suffers from an ailment, as He Most High says:

“Do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of slaughter. But whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head must offer compensation by fasting, charity, or sacrifice.”

The report of Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah is established by the agreement of the Muslims. During the ʿumrah of al-Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—passed by him while lice were falling from his head. He asked, “Are your lice troubling you?” He replied, “Yes.” He said, “Shave your head and sacrifice a sheep, or fast for three days, or distribute a faraq (a measure of food) among six needy people.” The authenticity of this hadith is agreed upon, and all Muslims have received it with acceptance.

The third kind is shaving the head as an act of worship, religious devotion, or asceticism, outside Hajj or ʿumrah. Examples include instructing someone who repents to shave his head; making a shaved head a distinguishing mark of people of devotion and religion, or part of the perfection of asceticism and worship; or considering someone who shaves his head better, more devout, or more ascetic than someone who does not.

Another example is trimming the hair of someone who repents, as some who claim spiritual leadership do when they guide someone through repentance: they cut some of his hair, and the shaykh appoints a bearer of scissors and a prayer rug. His praying on the rug and cutting people’s hair are then treated as part of the qualifications for spiritual leadership that make him fit to be an exemplar who guides

---

## Page 10523

those who repent.

This is an innovation that neither Allah nor His Messenger commanded. None of the imams of the religion considers it obligatory or recommended. Nor was it practised by any of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the Muslim shaykhs renowned for asceticism and worship—whether among the Companions, the Successors, their successors, or those who came after them, such as al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyād, Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, Ahmad ibn Abī al-Hawārī, al-Sarī al-Saqatī, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī, and others like them. These men did not cut anyone’s hair when he repented, nor did they instruct a penitent to shave his head.

All the inhabitants of the earth embraced Islam during the lifetime of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—yet he did not instruct them to shave their heads upon embracing Islam, nor did the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—cut anyone’s hair. Nor did he pray on a prayer rug. Rather, he led all the Muslims in prayer, praying on the same surfaces as they did and sitting on the same surfaces as they did. Nothing he sat on distinguished him from them, whether a rug or anything else. He would, however, sometimes prostrate on a small mat woven from palm leaves, because the mosque had no floor covering; they prayed on sand and pebbles. Most of the time, he prostrated directly on the ground, so that mud could be seen on his forehead—may Allah bless him and his family and grant him abundant peace.

Whoever regards innovations that are neither obligatory nor recommended as acts of devotion and obedience

---

## Page 10524

and a path to Allah, and regards them as completing the religion and as practices prescribed for the penitent, the ascetic, and the worshipper, is misguided, departing from the path of the Most Merciful and following in the footsteps of the devils.

The fourth type is shaving one’s head outside religious rites, without any need, and not as an act of devotion or religious observance. Scholars hold two views on this, both reported from Ahmad.

The first is that it is disliked. This is the position of Mālik and others.

The second is that it is permissible. This is the well-known position among the followers of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, because:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—saw a boy whose head had been partly shaved and said, ‘Shave it all or leave it all.’”

And:

“Young children were brought to him after three days, and he shaved their heads.”

Moreover, he prohibited shaving only part of the head, which indicates that shaving the entire head is permissible.

Those who hold the first view say that shaving the head is a distinguishing mark of the people of innovation. The Khawārij used to shave their heads, and some of them consider shaving the head part of completing repentance and religious devotion. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that:

“While the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was making a distribution in the year of the Conquest, a thick-bearded, shaven-headed man came to him.”

---

## Page 10525

He was asked:

Is a soldier who plucks the white hairs from his beard committing a sin by doing so?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Plucking grey hairs is disliked, whether for a soldier or anyone else, for a hadith states that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—“forbade plucking grey hairs and said, ‘They are the Muslim’s light.’”

He was asked:

If a man trims his nails or moustache, or combs his hair, while in a state of major ritual impurity, is there any blame upon him? Some have raised this matter, saying: “If someone in a state of major ritual impurity cuts his hair or nails, those parts of his body will be returned to him in the Hereafter. He will therefore rise on the Day of Resurrection bearing a share of major ritual impurity proportionate to what he removed, and each hair will bear a share of that impurity.” Is this so or not?

He replied:

It is authentically reported from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in the hadith of Hudhayfah

---

## Page 10526

and in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with them both—that when a person in a state of major ritual impurity was mentioned to him, he said: “The believer does not become impure.” In al-Hākim’s Sahīh, the wording is: “Whether alive or dead.”

I know of no evidence in Islamic law that removing one’s hair or nails while in a state of major ritual impurity is disliked. Indeed, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to a man who had embraced Islam: “Remove the hair from your time of unbelief and be circumcised.” He instructed the man who had embraced Islam to bathe, but did not instruct him to delay circumcision or hair removal until after bathing. The unqualified wording of his instruction therefore indicates that either order is permissible.

Likewise, a menstruating woman is instructed to comb her hair when performing her ritual bath, even though combing removes some hair. And Allah knows best.

## Page 10527

Chapter: Ablution

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about wiping the head during ablution:

“Some scholars require wiping the entire head, others require wiping a quarter of it, and others say that wiping some of its hair suffices. Which of these views should be considered correct? Please explain this to us.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. All the imams agree that the Sunnah is to wipe the entire head, as established in the authentic and good hadiths reported from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. None of those who described his ablution reported that he confined himself to wiping only part of his head. What some jurists—such as al-Qudūrī at the beginning of his compendium, and others—mention, namely that he performed ablution and wiped his forelock, is only part of the hadith recorded in the Sahīh on the authority of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—performed ablution in the year of Tabūk and wiped his forelock.”

For this reason, a group of scholars held that wiping part of the head is permissible, and this is

---

## Page 10528

the view of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, as well as one view within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

Others held that wiping the entire head is obligatory. This is the well-known position in the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and it is the correct view. Nothing in the Quran indicates that wiping only part of the head is permissible. For the Most High’s words, “And wipe your heads and your feet,” are comparable to His words:

“Then wipe your faces and your hands.”

Both verses use the word “wipe” and the preposition bā. If the verse concerning tayammum does not indicate wiping only part—even though tayammum is a substitute for ablution and involves wiping with earth, without prescribed repetition—how could the verse concerning ablution indicate this, when ablution is the primary rite and involves wiping with water, with which repetition is prescribed? No one who understands what he is saying would make such a claim.

Anyone who supposes that those who consider partial wiping sufficient hold this view because bā denotes a part, or indicates a common element of meaning, has misunderstood the imams, the language, and the meaning conveyed by the Quran.

The preposition bā indicates contact, and its inclusion always serves a purpose. When used with a verb that is already directly transitive, it conveys an additional meaning, as in His words:

“A spring from which Allah’s servants drink their fill.”

Had it said, “They drink from it,” this would not have indicated that their thirst was quenched. Thus, “drink” was invested with the meaning of “have their thirst quenched,” and so it says:

“Drink their fill from it.”

This indicates drinking that quenches thirst. The use of a verb to include the meaning of another verb, so that it takes the same preposition—as in His words:

“He has certainly wronged you in demanding that your ewe be added to his ewes,”

and His words, “And We helped him against the people

---

## Page 10529

who denied Our signs,” and His words:

“And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you,”

and similar examples—is frequent in the Quran. For the Basran grammarians, this dispenses with the strained claims of the Kufan grammarians that prepositions share meanings.

The same applies to wiping in ablution and tayammum. Had it said simply, “Wipe your heads” or “your faces,” this would not have indicated that anything adheres through wiping. For you may say, “I wiped so-and-so’s head,” even though your hand was not wet. But when it says, “Wipe your heads” and “your faces,” using the preposition bā, wiping is invested with the meaning of making something adhere. It thus conveys that, through this wiping, you make something adhere to your heads and faces. In the verse concerning tayammum, this indicates that earth must adhere to the face and hand. Hence His words:

“Then wipe your faces and hands with some of it.”

Those who permit wiping only part of the head base their position on the hadith. They then differed among themselves. Some said that wiping an area equal to the forelock suffices, as in one report from Ahmad and the position of some Hanafī scholars. Others said that wiping most of the head suffices, as in one report from Ahmad and the position of some Mālikī scholars. Some said that a quarter suffices, while others said an area equal to three fingers; these are two Hanafī positions. Some said three hairs, or part of them, while others said one hair, or part of it; these are two Shāfi‘ī positions.

As for those who require wiping the entire head—such as Mālik and Ahmad, according to the well-known position in

---

## Page 10530

their respective schools—their evidence is the apparent meaning of the Quran.

If their opponents concede that the entire prescribed area must be wiped in tayammum, then this applies all the more to wiping in ablution, both in wording and in meaning. It cannot be argued that complete coverage is obligatory in tayammum because it replaces washing the face, which must be washed entirely. A substitute takes the place of what it replaces in its legal ruling, not in its form. Thus, wiping over leather socks replaces washing the feet, yet complete coverage is not obligatory when wiping them, although it is obligatory when washing the feet. Their position is also supported by the widely transmitted Sunnah established through the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

As for the hadith of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, Ahmad and other jurists versed in hadith permit wiping over the turban, on the basis of the authentic, established hadiths concerning this. In Ahmad’s view, if a person wipes his forelock and completes the remainder by wiping over his turban, this unquestionably suffices. As for Mālik, his only answer to the hadith is to interpret it as a case in which the Prophet had an excuse that prevented him from uncovering his head, and therefore performed tayammum over the turban because of that excuse.

Whoever follows the Sunnah by wiping his forelock and turban has fulfilled the requirement when there is an excuse, without disagreement; according to the three, this also suffices without an excuse. Wiping the head once is sufficient by agreement, just as purifying each of the other limbs once is sufficient.

They differed over whether wiping the head three times is recommended. The majority hold that it is not recommended, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfa, and Ahmad according to the well-known position reported from him.

---

## Page 10531

Al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to one report from him, held that it is recommended, citing the authentic report that the Prophet performed each act of ablution three times. This wording is general. Sunan Abī Dāwūd also reports that he wiped his head three times. Moreover, the head is one of the parts included in ablution, so repeating its purification three times is prescribed, as with the other parts.

The first view, however, is more correct. The authentic hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, show that he used to wipe his head only once. For this reason, Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī said: “The authentic hadiths of ʿUthmān indicate that he wiped once.” This renders the report he transmitted about wiping three times unsound, for he explains that the authentic account is that the Prophet wiped his head once. This detailed account governs the interpretation of the summary statement:

“He performed each act of ablution three times.”

Similarly, the Prophet’s statement:

“When you hear the muezzin, say what he says,”

is a summary instruction, explained by Ibn ʿUmar’s hadith, according to which, at the calls to prayer and success, one says:

“There is no power and no might except through Allah.”

Thus, a specific, explanatory text governs the interpretation of a general, unelaborated one.

Furthermore, this is wiping, and repetition is not prescribed for wiping, as with wiping over leather socks, wiping in tayammum, and wiping over a splint. Drawing an analogy between one form of wiping and another is more appropriate than drawing an analogy between wiping and washing, for repeated wiping becomes like washing.

The practice of some people—wiping part of the head, or indeed merely part of the hair, three times—is an error that contravenes the agreed-upon Sunnah in two respects. First, wiping only part of the head is contrary to the Sunnah by agreement of the imams. Second, repeating the wiping is contrary to the Sunnah according to the correct view. Even those who recommend repetition—such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to one of his positions—do not say:

---

## Page 10532

“Wipe part of the head and repeat it.” Rather, they say: “Wipe the entire head and repeat the wiping.”

The imams do not disagree that wiping the entire head once is preferable to wiping part of it three times. Indeed, if wiping part is held to suffice, and a man avails himself of this concession, why would he repeat the wiping?

Moreover, Muslims disagree over whether it is permissible to wipe only part of the head and whether repeating the wiping is recommended. How, then, can one choose a practice that most of them consider insufficient and do not recommend, while abandoning a practice that all of them consider sufficient and most regard as preferable? And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Is it authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wiped his neck during ablution, or that any of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did so?

He answered:

It is not authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wiped his neck during ablution. Indeed, this has not been related from him in any authentic hadith. Rather, the authentic hadiths describing the ablution of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicate that he did not wipe his neck. For this reason, the majority of scholars—including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to the apparent position of their schools—did not recommend it. Those who recommended it relied on a report related from

---

## Page 10533

Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, or on a hadith with a weak transmission:

“He wiped his head as far as the back of the head.”

Such a report cannot serve as a reliable basis, nor can it counter what the hadiths indicate. Whoever omits wiping the neck has a valid ablution, by scholarly consensus. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Washing the feet during ablution is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through mass transmission. Both his practice and his command to do so have been transmitted. Among these is his statement authentically reported through several chains, including the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and ʿĀ’ishah:

“Woe to the heels from the Fire!”

One wording reads:

“Woe to the heels and the soles of the feet from the Fire!”

Whoever performs ablution as the people of innovation do—not washing the soles of his feet or his heels, but merely wiping their upper surfaces—then woe to his heels and the soles of his feet from the Fire.

Wiping over leather socks is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through mass transmission. Wiping over the feet has also been reported from him in circumstances of need, such as when a person is wearing sandals that are difficult to remove. As for wiping the feet when both are fully exposed, no one has reported this from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It contradicts the Book and the Sunnah. As for its contradiction of the Sunnah, that is evident

---

## Page 10534

and established by mass transmission. As for its contradiction of the Quran, Allah’s words,

“And wipe over your heads, and [wash] your feet up to the ankles,”

have two well-known readings: one with “feet” in the accusative, and the other with it in the genitive.

In the accusative reading, “feet” is coordinated with “faces” and “hands,” so the meaning is: “Wash your faces, your hands, and your feet up to the ankles, and wipe over your heads.” The genitive reading, however, does not mean “wipe your feet,” as some people suppose, for several reasons.

First, those among the early generations who recited it this way said: “The command comes back to washing.”

Second, if it were coordinated with “heads,” the command would be to wipe the feet, not to wipe over them. Yet in ablution and dry ablution, Allah commands wiping over the limb, not simply wiping the limb. Thus, the Most High says:

“And wipe over your heads.”

And He says:

“Then seek clean earth and wipe over your faces and hands with it.”

The recognized Quran reciters did not recite “your hands” in the accusative in the verse concerning dry ablution, as they did in the verse concerning ablution. Were it a matter of coordination, the two passages would be alike.

This is because His words, “And wipe over your heads,” and His words, “And wipe over your faces and hands,” require contact with what is being wiped, since the preposition bā’ denotes contact. This requires water and clean earth to reach the limbs being ritually purified. By contrast, saying, “Wipe your head and your foot,” does not require water to reach the limb.

This demonstrates that bā’ is a particle conveying a specific meaning, not a redundant addition as some people suppose. This contrasts with the following words:

---

## Page 10535

“Mu'āwiya, we are human, so be gentle—
we are neither mountains nor iron.”

Here, the particle bā’ serves to reinforce the meaning; removing it would not alter the sense. In the verse concerning purification, however, removing bā’ would alter the meaning. Coordination therefore cannot be with the syntactic position of the noun governed by it, but must instead follow that noun’s explicit inflection or refer back to an earlier noun.

Third: If coordination were with the syntactic position, the verse concerning dry ablution would have been read: “Wipe over your faces, and wipe your hands.” Thus, the verse contains what demonstrates the error of the commentator’s contention that his position is indicated by “Then wipe over your faces and your hands with it,” with “hands” in the accusative, since the two expressions are identical. Given their agreement on the genitive reading in the verse concerning dry ablution—although coordination with the syntactic position would have been possible had it been correct—it is clear that coordination follows the explicit inflection. Moreover, the verse concerning dry ablution contains no accusative noun with whose explicit inflection another noun could be coordinated, unlike the verse concerning ablution.

Fourth: He said:

“And your feet up to the two ankles.”

He did not say “up to the ankles,” using the plural. If it were supposed that coordination was with the syntactic position, as the other view maintains, and that the intended meaning was that each pair of feet has two ankles, with one ankle on each foot, the wording would have been “up to the ankle,” just as He said “up to the elbows,” since each arm has one elbow. Accordingly, the two ankles are the two bones projecting on either side of the lower leg, not the point where the sandal strap is fastened, at the junction of the leg and foot, as those who advocate wiping over the feet maintain. Thus, if Allah, blessed and exalted be He, commanded the feet to be purified only as far as the two projecting ankle bones,

---

## Page 10536

and the one who wipes does so up to the junction of the foot and lower leg, it is clear that he is acting contrary to the Quran.

Fifth: The two readings are like two verses. Observing the prescribed sequence in ablution is either obligatory or strongly recommended. When a limb to be wiped separates two limbs to be washed, interrupting the grouping of like with like, this indicates the prescribed sequence in ablution.

Sixth: The Sunnah explains the Quran, indicates its meaning, and expresses what it conveys; and it prescribes washing.

Seventh: Dry ablution was instituted as a substitute for ablution when needed: half of the limbs involved in ablution were omitted, and purification of the other half was made easier. Thus, what was to be wiped was omitted, and what was to be washed was instead wiped.

As for the other reading—the reading in which “and your feet” is in the genitive—it does not contradict the mass-transmitted Sunnah. The two readings are like two verses, and the established Sunnah does not contradict the Book of Allah; rather, it agrees with it and confirms it. It explains and clarifies it for those whose understanding falls short of comprehending the Quran. For the Quran contains subtle indications that escape many people, as well as passages stated in summary form which the Sunnah explains and clarifies.

---

## Page 10537

Wiping is a generic term denoting contact between what is used to wipe and what is wiped. The word itself neither affirms nor denies that the substance used flows.

Abū Zayd al-Ansārī and others said: “The Arabs say, ‘I have wiped myself for prayer,’” thus calling the whole of ablution “wiping.” However, when a general term encompasses two categories, the customary practice of the Arabs and others is to give one category a specific name and retain the general term for the other. For example, dābbah (“moving creature”) encompasses human beings and other creatures, but since human beings have their own specific name, the general term came to be applied to other creatures. The same is true of the term “animal.” Likewise, “blood relatives” encompasses everyone related by blood, but those entitled to inherit a prescribed share or through residuary succession have their own specific designation.

Similarly, the term “believer” encompasses someone who believes in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers, as well as someone who believes in superstition and false objects of worship. The latter category came to have its own specific name—“disbeliever”—while the term “faith” remained exclusive to the former. The same applies to bishārah (“announcing tidings”), and there are many similar examples.

The general term may then be used in both senses, sometimes with a contextual indication and sometimes without qualification. For example, if someone makes a bequest to his blood relatives, it encompasses his relatives, men and women alike.

Thus, the words of the Most High in the verse concerning ablution,

“Wipe over your heads and your feet,”

require that what is denoted by “wiping” be applied to both. Wiping in the restricted sense, without water flowing, and wiping accompanied by flowing water are both called “wiping.” The verse therefore requires the element common to both cases, and nothing in its wording precludes, in the case of the feet,

---

## Page 10538

the wiping being accompanied by flowing water. This is indicated by His words:

“Up to the ankles.”

He thus commanded that they be wiped up to the ankles.

Furthermore, wiping in the restricted sense is the flowing of water together with washing; these are two forms of wiping in the general sense, which means bringing water into contact with the part concerned. In such cases, Arabic usage allows one of two expressions to suffice, as in the saying:

“I fed her straw and cold water.”

Yet water is given to drink, not fed. Likewise, the poet says:

“I saw your husband in the fray,
Girded with a sword and spear.”

Yet a spear is not girded on. Another example is the saying of the Most High:

“There will circulate among them boys of everlasting youth,”

“With goblets, pitchers, and a cup,”

through to His words: “And fair maidens with beautiful, wide eyes.” Similarly, mentioning one of the two expressions sufficed here, although what was intended was washing. This is indicated by His words, “Up to the ankles,” and by the other Quranic reading, together with the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains.

Those who say that the feet are to be wiped without water flowing wipe them up to “the ankle bones,” not “the two ankle bones.” Such a person therefore contradicts each of the two readings, just as he contradicts the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains. Neither the apparent meaning nor any underlying meaning supports his position, nor does any known Sunnah. It is merely an error in understanding the Quran and ignorance of its meaning and of the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains.

The mention of wiping the feet suggests that the feet may be wiped, unlike the face and hands, which are not wiped under any circumstances. This is why, concerning wiping over the two leather socks worn on the feet, there are reports

---

## Page 10539

the like of which have not been reported concerning the face and hands. Yet the Sunnah, together with the indication of the Quran, establishes wiping the feet. Whoever wipes over his feet is an innovator who contravenes the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains and the Quran. No one may do so when washing is possible. When the foot is uncovered, it must be washed; when it is inside a leather sock, its ruling is as explained by the Sunnah.

This is comparable to the verse on prescribed shares of inheritance: the Sunnah explains the status of an heir who is a slave, an unbeliever, or a killer. There are numerous similar examples. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

There are three views concerning continuity between the acts of ablution:

The first: It is obligatory without exception. The followers of Imam Ahmad describe this as the apparent position of his school. It is also al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier view and one view within the school of [Mālik] (1).

The second: It is not obligatory at all. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah, one opinion reported from Ahmad, and al-Shāfiʿī’s later view.

I say: This third view is the strongest and the most consistent with the underlying principles of Islamic law

and with the principles of Ahmad’s school and those of others. This is because the evidence establishing its obligation applies only to someone who is negligent, not to someone unable to maintain continuity. The principal evidence in this matter is the hadith narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others, from Khālid ibn Maʿdān, from one of the Companions of the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him:

“He saw a man praying with a patch the size of a dirham on the top of his foot that the water had not reached. The Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—ordered him to repeat his ablution and prayer.”

This concerns a particular incident, and the person ordered to repeat his ablution was negligent: he could have washed that patch just as he could wash the rest. It remained unwashed only because he had neglected it and had not attended carefully to his entire ablution. His case resembles that of those who performed ablution while their heels remained visibly dry, to whom he called out at the top of his voice:

“Woe to the heels from the Fire!”

Likewise, the hadith in Sahīh Muslim, narrated from ʿUmar, states:

“A man performed ablution but left an area the size of a fingernail unwashed on his foot. The Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—noticed it and said, ‘Go back and perform your ablution properly.’ He went back and then prayed.”

Narrated by Muslim.

Those performing ablution frequently neglect to wash the whole foot. Indeed, many misguided people have come to believe that it is not to be washed: one group among the Shīʿah holds that the obligation is to wipe its upper surface, while one group among the Muʿtazilah allows a choice between wiping and washing.

Those who do not regard continuity as obligatory rely principally on a report from Ibn ʿUmar:

“He performed ablution [washing his face and hands and wiping his head. Then he was called to offer the funeral prayer; when he entered the mosque, he wiped over his leather socks and then offered the funeral prayer] (1).

## Page 10542

in succession, owing to the lack of sufficient water.” The principles of the Sharia support this. Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Someone unable to maintain continuity—because water is scarce, has spilled, or has been wrongfully seized from him after he obtained it; because the source or place from which he and others draw water, such as a pipe or well, supplies him with water only at widely separated intervals; or for similar reasons—can fulfill the command only by washing whatever he can with the water available. If he does this and then washes the remaining parts with water he subsequently obtains, he has feared Allah as much as he is able and has fulfilled as much of the command as he can.

This is further clarified by the fact that, if he were entirely unable to wash the required body parts because no water was available, that obligation would be waived, and his duty would instead be tayammum (dry ablution). If he could wash only some of them, three opinions are reported:

One holds that he should perform tayammum alone, so as not to combine a substitute with that for which it substitutes.

Another holds that he should use whatever water he can and perform tayammum for the remaining parts. This is the well-known position in Ahmad’s school and those of others.

A third holds that he should use that water for ritual bathing, but not for ablution, as is reported from Abū Bakr. This rests on the view that continuity is obligatory in ablution but not in ritual bathing.

---

## Page 10543

The proponent of this view said: “Thus, using some of the water is beneficial for ritual bathing, but not for tayammum.”

They deemed this argument weak on the grounds that a person must do whatever he can. This shows that, in their view, such washing is a beneficial act of purification when one’s ability is limited, whether in ablution or ritual bathing. Accordingly, once water becomes available, he need not wash again the parts he has already washed in ablution, just as he need not repeat prayers performed with tayammum or repeat what he has already washed in ritual bathing. This accords with the well-known distinction drawn by Ahmad’s followers between ablution and ritual bathing, as we shall explain, Allah willing. For he has done what he was commanded to do, in the manner commanded; whoever complies with the command has fulfilled his obligation and need not repeat the act.

This becomes clearer when we consider that, while unable, he was not commanded to wash the second body part. Rather, he was only commanded to obtain purifying water with which he could wash it, or to defer washing it until he became able. Meanwhile, he can wash the first body part, and this is the portion of the command he can fulfill, so he must do so. Likewise, if he can wash only some body parts, or only part of a single body part, he must wash whatever he can—as in the case of someone whose hand has been severed together with part of the forearm.

The same reasoning applies to the case we mentioned: if a wound, illness, or some other condition exempts one of his body parts from the obligation of washing, and he washes the healthy part, then suppose the pain subsides after the part already washed has dried. If he then washes the remainder, he has done what he is able to do.

---

## Page 10544

Moreover, fasting the two months consecutively is obligatory according to the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and scholarly consensus. Yet Muslims agree that interrupting the fast for an unavoidable excuse—such as menstruation—does not break the required continuity.

Ahmad’s position on this is more accommodating than that of others. In his view, if continuity is interrupted by a legally recognized excuse that makes its maintenance impossible, even though the excuse could have been avoided—such as when the two months are interrupted by the Ramadan fast, the day of Eid al-Fitr, the day of sacrifice, the days of Minā, illness, postnatal bleeding, or the like—this does not invalidate the required continuity. If, however, someone breaks the fast for an excuse that permits doing so, such as travel, there are two views within his school. This reasoning applies all the more to ablution when its continuity is interrupted for a legally recognized excuse, even if that excuse could have been avoided.

Moreover, continuity is obligatory when reciting al-Fātihah. They said that if someone recites part of it and then remains silent for a long time without an excuse, he must recite it again from the beginning. But if he remains silent to listen to the imam’s recitation, or interrupts his recitation with a prescribed remembrance—such as saying “Āmīn” or the like—its continuity is not invalidated. Rather, he completes the recitation without starting over. The case of ablution is exactly the same, since he has interrupted it for a legally recognized excuse. It is well known that continuity in speech is more strictly required than continuity in actions.

Moreover, Ahmad’s expressly stated position concerning contracts is likewise: continuity between offer and acceptance is obligatory, such that if acceptance is delayed after the offer—until

---

## Page 10545

they turn from that discussion to another subject or physically part—then a fresh offer is required. Ahmad expressly stated that if a marriage offer is made to an absent person, and a messenger goes to him and he accepts during the sitting in which the offer is conveyed, the contract is valid. Some of his followers therefore supposed that this constituted a second position of his: that acceptance may be delayed without restriction, even when the parties had been in the same gathering, then separated and allowed a lengthy interval to elapse. This is the position reported in works such as al-Hidāyah, al-Muqni', al-Muharrar, and others: that acceptance in marriage remains valid even after the gathering has ended.

That is mistaken, as my grandfather pointed out—as I recall—in his major work. There is no distinction here between marriage, sale, and lease contracts. The distinction between the two situations is clear, and other jurists, such as Abū Yūsuf and others, also recognize it. This distinction is among the soundest positions. It seems likely that Ahmad’s expressly stated position concerning ablution follows the same distinction, but I have not yet examined his statement on ablution closely. For often two positions are reported from him in such matters, whereas his explicit statements distinguish between different circumstances—and that distinction is correct—as in the questions of giving equivalent values and of killing the testator.

Moreover, continuity is more firmly required in circumambulation and in walking between Safā and Marwah than in ablution. Nevertheless, one may interrupt circumambulation for an obligatory prayer that is commencing or a funeral prayer that is taking place, then resume the circumambulation without starting over. Ablution is therefore all the more deserving of this allowance. Accordingly, if he were to perform ablution after

---

## Page 10546

ablution, and then an obligatory duty arose that prevented him from completing it—such as rescuing someone from drowning or enjoining right and forbidding wrong—and he discharged that duty, he could then complete his ablution, just as with circumambulation, and with even greater reason. The same applies if an illness were to prevent him from completing his ablution. Moreover, the principles of the Sharia distinguish throughout between those who are able and those who are unable, and between those who are negligent or transgress the limits and those who are neither negligent nor transgressive. Distinguishing between them is a fundamental, authoritative principle. It is the middle course followed by the balanced community, and through it the just position between two divergent views becomes clear.

I have examined as many questions as Allah has willed in which the opposing positions diverge between denial and affirmation, until they resemble questions of sectarian controversy and opinions to which factions cling. These include questions discussed in the various approaches to the disagreements between Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi'ī, and among the four imams, as well as other questions.

I have found that, in many of them, the correct position lies in the middle. Examples include removing ritual impurity with something other than water; issuing judgment on the basis of a refusal to take an oath; paying equivalent values in zakat; praying at the beginning of the prescribed time; reciting behind the imam; specifying one’s intention and forming it during the night; selling goods that are not present; avoiding ritual impurity during prayer; questions of partnership, such as labor partnerships, credit partnerships, and mufāwadah partnerships; and the qualifications of a judge. This is likewise the authoritative principle in matters of transmitted doctrine and belief, which are called

---

## Page 10547

questions of fundamentals, or the fundamentals of religion, or the fundamentals of speculative theology. In these matters, people follow conjecture and their own desires. We have also established what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, in these and other matters, concerning the distinction between someone who believes both inwardly and outwardly and a hypocrite who conceals unbelief, professing faith outwardly but not inwardly. We have likewise established that believers are pardoned for mistakes and forgetfulness.

In most of the sharply divergent disputes in these matters, the truth lies in the middle position: questions of divine oneness and attributes; divine decree and justice; religious designations and rulings; faith and Islam; divine promise and threat; and enjoining right and forbidding wrong, rising against rulers and their ways, or cooperating with them in obedience to Allah. Rulers are to be enjoined to do right and forbidden to do wrong as far as possible, while rebellion and civil strife are to be avoided. The same applies to similar matters subject to partisan passions.

Furthermore, the principal analogy concerning prescribed sequence and continuity is the analogy with prayer. Prayer requires a prescribed sequence: prostration may not precede bowing. It also requires continuity: its parts may not be separated by anything incompatible with it. Moreover, prayer is a single act of worship whose parts are connected, with no interval whatsoever between them that would allow a choice between performing them consecutively or separately. Yet even so, if its parts are separated for a valid excuse, such as extensive movement out of necessity—as in the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar:

“The first group, after praying one rak‘ah, goes to face the enemy. When the second group has prayed the second rak‘ah, it too goes to face the enemy; then back came

---

## Page 10548

the first group to its place, where it completed the prayer; then the second group did likewise.” This manner of praying is described in the two Sahīh collections. It is permissible and not disliked according to the leading hadith scholars, such as Ahmad and others. It is also Abū Hanīfah’s preferred form of prayer in circumstances of fear, since it differs from prayer in safety only in turning away from the direction of prayer and making extensive movements. Both are permissible for a valid excuse.

A similar case is someone whose ablution is involuntarily invalidated. Most scholars—including Abū Hanīfah and Mālik, as well as al-Shāfi‘ī according to one opinion and Ahmad according to one transmitted position—hold that he should renew his ablution and resume his prayer from where he left off, provided that he has not invalidated it through deliberate speech or the like. This is reported from most of the Companions. There are also two reports with disconnected chains from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) concerning this. Al-Shāfi‘ī and others accept such a report as evidence when the majority of the Companions have acted upon it.

Likewise, if someone inadvertently gives the salām to end his prayer—as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) did in the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn—and then completes the prayer, this interruption and separation between its parts does not prevent its completion. In that incident, the prayer was interrupted by his rising and going to the wooden beam, leaning against it, interlacing his fingers, and resting his cheek upon them; by his speech and that of the man who alerted him, questioned him, and told him that he had not forgotten and that the prayer had not been shortened; and by the replies of those who agreed with the man who had alerted him.

It is well known that, had he done this deliberately, it would have invalidated the prayer, without dispute. Thus, if prayer—which has only been prescribed as a continuous act—is treated differently when its parts are separated for a valid excuse and when they are separated without one, how can separating the acts of ablution be treated alike with and without a valid excuse, even though ablution

---

## Page 10549

consists of separate acts which, by consensus, need not be performed as one uninterrupted act.

No one may object: “If someone performs extensive movements for a valid excuse, as in the prayer of fear, or inadvertently gives the salām, he is still legally considered to be praying. The proof is that if he were then deliberately to engage in conversation or speech that invalidates prayer, make extensive movements unnecessarily, turn his back to the direction of prayer unnecessarily, or uncover his private parts, his prayer would become invalid. Were he no longer praying, these things would not invalidate his prayer. This therefore does not constitute a breach of the required continuity.”

The answer is that this is, in fact, among the strongest proofs of what we have said. It is well known that these actions and the lengthy interruption excused in his case—such as going to face the enemy and then returning to his position, or someone who inadvertently gave the salām rising and going to one side of the mosque and leaning against it—are neither obligatory nor recommended acts of prayer. Nor can they be included among such acts in the way that prolonging the standing, bowing, prostration, or sitting can. These four postures are themselves acts of prayer. Prolonging them, or introducing into them minor movements that are not prescribed in prayer, does not prevent them from remaining part of the prayer.

Those other actions, however, are not acts of prayer. The worshipper was commanded to perform extensive movements during the prayer of fear only for the sake of jihad, and comparable actions done inadvertently are excused because Allah has pardoned this community for mistakes and forgetfulness. Thus, an interruption between the successive parts of prayer occurs sometimes through an action that necessitates altering its form, and sometimes through an action for which the person incurs no sin

---

## Page 10550

because he is not required to refrain from it. This resembles an interruption in consecutive fasting: sometimes through an obligatory fast or an obligatory breaking of the fast, and sometimes through menstruation, postnatal bleeding, or an illness that renders one unable to fast. Hence Ahmad applied this principle consistently. If such an interruption occurred without an excuse, it would invalidate the prayer by consensus. There is therefore even greater reason not to treat interruptions in ablution with and without an excuse alike.

As for his still being legally considered to be praying, this means that he may interrupt the prayer only in ways that are excused within it. If he does something incompatible with prayer—such as deliberate speech, extensive movement, or turning his back to the direction of prayer without an excuse—he has separated its parts by an act incompatible with it, without an excuse. His prayer is therefore invalidated, just as it would be if he prayed two rakʿahs and then deliberately gave the salām. He may not simply perform the remaining two rakʿahs; rather, he must begin the prayer anew. If, however, he gave the salām inadvertently, he resumes from where he left off, as established by the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains and by the scholars’ agreement on this.

The person giving the salām is merely leaving the prayer and adding to the prescribed act. If he does this deliberately, he is not permitted to do so; the only objection here is that he has interrupted the prayer. Do you not see that the sole difference between performing witr as three uninterrupted rakʿahs and performing three rakʿahs with a separation between the first two and the final one is the separation itself?

Hence they say: the two rakʿahs are separated from the final single rakʿah by a salām, or they are not separated by a salām. Some scholars of Iraq do not permit this separation, treating witr like the Maghrib prayer. They hold that the night’s odd-numbered prayer must be like the day’s odd-numbered prayer: uninterrupted, without separation. Some scholars of the Hijaz, on the other hand, permit only separation, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Night prayer

---

## Page 10551

is offered two rakʿahs at a time. Then, if you fear the approach of dawn, pray one rakʿah as witr.” The jurists among the scholars of hadith prefer separating them, because of the authenticity and abundance of the reports supporting this, although they also permit joining them.

The point here is that they mention no difference between the two forms of witr except that one is uninterrupted and the other separated. This is precisely the distinction between continuity and separation. Thus, deliberately giving the salām invalidates an obligatory prayer, or any similar prayer prescribed to be uninterrupted, only because it separates one part of the prayer from another. If someone does this inadvertently, however, his prayer is not invalidated.

Anything incompatible with prayer—whether an action or extensive movement, deliberate speech, or failure to fulfil one of its conditions, such as facing the direction of prayer, covering the parts of the body that must be covered, or the like—also separates its parts, besides being incompatible with it. Such an act can bring a person out of prayer, just as the salām does. Hence some scholars of Iraq held that a person leaves prayer through anything incompatible with it, just as he leaves it through the salām. However, the jurists among the scholars of hadith and the scholars of the Hijaz disallowed this, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The key to prayer is purification; its prohibitions begin with the opening declaration of Allah’s greatness and are lifted by the salām.”

There are also other grounds establishing that one may enter prayer only in the prescribed manner and leave it only in the prescribed manner.

Several points further clarify this discussion:

First: Those who permit witr to be offered as three rakʿahs with a separation—such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad

---

## Page 10552

and others—hold that a prayer bearing a single name may have its parts separated by deliberately giving the salām, as with witr, the forenoon prayer, the Ramadan night prayers, and the four rakʿahs before the noon prayer. Their preference in all prayers is that they be offered two rakʿahs at a time, except for the forms Ahmad exempts in which separation is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as witr offered as five, seven, or nine rakʿahs. In these cases, he prefers the practice established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They say that the minimum witr is three rakʿahs offered with a separation. It is established in the authentic collections, through several routes from ʿĀʾishah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would offer eleven rakʿahs of witr at night, separating each pair of rakʿahs.”

She thus called the entire prayer witr despite the separations. The followers of Abū Hanīfah may dispute this with them, since they consider the prescribed Sunnah practice for the four rakʿahs before the noon prayer to be uninterrupted prayer, as they do for three rakʿahs of witr. Likewise, whenever a prayer of four or eight rakʿahs is mentioned, they understand it to be concluded with a single salām.

Second: If someone speaks after inadvertently giving the salām during prayer, as in the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn, the legal implications of that report are well known. Those who disagree maintain that it has been abrogated. This is the position of the followers of Abū Hanīfah and a group among Ahmad’s followers, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā. They hold that speaking invalidates the prayer without exception, even when it occurs after an inadvertent salām, on the grounds that the person is still in prayer. The majority, however, hold that the report remains in force. This is the correct view, and it is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position in

---

## Page 10553

most of his responses. He accepted this report and derived legal rulings from it; he neither ceased to act upon it nor declared it abrogated.

It is established that the narrator best known for reporting this incident, who stated that he offered that prayer with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was Abū Hurayrah. He mentioned in his account that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led them in the prayer. He had only embraced Islam, seen the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and prayed behind him from the year of Khaybar onward. The incident took place in the Prophet’s mosque, certainly after his return from Khaybar. This was unquestionably after speaking during prayer had been prohibited, for it is established in the two Sahīh collections that Ibn Masʿūd said:

“We used to greet the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while he was praying, and he would return our greetings. When we returned from our stay with the Negus, I greeted him, but he did not return my greeting. We said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, we used to greet you during prayer, and you would return our greetings.’ He replied, ‘Prayer demands one’s full attention.’”

This shows that speaking during prayer had been prohibited by the time they returned from their stay with the Negus.
