## Page 10751

Chapter: Tayammum (Dry Ablution)

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

All praise is due to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whoever He leads astray, none can guide. We bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, and we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Allah Most High said:

“O you who believe, when you rise to pray, wash your faces and your arms up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves. But if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

---

## Page 10752

In its linguistic sense, tayammum means making for something. An example is Allah Most High’s saying:

“Do not deliberately choose the inferior part of it to give away, when you yourselves would not accept it except by overlooking its defects.”

And His saying:

“Nor those making for the Sacred House.”

Another example is the verse of Imru’ al-Qays:

I made for the water this side of Dārij,
Where shade leans over it, its waterweed thick upon the surface.

However, when Allah Most High said:

“Then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it,”

the tayammum commanded here meant seeking clean earth in order to wipe oneself with it. Thus, in the customary usage of jurists, the word tayammum, when used without qualification, came to denote this particular act. The word may also refer to the actual wiping of the hands and face: the act intended by tayammum was itself called tayammum.

This tayammum commanded in the verse is one of the distinctive privileges of the Muslims, and one of the ways in which Allah has favored them over other nations. In the two Sahīh collections, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been granted five things that no prophet before me was granted: I have been aided by fear cast into the enemy at a distance of a month’s journey; the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, so whenever the time for prayer comes upon any man of my community, let him pray; spoils of war have been made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; I have been granted intercession; and whereas a prophet would be sent specifically to his own people, I have been sent to all humanity.”

This is al-Bukhārī’s wording.

---

## Page 10753

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been favored over the prophets in six ways: I have been granted concise speech rich in meaning; I have been aided by fear cast into the enemy; spoils of war have been made lawful for me; the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification; I have been sent to all creation; and I have been made the seal of the prophets.”

Muslim also reported from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been favored over other people in three ways: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the whole earth has been made for us a place of prayer; and its soil has been made for us a means of purification when we cannot find water.”

‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb reported from his father, from his grandfather, who said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification. Wherever the time for prayer comes upon me, I perform tayammum and pray. Those before me regarded that as a grave matter; they prayed only in their churches and synagogues.”

Allah Most High’s words, “Then seek clean earth,” contain an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, as do His words:

“Allah commands you to slaughter a cow,”

“Then the freeing of a slave,”

“Then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when you return,”

and:

“Whoever cannot find the means must fast three days.”

Such expressions are termed unrestricted. They convey general applicability by way of alternatives, not collective inclusion. This indicates that one may perform tayammum with whatever clean earth happens to be available. Here, “clean” means ritually pure. Dust that can be stirred up is, by consensus, included in what the text denotes. As for anything else, there is disagreement, which we shall discuss, if Allah Most High wills.

---

## Page 10754

Concerning His words:

“Then wipe your faces and your hands with it,”

all seven canonical reciters agree on reading aydīkum (“your hands”) with the yā unvowelled. This differs from His words concerning ablution, “and your feet,” which some of the seven read as arjulakum, in the accusative. They explain that it is coordinated with the parts to be washed, the implied wording being: “Wash your faces and your hands, and your feet up to the ankles.” This was also stated by ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others among the early generations.

Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said:

“Al-Hasan and al-Husayn recited to me, ‘And your feet up to the ankles,’ reading arjulikum in the genitive. ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib heard this while adjudicating disputes between people. He said, ‘Wa-arjulakum’—meaning in the accusative—and said, ‘This is an instance of words being placed earlier or later than their underlying syntactic order.’”

Likewise, Ibn ‘Abbās read it in the accusative and said, “The command has returned to washing.”

This cannot be coordination according to syntactic position, as some suppose, as in the poet’s words:

Mu‘āwiyah, we are only human, so be gentle;
We are neither mountains nor iron.

Such a construction is permissible only with a particle of emphasis, akin to structural elements. It is not permissible, however, with particles that convey meaning. Here, the preposition bā denotes contact, not emphasis. This is why the reciters did not read wa-aydiyakum (“and your hands”) here as they read wa-arjulakum (“and your feet”) there.

For had He said, “Wipe your faces and your hands,” or “Wipe with them,” mere wiping would have sufficed, without conveying the purifying substance to the head. That, however, contradicts the consensus. Since the bā denotes contact, it indicates that the substance used for wiping must actually make contact. This in turn indicates

---

## Page 10755

that a purifying substance must be used. Thus, none of the early scholars or leading authorities on Arabic held that this bā has a partitive meaning. Nor did al-Shāfiʿī say that a partitive meaning is derived from the bā. Indeed, Imām al-Haramayn and other scholars of his school rejected this, appealing to the statements of the leading authorities on Arabic in support of their rejection. Those who held that view, however, relied on other evidence.

Allah Most High says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship on you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

This verse indicates that earth is a means of purification, as the authentic Sunnah explicitly states in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.”

Abū Dharr reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he cannot find water for ten years. But when he finds water, let him apply it to his skin, for that is better.”

Reported by Imam Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Tirmidhī, whose wording this is. He said: “A good and authentic hadith.”

Muslims agree that someone who cannot find water while traveling is to perform tayammum (dry ablution) and pray until he finds water. Once he finds water, he must use it. Likewise, concerning tayammum for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, the four imams and the overwhelming majority of earlier and later scholars held

---

## Page 10756

that he should perform tayammum if he cannot find water while traveling, until he finds water; once he finds it, he must use it. It has been reported that ‘Umar and Ibn Mas‘ūd rejected tayammum for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, and it has also been reported that they retracted that view. Permitting it is the position of most of the Companions, including ‘Alī, ‘Ammār, Ibn ‘Abbās, Abū Dharr, and others. It is supported by verses from the Book of Allah and five hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

These include the hadiths of ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir and ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, both recorded in the two Sahīhs; the hadith of Abū Dharr, which al-Tirmidhī graded authentic; the hadith of ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās; and the hadith concerning the man who suffered a head wound and was given a legal ruling, about whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“They killed him—may Allah kill them! Why did they not ask when they did not know? The only cure for ignorance is to ask.”

An authentic report relates that ‘Umar said:

“We were with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He asked for water for ablution and performed ablution. The call to prayer was made, and he led the people in prayer. When he finished praying, he noticed a man sitting apart who had not prayed with the others. He said, ‘What prevented you, so-and-so, from praying with the others?’ He replied, ‘I am in a state of major ritual impurity, and there is no water.’ He said, ‘Use clean earth, for it is sufficient for you.’”

Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent me on an errand. I entered a state of major ritual impurity but could find no water, so I rolled in the earth as an animal rolls. Then I came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and told him what had happened. He said, ‘It would have sufficed for you to do this with your hands.’ Then he struck the ground with both hands

---

## Page 10757

once, then wiped his left hand over his right, the backs of both hands, and his face.” This is Muslim’s wording.

Section

The scholars have differed concerning tayammum: does it temporarily remove ritual impurity until one is able to use water? Or does ritual impurity remain, while prayer is nevertheless valid despite the presence of the impurity that would otherwise prevent it? This is a theoretical question.

They have also differed over whether tayammum takes the place of purification with water: may one perform it before the prayer time begins, just as one may perform ablution beforehand, and pray as many obligatory and voluntary prayers with it as one wishes, just as with purification using water? Does it remain valid when the prayer time ends, just as ablution remains valid? There are two well-known views on this, and this disagreement has practical consequences.

Abū Hanīfa’s position is that one may perform tayammum before the prayer time begins, that it remains valid after that time ends, and that one may pray with it as much as one wishes, just as with purification using water. This is also the view of Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basrī, al-Zuhrī, al-Thawrī, and others. It is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

The second view is that one may not perform tayammum before the prayer time begins, and that it does not remain valid after that time ends.

---

## Page 10758

Among those who hold this view, some say that one must perform tayammum for each prayer time; others say that one must perform it for each obligatory prayer and may not offer two obligatory prayers with the same tayammum. Some have gone to extremes, saying that one must also perform tayammum for every voluntary prayer. Broadly speaking, this is the well-known position in the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad.

They argue that tayammum is a form of purification permitted out of necessity, and that a ruling dependent on necessity is limited to the extent of that necessity. Thus, if someone performs tayammum at a time when there is no need for it, it is invalid, just as it would be if performed when water is available.

They also argue that Allah has commanded everyone who rises for prayer to perform ablution, or tayammum if water cannot be found. The apparent wording of this command would require everyone who rises for prayer to perform ablution or tayammum, as applicable. However, an authentic report establishes that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered all the prayers with a single ablution.”

Muslim related this in his Sahīh. The Sunnah thus establishes that ablution may be performed before the time when it becomes obligatory, whereas tayammum remains subject to the apparent wording of the command. Some explain this by saying that one is commanded to seek water for every prayer, and that this invalidates one’s tayammum. Views similar to theirs have been reported from ʿAlī, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs, and Ibn ʿUmar.

Our argument is that the Quran and Sunnah establish that earth is a means of purification, just as water is a means of purification. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. But when you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

He thus declared it a means of purification whenever water is unavailable, without qualification. This indicates that it is a means of purification

---

## Page 10759

for the person who performs tayammum. Since he declared the person who performs tayammum purified, just as the person who performs ablution is purified, without restricting this to a particular time or saying that the end of the prayer time invalidates it—as he did state that the ability to use water invalidates it—this indicates that earth takes the place of water when water is unavailable. This is also what the foundational principles require.

Tayammum is a substitute for water, and a substitute takes the place of the original in its rulings, even if it differs in form. Thus, fasting two months substitutes for freeing a slave; fasting three days and seven days substitutes for the sacrificial offering required for tamattu‘ Hajj; and fasting three days as expiation for an oath substitutes for expiation through material means. A substitute takes the place of the original.

This conclusion is binding upon anyone who draws an analogy between tayammum and purification with water regarding their manner of performance, and consequently requires wiping up to the elbows, even though the verse concerning tayammum is unqualified. Similarly, ‘Ammār reasoned by analogy when he rolled in the dust as an animal rolls, wiping his entire body just as he would wash his entire body. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that this analogy was invalid, and that the tayammum which suffices in place of ablution also suffices for purification from major ritual impurity: wiping the face and hands.

A substitute does not share the form of the original; rather, it shares its ruling. Tayammum consists of wiping two parts of the body—the two that are washed in ablution—while the two parts that are wiped are omitted. Tayammum for major ritual impurity is likewise confined to these two parts, unlike the full ritual bath. Tayammum does not involve rinsing the mouth or drawing water into the nose, unlike ablution; and tayammum

---

## Page 10760

does not involve any recommendation to perform its actions twice or three times, unlike ablution. Tayammum differs from ablution in several aspects of its form, but has the same legal effect, because it is a substitute for it. It must therefore take its place, as all substitutes do. This is what the revealed text and analogy require.

If it is said, “Ablution removes ritual impurity, whereas tayammum does not,” there are two answers.

First, whether tayammum removes ritual impurity or not, the Lawgiver has made it a means of purification that takes the place of water when water is unavailable. It must therefore carry the same rulings of purification as water, unless evidence from Islamic law establishes otherwise.

The second answer is that saying tayammum removes ritual impurity or does not remove it involves no disagreement over practice; the disagreement is merely conceptual and terminological. Those who say that it does not remove ritual impurity argue that, if it did, a person would not need to renew his purification upon becoming able to use water. Yet the revealed text and scholarly consensus establish that tayammum is invalidated by the ability to use water.

Those who say that it removes ritual impurity mean only that it removes it temporarily, until the person becomes able to use water. Thus, they do not disagree over any practical ruling of Islamic law. Rather, their disagreement goes back to a principle of legal theory concerning the question of exceptions to an effective cause, and whether

---

## Page 10761

the suitability of an effective cause is undermined by a countervailing consideration, and whether an impediment opposing a causative factor negates it or not, in respect of its causal efficacy while the factor itself remains.

To clarify the nature of this disagreement: the term “effective cause” may mean the complete cause—the totality of what necessarily entails a ruling, such that whenever it exists, the ruling exists without fail. In this usage, the term includes what completes the cause, its conditions, and the absence of any impediment. According to one view, this is because the absence of an impediment necessarily entails a positive attribute; according to another, it is because an absence may form part of what completes the causative factor. Whenever such a cause admits an exception and is invalidated, with the ruling existing without it, this demonstrates its unsoundness.

For example, if someone explained the shortening of prayer by the mere existence of an excuse, he would be told:

“This is incorrect. The sick and others with valid excuses do not shorten their prayers; only travellers do so. Thus, shortening prayer accompanies travel, being present when travel is present and absent when it is absent.” When a ruling accompanies an attribute in both its presence and its absence, this indicates that the attribute is what the ruling depends upon. Likewise, if someone explained the obligation of zakat by the mere possession of the minimum threshold of wealth, he would be told: “This is disproved by possessing that wealth before a year has elapsed.”

The term “effective cause” may also mean that which calls for a ruling, even though the ruling depends upon certain conditions being fulfilled and impediments being absent.

This may also be expressed by the term “cause,” as when it is said:

“The causes establishing entitlement to inheritance are

---

## Page 10762

three: kinship, marriage, and patronage.”

According to Abū Hanīfa, and according to one of the two reports from Ahmad, entitlement to inheritance is also established through a pact of mutual allegiance and other means. Here, the ruling may fail to follow from the effective cause because of an impediment, such as slavery, killing, or difference of religion. When “effective cause” is intended in this sense, it may admit exceptions owing to missing conditions and the presence of impediments.

However, if the person advancing the causal explanation does not identify a relevant distinction between the counterexample and the other cases, his explanation is invalid. For the ruling sometimes accompanies the attribute, as in the original case; sometimes fails to accompany it, as in the original case; and sometimes differs from it, as in the counterexample. Unless the person presenting the argument demonstrates that the new case resembles the original case rather than the counterexample, there is no stronger justification for assimilating it to the original case and affirming the ruling than for assimilating it to the counterexample and denying the ruling. The attribute exists in all three cases: the ruling accompanies it in one but not the other, while its application to the third remains uncertain.

This is like three people participating in a killing. The victim’s relatives execute one but spare another, either because he pays blood money or because he had previously done them a kindness. As for the third, it is not known whether his situation resembles that of the one executed or the one pardoned. We cannot place him in either category without evidence showing that he resembles one rather than the other.

Once this is understood, legal theorists and jurists disagree over the permissibility of consuming carrion

---

## Page 10763

in cases of necessity. Some say:

“What is forbidden has been made permissible despite the continued presence of the cause that prohibits it, namely its properties as nourishment.”

Others say:

“Necessity has not removed the ruling arising from the cause—namely prohibition—by removing its capacity to entail prohibition. Thus, nothing prohibiting remains in this situation, since prohibition cannot cease while its fully sufficient cause remains.”

The dispute can be resolved as follows: if “the prohibiting cause” means the fully sufficient cause, which necessarily entails prohibition, then this ceases to exist in a situation of dire hunger. For something cannot exist without that which necessarily follows from it. Permissibility is established in this situation, so the cause that necessarily entails prohibition cannot be present. If, however, “cause” means that which would entail prohibition were it not for an overriding countervailing factor, then this undoubtedly exists when prohibition applies. But the overriding countervailing factor has removed its capacity to entail prohibition, so it no longer entails prohibition in this situation. If the dire hunger is assumed to cease, the cause resumes its effect because the factor opposing it has ceased.

The same reasoning applies to whether dry ablution removes ritual impurity or not, for this depends on the position of those who say that it removes ritual impurity. Once it becomes clear to someone holding this position that it removes ritual impurity temporarily, until one is able to use water, whereupon the impurity returns, this meaning is not impossible. The revealed law has indicated it by making earth a means of purification. Water serves as a means of purification when it removes ritual impurity; otherwise, while major ritual impurity remains

---

## Page 10764

purification cannot be attained. Thus, the proponent of this view merely says:

“It removes ritual impurity temporarily, until one is able to use water, whereupon the impurity returns.”

This is possible, not impossible. The revealed law has indicated this by making earth a means of purification. It can only be a means of purification if it removes ritual impurity; otherwise, while ritual impurity remains, it cannot be a means of purification.

As for someone who says, “It does not remove ritual impurity, but merely permits prayer, while ritual impurity remains the impediment to prayer”: if he means that it is a fully sufficient impediment, as it is when water is available, then he is mistaken. A fully sufficient impediment necessarily prevents prayer, whereas someone who has performed dry ablution is permitted to pray and is not prevented from doing so. Something cannot exist without that which necessarily follows from it. If, however, he means that the cause preventing prayer remains present but does not take effect because a legally prescribed purification has removed its prohibitive effect, and that this prohibitive effect returns once one becomes able to use water, then this is correct.

Likewise, if someone who says, “It removes ritual impurity,” means that it removes it just as water does, so that it cannot return without another cause arising, then he is mistaken. It is established by explicit scriptural text and consensus that once a person becomes able to use water, he must use it, even if no second state of major ritual impurity has arisen since the first. This is unlike purification with water.

But if he says, “By its removal, I mean the removal of the impediment’s prohibitive effect, so that it no longer prevents prayer until water becomes available,” then he is correct. There is no disagreement between the two positions concerning the practical rulings of the revealed law.

---

## Page 10765

Accordingly, it may be said:

On either view, ritual impurity no longer constitutes an impediment once purification through dry ablution has been attained. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—made earth a means of purification just as he made water a means of purification. However, he limited its purifying effect to the period before water becomes available, imposing no other condition for its being a means of purification. Thus, someone who has performed dry ablution has become ritually pure, and the impediment’s prohibitive effect upon prayer has been lifted until water becomes available. As long as water remains unavailable, that prohibitive effect remains absent, provided no fresh cause arises requiring purification, just as it would require purification with water.

Earth is therefore a means of purification before, after, and during the prayer time, just as water is a means of purification in all three circumstances. There is no legally significant difference between these cases, except when one becomes able to use water. Whoever declares dry ablution invalid when the prayer time ends has therefore contradicted what the evidence entails.

Moreover, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—made this a general concession for his community. He did not distinguish between performing dry ablution with the intention of offering an obligatory or voluntary prayer, or that particular prayer rather than another, just as he made no such distinction concerning ablution with water. The two must therefore be treated alike. There is disagreement concerning ablution with water before the prayer time begins, but the disagreement concerning dry ablution is better known.

Since the authentic Sunnah establishes that one of these two forms of purification is permissible before the prayer time begins, the same applies to the other. In either case, the person has purified himself by doing what Allah commanded. For this reason, the great majority of scholars permit someone who has performed ablution or a full ritual bath to pray behind someone who has performed dry ablution. This is what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs did, and the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—approved it. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise had intercourse with a slave woman of his and then led his companions in prayer after performing dry ablution. This is the position of the four imams, as well as that of Abū

---

## Page 10766

Yūsuf and others. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, however, did not permit this, on the grounds that the state of someone who has performed dry ablution is deficient.

Furthermore, the beginning or end of the prayer time, without any new cause arising, has no effect in invalidating obligatory purification, since the state of the purified person is the same before and after the prayer time begins. The Lawgiver is wise: He establishes and sets aside rulings only for reasons appropriate to them. Just as He does not invalidate purification on account of place, He does not invalidate it on account of time or other circumstances that have no legal significance.

If it is said:

“This is contradicted by the purification of someone who wipes over his leather socks, that of a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, and that of people with continuous causes of ritual impurity.”

The answer is:

Purification by wiping over leather socks is not obligatory. Rather, a person has the choice between wiping over them and removing them and washing his feet. This is why the Lawgiver imposed a time limit upon it. He did not tie that limit to the beginning or end of a prayer time; rather, because it is a concession, not a binding requirement, He prescribed a fixed duration for it: three days for a traveller, and one day and one night for a resident. This is also why wiping over leather socks is not permissible for major ritual purification.

By contrast, since purification by wiping over a splint is a binding requirement, no time limit was imposed upon it. A person may continue wiping over it until he removes it, and may do so for both minor and major ritual purification, just as dry ablution may be performed for both minor and major ritual impurity. It is therefore more appropriate to draw an analogy between dry ablution and wiping over a splint than between dry ablution and wiping over leather socks.

---

## Page 10767

As for people with continuous causes of ritual impurity, such as a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, the cause that necessitates ritual impurity is present in their case: impure matter issuing from either the front or rear passage. Out of necessity, however, the Lawgiver has permitted them to pray despite this, so the concession may be time-limited. Thus, if a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding purifies herself and no discharge occurs, her purification is not invalidated when the prayer time ends. It is invalidated only if discharge has occurred during that time: she may pray with that purification until the prayer time ends, but thereafter she may no longer do so, because something that invalidates purification has occurred. This differs from someone who has performed dry ablution, since nothing has occurred after his dry ablution to invalidate his purification.

Dry ablution is like ablution with water: nothing invalidates it except what invalidates ablution with water, so long as the person remains unable to use water. This argument proceeds on the basis of our position, and that of those who agree with us, concerning the time limit for wiping over leather socks and the invalidation of ablution in the case of a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding. This is the position of the three imams: Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. As for someone who does not regard purification as invalidated by this, or does not impose this time limit, such as Mālik, a person holding that position cannot invoke either case as a counterargument. Neither is subject to a time limit in his view, so dry ablution has still stronger grounds for not being time-limited.

As for the assertion:

“A person who rises to pray is commanded to perform one of the two forms of purification.”

The reply is:

Yes, he is obliged to do so. But if he has purified himself beforehand, then he has already

---

## Page 10768

done well and fulfilled the obligation beforehand, just as if he had performed ablution with water beforehand. Remaining in a state of purity from before the prayer time until it begins is better than remaining in a state of ritual impurity. Likewise, if someone who performs dry ablution has purified himself in advance, he has done well, since being in a state of purity before the prayer time is better than being without it. The Quran and Sunnah establish that dry ablution is a form of purification. Indeed, an authentic report states:

“A man greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but he did not return his greeting until he had performed dry ablution. He then returned the greeting and said, ‘I disliked mentioning Allah except in a state of purity.’”

If he has purified himself before the prayer time, he has done well and done something better than what was obligatory upon him. He is like someone who purifies himself for prayer before its time, someone who gives more than the obligatory amount in zakat or other payments, or someone who goes beyond what is obligatory in bowing and prostration. All this is good, provided it does not involve something prohibited, such as adding a fifth unit to the prayer. Performing dry ablution when water is unavailable is good, not forbidden. Hence, it is permissible before the prayer time for voluntary prayer, touching a copy of the Quran, and reciting the Quran.

As for the reports cited from some of the Companions, some are weak, while others are contradicted by statements of other Companions. There is no consensus on this issue. Allah Most High has said:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and leads to the best outcome.”

---

## Page 10769

Section

As for sa'īd (earth), there are several opinions. One holds that dry ablution is permissible with any substance of the same nature as earth, even if none of it adheres to the hand, such as arsenic, lime, gypsum, or smooth rock. Substances that are not of this nature, such as metals, may not be used for dry ablution. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah. Muhammad agrees with him, but stipulates that the material be mu'abbir, on the basis of His words, “from it.”

Another opinion permits dry ablution with earth and whatever is connected to it, even trees, just as this view permits the use of stones and clods of earth, as does Abū Hanīfah. This is Mālik’s view. Two opinions are transmitted from him concerning snow. According to one, dry ablution with it is permissible; this is also the view of al-Awzā'ī and al-Thawrī.

Another opinion permits the use of soil and sand. This is one of Abū Yūsuf’s two views and one of the two opinions transmitted from Ahmad. It is also reported from Ahmad that sand may be used when soil is unavailable.

Another opinion holds that dry ablution is permissible only with ritually pure soil whose dust adheres to the hand. This is the view of Abū Yūsuf and al-Shāfi'ī, and the other opinion transmitted from Ahmad.

---

## Page 10770

Those who hold this view adduced His words:

“Then wipe your faces and hands with some of it.”

This can only apply to something that adheres to the face and hands, whereas rock adheres to neither. They also cited Ibn ‘Abbās’s statement: “Pure earth means soil used for cultivation.” They further adduced the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The earth has been made a place of prayer for me, and its soil has been made a means of purification.”

They argued that he extended the ruling concerning prayer to the whole earth, but restricted the ruling concerning purification to its soil.

They also argued that, among all liquids, purification with water is restricted to what is water in its original nature; likewise, purification with soil is restricted to what is soil in its original nature. These are the two basic substances from which Adam was created: water and soil. They are the two simple elements, unlike other liquids and solids, which are compounds.

Those holding the first view adduced the Most High’s word:

“Ground.”

They explained that sa‘īd denotes whatever rises upon the earth’s surface, and thus encompasses everything upon it, as indicated by the Most High’s words:

“We will surely turn whatever is upon it into barren ground,”

and His words:

“And it becomes smooth, slippery ground.”

Those who did not restrict the ruling to soil adduced the words of the Prophet (may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace):

“The earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for me. So whenever the time for prayer comes upon any man of my community, let him pray.”

Another narration states:

“His place of prayer and his means of purification are at hand.”

This makes clear that wherever a Muslim may be, his place of prayer and his means of purification are at hand.

---

## Page 10771

It is well known that much of the earth contains no cultivable soil. If dry ablution with sand were impermissible, this would contradict the hadith. This is the argument of those who permit dry ablution with sand but not other materials, or who also include saline ground, since some land is saline. Such differences in soil are like its differences in colour, as indicated by the Prophet’s words (may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah created Adam from a handful that He took from all parts of the earth. His descendants therefore reflected that handful: among them are the black, the white, and those in between; the easygoing, the harsh, and those in between; and the wicked, the good, and those in between.”

Adam was created only from soil. Both good and poor soil—that which brings forth its vegetation by its Lord’s permission, and that which is poor and yields only scantily—may be used for dry ablution. Thus, it is clear that ‘good’ here means ritually pure. This is unlike rocks and trees, which are not of the same kind as soil and do not adhere to the hand. Arsenic and lime, by contrast, are minerals found in the earth, though they are not malleable as gold, silver, lead, and copper are.

---

## Page 10772

The shaykh and imam, the scholar and mufti of the people, the independent jurist and leading authority in Islamic law, Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Halīm ibn ʿAbd al-Salām Ibn Taymiyyah al-Harrānī—may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him—said:

Allah, the Almighty and Majestic, says:

“O you who believe, when you rise to pray, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe over your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of sexual impurity, purify yourselves. If you are ill or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have had contact with women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

This address entails that everyone who rises to pray is commanded to perform the washing and wiping mentioned—that is, ablution.

A group of scholars held that this is a general statement whose scope has been restricted.

---

## Page 10773

Another group held that it requires everyone who already has ablution to perform it anew. Both views are weak.

As for the first group, some said that what is meant here is someone rising from sleep. This view is well known from Zayd ibn Aslam and those who agreed with him among the scholars of Medina, including Mālik’s followers and others.

They said that, through this wording, the verse requires ablution of someone who has slept; of someone who has relieved himself, through His words:

“Or one of you has relieved himself”;

and of someone who has touched women, through His words:

“Or you have had contact with women.”

These are the usual causes of ritual impurity, and in their view they are what necessitate ablution.

Some of them said that the verse’s clauses are not in their intended order, which would be:

“When you rise to pray after sleeping, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have had contact with women.”

The response is this: as for the verse applying to someone rising from ordinary sleep, its apparent wording does encompass him. But the claim that it applies exclusively to him, so that it does not encompass someone who was already awake and rose to pray, is weak. Rather, the verse encompasses the latter in both wording and meaning.

For most prayers, people rise to pray while already awake, not after sleeping:

---

## Page 10774

such as the afternoon, sunset, and night prayers. The same is true of the noon prayer in winter. For the dawn prayer, however, they rise from sleep, as they do for the noon prayer after a midday nap. The verse encompasses all these cases.

It may, however, be argued:

If the verse commands someone rising from sleep to perform ablution because he has passed wind involuntarily, then its command applies all the more to someone rising to pray who has passed wind while awake. On this interpretation, the verse applies to someone who is awake through its implicit, a fortiori meaning.

If, alternatively, it is said that the wording is general and encompasses this case through the general scope of the words themselves, then these are two defensible interpretations. On either interpretation, the verse is general in scope. It also encompasses rising to perform voluntary prayers by night or day and rising to perform the funeral prayer, as we shall explain, if Allah wills.

If it encompasses all these cases, there is no basis for restricting its scope.

Another group said:

The implied wording is: “When you rise to pray while in a state of ritual impurity, or after having invalidated your ablution.” For someone who already has ablution is not required to perform it again. All of this is reported from al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him. Yet al-Shāfiʿī requires renewal in the case of dry ablution, for the apparent meaning of the Quran requires ablution and dry ablution of everyone who rises to pray, which conflicts with this interpretation.

---

## Page 10775

If he did indeed say this, then he held two opinions. Some Quran commentators attribute this view to the jurists generally, both earlier and later, because they agree on the ruling. They thus treat agreement on this ruling as agreement that these words are implicitly understood, as Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī does. He said:

“Scholars hold two views concerning the meaning of the verse. The first is: ‘When you rise to pray while in a state of ritual impurity, wash…’ Thus, ritual impurity is understood as an implicit condition for ablution to be obligatory. This is the view of Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, Abū Mūsā, and Ibn ‘Abbās—may Allah be pleased with them—and of the jurists.”

He said:

“The second is that the wording remains unrestricted, with nothing implicitly understood. Ablution is therefore obligatory for everyone intending to pray, whether in a state of ritual impurity or not. This is reported from ‘Ikrimah and Ibn Sīrīn. They are also reported to have held that this ruling has not been abrogated.

“A number of scholars are reported to have held that this was obligatory by virtue of the Sunnah. This is the report narrated by Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with him:

‘The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed five prayers on the day of the conquest with a single ablution. He said: “I did so deliberately, O ‘Umar.”’”

I say: As for the ruling—that someone who performs ablution for a prayer may pray using that

---

## Page 10776

ablution for another prayer—this is the view of the great majority of earlier and later scholars; dissent on this is exceptional. It is known through mass transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he did not require anyone who had prayed and then rose for another prayer to perform ablution again. For it is established through mass transmission that:

“He led the Muslims in the noon and afternoon prayers on the day of ‘Arafah, combining the two prayers.”

Many thousands prayed behind him, their number known only to Allah. After concluding the noon prayer with the salutation, he led them in the afternoon prayer. Neither he nor anyone else performed fresh ablution, nor did he command the people to do so, nor has anyone reported any such thing. This indicates that renewing ablution is not recommended in all circumstances.

Is renewing ablution recommended for each of the five daily prayers? This is disputed, and two positions are reported from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him.

Likewise, when he arrived at Muzdalifah:

“He led them in the sunset and night prayers, combining them,”

without renewing his ablution for the night prayer. On both occasions, he and those praying behind him rose for one prayer after another, and he had a separate call to commence prayer given for each prayer. The same applies to all the other hadiths concerning the combining of prayers established in the two Sahīh collections, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Abbās, and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them. They all indicate that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the Muslims behind him—performed the second of the two combined prayers in the state of ritual purity they had for the first, without performing fresh ablution for it.

---

## Page 10777

Likewise, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, through reports from Ibn ‘Abbās, ‘Ā’ishah, and others, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“would perform ablution for the night prayer, then offer the dawn prayer with that same ablution,”

even though he would sleep until he snored. He would say:

“My eyes sleep, but my heart does not sleep.”

Thus, it is established with the utmost authenticity that he would sleep and then offer the obligatory prayer with the same ablution he had performed for the voluntary prayer. How, then, can it be said that he performed ablution for every prayer?

It is also established in the Sahīh that:

“He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered the noon prayer. Then the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to him, and attending to them kept him from offering the two rak‘ahs after the noon prayer until he had offered the afternoon prayer, without performing fresh ablution.”

Sometimes he would offer an obligatory prayer followed by a voluntary prayer; sometimes a voluntary prayer followed by an obligatory prayer; and sometimes one obligatory prayer followed by another—all with a single ablution. Likewise, at night in Ramadan, the Muslims offered multiple prayers behind him with a single ablution. During his lifetime, the Muslims would perform ablution and then continue praying so long as their ablution remained unbroken, as related in authentic hadiths. It has not been reported from him—through either a sound or a weak chain of transmission—that he commanded them to perform ablution for every prayer.

---

## Page 10778

Thus, the claim that this is recommended requires evidence. As for the claim that it is obligatory, it contradicts the mass-transmitted Sunnah of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Companions. The report attributing a contrary view to ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, is not established; rather, what is established from him is the opposite.

‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, is far too eminent for a matter like this to have escaped his knowledge. Fabricated reports attributed to ‘Alī are numerous and well known—more numerous than those attributed to others. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, despite his extensive knowledge of the reports from the Companions and the Successors, denied that there was any disagreement on this matter.

Ahmad ibn al-Qāsim said:

“I asked Ahmad about someone who offered more than five prayers with a single ablution. He replied, ‘There is nothing wrong with that, provided his ablution remains unbroken. I did not think anyone had objected to this.’”

Al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would perform ablution for every prayer. I asked, ‘What did you yourselves do?’ He replied, ‘A single ablution would suffice for any of us so long as he did not invalidate it.’”

This concerns the five daily prayers offered separately. For this reason, Ahmad held this to be recommended according to one of his two opinions, even though the Prophet would sometimes offer several prayers with a single ablution. As related in Sahīh Muslim, Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“On the day of the Conquest, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered five prayers with a single ablution and wiped over his leather socks. ‘Umar said to him, ‘I

---

## Page 10779

saw you do something you had not done before?’ He replied, ‘I did it deliberately, O ‘Umar.’”

The Quran also indicates, in several ways, that someone who already has ablution is not obliged to perform it again.

First: He, glorified be He, said:

“If you are ill, on a journey, have relieved yourselves, or have touched women, and cannot find water, then perform dry ablution with clean earth.”

He thus commanded anyone who has relieved himself and cannot find water to perform dry ablution with clean earth. This indicates that relieving oneself makes dry ablution obligatory. If ablution were obligatory both for someone who had relieved himself and for someone who had not, then dry ablution would have an even stronger claim to be obligatory, for many jurists require dry ablution for every prayer. On that view, relieving oneself would make no difference: whenever someone rose to pray, ablution or dry ablution would be obligatory, even if he had not relieved himself. Conversely, if he relieved himself but did not rise to pray, neither ablution nor dry ablution would be obligatory. According to their position, therefore, mentioning the act of relieving oneself would serve no purpose.

Second: He, glorified be He, addressed the believers, for all people enter a state of ritual impurity. Urination and defecation are habitual bodily functions, and every descendant of Adam is subject to ritual impurity.

Their default state is minor ritual impurity. Each person has been accustomed to these bodily functions since infancy and thus remains in a state of ritual impurity, unlike major ritual impurity, which only occurs to them

---

## Page 10780

at puberty. Their default state is freedom from major ritual impurity, just as their default state is the absence of minor ritual purification. For this reason, He said:

“When you rise for prayer, wash your faces.”

Then He said:

“And if you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

He commanded them to perform minor ritual purification without qualification, because the default is that they are all in a state of minor ritual impurity before performing ablution. Then He said:

“And if you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

None of them is in a state of major ritual impurity unless he has entered that state. For this reason, He, glorified be He, distinguished between the two.

Third: It may be said that the verse establishes the obligation of ablution when a believer rises for prayer. This indicates that rising for prayer is the cause that makes ablution obligatory, and that when he rises for prayer, it becomes an obligation admitting of no delay. If he has already performed ablution, he has fulfilled this obligation before further delay became impermissible. Likewise, He said:

“When the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah.”

This indicates that the call makes proceeding to Friday prayer obligatory. At that point, it must be done without delay, and one may not be distracted from it by trade or anything else. If someone proceeds to it before the call, he has hastened to good deeds and set out before further delay became impermissible. Would any rational person say that he must return home so that he can set out when the call is made?

The same applies to ablution: a Muslim may have performed ablution for the noon prayer before the sun passes its zenith, for the sunset prayer before sunset, or for the dawn prayer before dawn breaks, although he only rises for prayer after its time has begun. Anyone who says that he must repeat his ablution is

---

## Page 10781

like someone who says that a person who arrives for Friday prayer before the call must make the journey again. During their Prophet’s lifetime, the Muslims used to perform ablution for the dawn prayer and other prayers before their prescribed times began. The same applies to the sunset prayer: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would offer it promptly, praying as soon as the sun disappeared from view. Many of his Companions lived far from the mosque. Had they not performed ablution before sunset, they would not have caught the beginning of the prayer with him; indeed, they might have missed it entirely because of the distance. He himself, peace and blessings be upon him, did not perform ablution after sunset, nor did those present with him in the mosque, and he did not instruct anyone to renew his ablution after sunset. All this is known with certainty.

I know of no reliably established dissent from the Companions on this point—no view that someone who performs ablution before the prayer’s time begins must repeat it once its time has begun. Nor is renewing ablution recommended for someone in this situation.

The jurists discussed only whether someone who has already prayed with his first ablution is recommended to renew it. As for someone who has not yet prayed with it, repeating his ablution is not recommended. Rather, renewing ablution in such circumstances is a religious innovation contrary to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and to the practice of the Muslims during his lifetime and thereafter, down to the present day.

Thus it is clear that, before rising for prayer, such a person has already fulfilled this obligation before further delay becomes impermissible, just like someone who sets out for Friday prayer before the call, or someone who repays a debt before it falls due. For this reason,

---

## Page 10782

al-Shāfiʿī and others said that if a boy performs a prayer and then reaches puberty, he need not repeat it, because it is that very prayer which he performed before it became obligatory upon him. This is also one position within Ahmad’s school, and it is stronger than the view that repetition is obligatory. Those who require repetition draw an analogy with Hajj, but there is a distinction between the two, as explained at length elsewhere.

What we have said about ablution applies equally to tayammum (dry ablution). Thus, scholars have said that dry ablution is like ablution: it is a means of purification for a Muslim so long as he cannot find water. Even if he performs dry ablution before the prayer time and does so for a voluntary prayer, he may use it to offer an obligatory prayer and other prayers. This is the position of Ibn ʿAbbās.

It is also the position of many scholars, including Abū Hanīfah and others, and one of the two views reported from Ahmad. The other view—that dry ablution must be performed for each prayer—is the well-known position in the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. It is a view that has not been reliably established from anyone else among the Companions, as explained at length in its proper place.

Thus the verse is definitive, praise be to Allah. It retains its stated meaning: everyone who rises to pray is commanded to perform ablution. If he has already performed ablution, he has done well, fulfilled the obligation before further delay becomes impermissible, and hastened to good deeds, like someone who sets out for Friday prayer before the call. It is therefore clear that the verse contains neither ellipsis nor any restriction of its general scope, nor does it indicate

---

## Page 10783

an obligation to perform ablution twice. Rather, it indicates the ruling established by mass-transmitted reports of the Sunnah and upheld by the Muslim community: that ablution is obligatory for anyone who prays.

Thus, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah does not accept the prayer of any of you who has broken his ablution until he performs ablution again.”

A man from Hadramawt asked, “What breaks ablution, Abū Hurayrah?” He replied, “Passing wind, silently or audibly.”

In Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, it is reported from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah does not accept prayer without purification, nor charity from misappropriated property.”

This accords with the noble verse, for it indicates that purification is indispensable. Whoever has ablution is already in a state of purification; only someone whose ablution has been broken needs to perform it. As he said:

“Allah does not accept the prayer of any of you who has broken his ablution until he performs ablution again.”

If someone performs ablution and then breaks it, the verse indicates that he is commanded to perform ablution when he rises to pray. If he has already performed ablution, he has done what he was commanded to do.

This is like saying, “Do not pray except with ablution,” or, “Do not pray until you have performed ablution,” and similar expressions. These make clear that he is commanded to perform ablution for prayer generally, encompassing all its kinds and individual instances. He is not commanded to perform a separate ablution for each kind or instance, distinct from the ablution for another. Nor does the wording indicate any such requirement. However, this line of reasoning does not establish that ablution may precede prayer in general, as in the case of someone who embraces Islam

---

## Page 10784

and performs ablution before the sun passes its zenith or sets, or someone who breaks his ablution and performs it again before the prayer time begins. The preceding line of reasoning, by contrast, encompasses all these cases.

Section

Allah Most High says:

“When you rise to pray, wash…”

This requires everyone who prays to perform ablution time after time; it therefore entails repetition. Muslims agree on this concerning purification. He said: This is established by the mass-transmitted Sunnah. Indeed, it is known of necessity within the Muslim religion, as received from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he did not command us to perform ablution for only one prayer. Rather, he commanded a person to have ablution whenever he prays. If someone were to offer one prayer with ablution and then intend to offer all his remaining prayers without ablution, he would be called upon to repent: either he repents or he is put to death.

What concerns us here, however, is how the verse indicates this. It does so through the word “prayer,” which is a generic noun here, not a reference to a single prayer. Thus, He commands a person to perform ablution whenever he rises to perform prayer as a category, and that category encompasses every prayer he offers throughout his life.

If it is said: “This establishes the universal scope of the category, but where does repetition come from? For when

---

## Page 10785

he rises to offer any prayer, he performs ablution; but what establishes that he must perform ablution when he rises to offer it on another day?”

The answer is: On that second day, he is again rising to pray. He is commanded to perform ablution whenever he rises to offer anything designated as prayer. Thus, whenever this occurs, the command to perform ablution applies, and ablution is obligatory for him.

This is like the words of Allah Most High:

“Establish prayer at the decline of the sun.”

What is meant is the sun’s decline as a recurring event, for which he is commanded to establish prayer.

Likewise, His words:

“Glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise and before sunset.”

This encompasses every sunrise and sunset; it does not mean a single sunrise. It is as though He said: “Before every sunrise and before every sunset; establish prayer whenever the sun declines, and rise to offer every prayer having performed ablution for it.”

Scholars have differed over whether an unrestricted command entails repetition. There are three positions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

One holds that it entails repetition. This is the view of a group that includes al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn ʿAqīl.

Another holds that it does not entail repetition. This is the view of many, including Abū al-Khattāb.

The third holds that, if the command is tied to a cause, it entails repetition. This is the position explicitly stated by Ahmad, as in the verses concerning purification and prayer.

---

## Page 10786

If it is objected, “But this does not recur in conditional divorce or manumission,” the answer is: The emancipation of the same person cannot recur. Likewise, the conditional divorce itself cannot recur. Rather, a second divorce has a different legal effect from the first, and divorce is limited to three pronouncements.

However, if someone makes a vow, saying, “I owe it to Allah, if He grants me a child, to free a slave on the child’s behalf; and whenever He grants me wealth, to pay its zakat or give a tenth of it in charity,” the obligation recurs. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

Section

Allah Most High says:

“If you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have touched women…”

This verse has puzzled some people. A group of them said that “or” means “and,” interpreting the wording as: “and one of you has relieved himself, and you have touched women.”

They argued that “or” would imply that illness and travel each necessitate dry ablution, just as relieving oneself and touching women do.

This, however, is contrary to the meaning of the verse.

---

## Page 10787

For “or” differs from “and”: “and” combines the two coordinated elements and includes both, whereas “or” does not require their combination but affirms one of them. This may leave the other permissible, as in the sayings, “Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sīrīn,” and “Study jurisprudence or grammar.” The alternative acts of expiation are another example: one may choose between them, although performing them all is permissible. Alternatively, the choice may be exclusive, as when a sick person is told, “Eat this or that.”

Likewise, in a statement, “or” affirms one of the two alternatives, either without the addressee knowing which—which constitutes doubt—or with his knowledge—which constitutes deliberate ambiguity, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.”

Nevertheless, the meaning he intended is the soundest: the instruction to perform dry ablution applies to the sick person and the traveller even if he has relieved himself or had intercourse. Their interpretation should not, however, be understood to mean that dry ablution is permitted only in these two cases. Rather, the implication is that following a wet dream or minor ritual impurity not caused by defecation, dry ablution is all the more appropriate.

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded everyone rising for prayer to perform ablution, He also commanded them to purify themselves if they were in a state of major ritual impurity. Among them are those whose minor ritual impurity arose from something other than defecation, such as waking from sleep or passing wind. Others are in a state of major ritual impurity not through intercourse but through a wet dream. Thus, the verse encompasses everyone in a state of minor ritual impurity and everyone in a state of major ritual impurity.

Allah Most High then said:

“If you are ill or on a journey”

“then perform dry ablution.”

He thus permitted dry ablution for a person in a state of minor or major ritual impurity if

---

## Page 10788

he is ill or on a journey and cannot find water. Dry ablution is a concession, so one might suppose that it is permitted only for less severe forms of minor and major ritual impurity, such as those caused by passing wind and wet dreams, rather than defecation and intercourse. People regard performing dry ablution and praying in the latter circumstances as a daunting matter and shrink from it. Indeed, some of the foremost Companions rejected dry ablution altogether for someone in a state of major ritual impurity.

Many people are reluctant to pray with dry ablution when they are ritually impure, for making earth a means of purification like water is one of the special favors Allah has bestowed upon Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his community. Those whose faith is not firmly established do not consider this permissible. Allah, glorified is He, therefore made clear that dry ablution is prescribed even when minor ritual impurity is aggravated by defecation and major ritual impurity by intercourse.

The sense is: “If you are ill or travelling, or if—in addition to that—one of you has returned from relieving himself or you have had intercourse with women.” The intention is not to treat defecation and intercourse as cases unaccompanied by illness or travel. For He has already addressed the case of those who have relieved themselves or had intercourse with women, while neither ill nor travelling, in His words:

“When you rise for prayer, wash your faces,”

and His words:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, then purify yourselves.”

Thus, the verse indicates that ablution and a full ritual bath are obligatory for the healthy and the non-traveller.

Furthermore, He may have singled out defecation and intercourse because a person might not perform dry ablution in such circumstances, although he would for something less severe, such as passing wind and

---

## Page 10789

wet dreams. For passing wind is like sleep, and wet dreams occur during sleep. In these cases, minor and major ritual impurity arise while a person is asleep.

If he is commanded to perform ablution and a full ritual bath in that situation, then these are all the more obligatory when such impurity arises while he is awake. For a sleeping person is not held accountable, unlike someone who is awake. Yet the verse indicates that purification is obligatory even when minor or major ritual impurity arises involuntarily, as when a sleeping person loses his state of purity or has a wet dream.

Since the verse indicates that purification with water is obligatory in that situation, it is all the more obligatory when ritual impurity results from a person’s voluntary action or arises while he is awake. Dry ablution, however, is different. Permitting dry ablution for someone with a valid excuse who becomes ritually impure during sleep through a wet dream or passing wind does not necessarily entail permitting it for someone whose ritual impurity results from his voluntary action. Thus, the Most High said:

“Or one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women,”

to make clear that dry ablution is permissible for these two persons, even if their ritual impurity arises while they are awake and through their own actions, and even if it is severe.

If “or” meant “and,” the statement would mean that dry ablution is permissible only when both conditions—illness and travel—are present, together with returning from relieving oneself and having a wet dream. This would entail that it is not permissible following a wet dream, nor following minor ritual impurity unaccompanied by defecation, such as that of someone who has slept or passed wind. For when a ruling is made contingent upon two conditions, it does not apply when only one is present. This is certainly not what is intended; rather, it is the very opposite of

---

## Page 10790

the truth; for if dry ablution is permitted after defecation, which occurs voluntarily, it is all the more permissible when ritual impurity is minor and involuntary.

It thus becomes clear that the meaning of the verse is:

“If you are ill or on a journey, perform dry ablution, even if, in addition, one of you has returned from relieving himself or you have had intercourse with women.”

This is like saying: “Even if you are ill or travelling.” The underlying wording is:

“And if you who rise for prayer—while ill or travelling—have returned from relieving yourselves or have had intercourse with women…”

This is why those who said that the verse addresses people rising from sleep explained its underlying wording as follows:

“When you rise for prayer, or one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women.”

For He, glorified be He, first mentions their actions in His words:

“When you rise,”

and:

“Or one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women”—

three actions in all. His words:

“And if you are ill or on a journey,”

describe their circumstances; that is, if they are in this condition. It is as though He were saying:

“If you are unable to use water—either because it is unavailable or because you fear harm from using it—then perform dry ablution when you rise from sleep for prayer, or one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women.”

However, the view we have preferred is that His words, “When you rise,” are general in scope: either in both wording and meaning, or in meaning alone.

---

## Page 10791

Accordingly, the meaning is:

When you rise for prayer, perform ablution, or bathe if you are in a state of major ritual impurity; and if you are ill or travelling, or have done something that more clearly entails ritual impurity—returned from relieving yourselves or had intercourse with women—

For the underlying wording is:

If you are ill or travelling and have risen for prayer, or, besides rising for prayer while ill or travelling, you have performed these two acts: relieving yourselves and having intercourse. Thus, your rising for prayer, illness, travel, and one of these two acts will have come together. Rising requires purification, while the excuse permits dry ablution; and this is the rising in question. Thus, when you rise, dry ablution becomes obligatory if it is merely rising, or if one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women.

Some people, however, take His words, “Or one of you has returned” and “Or you have had intercourse,” as coordinated with His words, “When you rise.” The underlying wording would then be: “When you rise, or one of you has returned, or you have had intercourse.” This, however, conflicts with the arrangement of the verse, which requires that this fall within the consequent of the conditional statement.

As for His words:

“If you are ill or on a journey, or one of you has returned from relieving himself, or you have had intercourse with women, and you find no water, then perform dry ablution,”

the interpretation just mentioned is close in meaning. The underlying wording, however, is:

If, when you rise for prayer, you are ill or on a journey, or if, in addition, one of you has returned from relieving himself or you have had intercourse with women.

Thus, it distinguishes between a circumstance on its own and a combination of circumstances. It means:

If you are ill or on a journey, rising for prayer merely by rising

---

## Page 10792

from sleep or ordinary sitting; or if, in addition, one of you has returned from relieving himself or you have had intercourse with women.

Thus, His words, Exalted is He:

“If you are ill or on a journey,”

address those who have been told:

“When you rise for prayer, wash,”

and:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

The meaning is: You who rise for prayer, perform ablution. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, bathe. If you are ill or travelling, perform dry ablution. Or if, alongside these two circumstances—rising for prayer while in a state of minor or major ritual impurity, and being ill or travelling—you have returned from relieving yourself or have had intercourse with women, then perform dry ablution if you have a valid excuse.

To clarify: this is an instance of coordinating a specific case with a general category, singling it out for mention because of its distinctive character. Its being singled out implies that distinction. In such cases, one may say that it is included in the general category and then mentioned specifically. Alternatively, one may say that its separate mention excludes it from the general category.

This occurs in coordination with “or.” As for coordination with “and,” examples include His words, Exalted is He:

“His angels and His messengers, Gabriel and Michael,”

and:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah and Abraham,”

to the end of the verse. Another example is His statement:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing,”

and similar passages. As for “or,” examples include His words, Exalted is He:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins,”

and His words: “And whoever does

---

## Page 10793

evil or wrongs himself, then seeks Allah’s forgiveness, will find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.” And His words:

“Whoever commits an offence or a sin, then accuses an innocent person of it, has burdened himself with slander and manifest sin.”

And His words:

“But if anyone fears bias or sin on the part of a testator.”

Bias means deviation from what is right, even when deliberate. Most Quran commentators explain “bias” as inadvertent error and “sin” as deliberate wrongdoing. Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said: “Bias is departure from what is right. The term may apply both to someone who errs inadvertently and to someone who acts deliberately. However, the commentators associate ‘bias’ with the former and ‘sin’ with the latter.”

A similar example is His statement:

“And do not obey any sinner or disbeliever among them.”

A disbeliever is also a sinner, but this coordinates a specific case with a general category. It has also been said that these are two descriptions of the same person, which is more emphatic. Coordinating two descriptions of the same subject occurs in His words:

“Who created and fashioned, and who determined and guided.”

And His words:

“He is the First and the Last, the Ascendant and the Intimate.”

And His words:

“Successful indeed are the believers, who are humble in their prayers, who turn away from idle talk, who pay zakah, and who guard their chastity.”

There are many similar examples.

Ibn Zayd said: “The sinner, the guilty, the unjust, and the disbeliever—all these refer to the same person.”

Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: “He may choose either of these two descriptions to identify the person whom he must not obey, since each of them is both a sinner and a disbeliever

---

## Page 10794

and the community was not so numerous that sin predominated over acts of disobedience.”

He said: “The wording merely requires that the leader be forbidden to obey a sinner from among the disobedient or a disbeliever from among the polytheists.”

Abū ‘Ubaydah and others said: “No choice is offered here; ‘or’ means ‘and’.” A number of scholars, including al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī, said likewise.

Al-Mahdawī said: “That is, do not obey anyone who sins or disbelieves. The inclusion of ‘or’ requires that neither be obeyed individually. Had He said, ‘And do not obey either of them, a sinner or a disbeliever,’ the prohibition would apply only when both descriptions were combined.”

It may also be said that the “disbeliever” is someone who denies the truth, even if he has striven to reach the correct judgment but erred. Thus, the former is broader in one respect, and the latter is broader with respect to adherence (1).

Allah’s words also belong to this category:

“If you are ill, on a journey, have relieved yourselves, or have had contact with women.”

For He addressed the believers, saying:

“When you rise for prayer, wash…”

As explained earlier, this includes those in a state of minor ritual impurity. He then said:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

Then He said: “And if you—while in a state of minor or major ritual impurity—are ill or on a journey, and cannot find water, then perform dry ablution.”
