## Page 10795

And this includes everyone in a state of minor ritual impurity, whether he has relieved himself or not, such as someone who has awakened from sleep or someone who passes wind while awake. It also includes everyone in a state of major ritual impurity, whether caused by a wet dream or intercourse. Thus He said:

“And if you are in a state of minor or major ritual impurity and are ill or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself”—this is a particular kind of minor ritual impurity—“or you have had contact with women”—this is a particular kind of major ritual impurity.

It may then be said that the term “one in a state of major ritual impurity” encompasses both kinds, while the person who has had intercourse is singled out for mention. Likewise, “one who rises for prayer” encompasses both someone who has relieved himself and someone whose ritual purity has been invalidated otherwise, but the former is singled out for mention. This is like His words:

“Whoever fears partiality or sin on the part of a testator.”

Here, the sinner is someone who acts deliberately. Singling him out for mention—even if he is already included—clarifies the ruling concerning him specifically, lest anyone suppose that he falls outside the general wording. If, however, he is not included, then he constitutes another category.

The implied wording is: “If you are ill or on a journey, then perform dry ablution.” This is the meaning of the verse.

Section

In His words:

“Or one of you has relieved himself,”

He mentions minor ritual impurity. Coming “from the place of relief” means coming from the place where one relieves oneself. They used to

---

## Page 10796

go to low-lying places, known as al-ghā’it. This is like saying, “He has come from the lavatory,” or “He has come from the privy,” and similar expressions. All these expressions refer to someone returning after relieving himself by urinating or defecating. Wind accompanies both.

The jurists have disagreed: does passing wind invalidate ablution because it carries some faecal matter with it, in which case it would not constitute a separate category? Or does it carry no faecal matter, but itself invalidate ablution? Muslims agree that passing wind invalidates ablution. The Quran indicates this in His words:

“When you rise,”

whether this means rising from sleep or rising in general. Rising from sleep is intended in either case, and sleep invalidates ablution only because of the passing of wind. This is the position of the four imams and the majority of earlier and later scholars: sleep itself does not invalidate ablution, but is a circumstance in which passing wind is likely.

One group, however, held that sleep itself invalidates ablution, whether one sleeps a little or a great deal. This is a weak view. It is authentically reported in the two Sahīh collections:

“The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would sleep until he snored, then rise and pray without performing ablution, and would say, ‘My eyes sleep, but my heart does not.’”

This indicates that, through his heart—which did not sleep—he knew that he had not invalidated his ritual purity. If sleep itself were like urination, defecation, or passing wind, it would invalidate ablution just as the other nullifiers do. It is also authentically reported in the two Sahīh collections:

“The Companions would wait for the prayer until

---

## Page 10797

their heads nodded. Then they would pray without performing ablution, while they were in the mosque waiting to pray ʿIshā’ behind the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported:

“One night, the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was occupied and delayed ʿIshā’ until we fell asleep in the mosque, then woke up, then fell asleep again, then woke up. The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) then came out to us and said, ‘No one else on earth tonight is waiting for the prayer except you.’”

Muslim also relates that he said:

“One night, we waited for the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) for the late-evening prayer, ʿIshā’. He came out to us when a third of the night, or some portion of it, had passed—we did not know what had occupied him, whether something concerning his family or something else. When he came out, he said, ‘You are indeed waiting for a prayer for which the followers of no other religion are waiting. Were it not burdensome for my community, I would lead them in this prayer at this hour.’ Then he instructed the caller to prayer, who pronounced the call to commence the prayer, and he prayed.”

Muslim also relates from ʿĀ’ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said:

“One night, the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) delayed ʿIshā’ until most of the night had passed and those in the mosque had fallen asleep. Then he came out and prayed, and said, ‘This is indeed its proper time, were it not that I would cause hardship for my community.’”

These authentic hadiths establish that they slept, and some versions state, “They

---

## Page 10798

fell asleep, then woke up, then fell asleep again, then woke up.” Those who prayed behind him were a large congregation; they had waited a long time and had fallen asleep.

He did not seek further details from anyone. He was not asked, nor did he ask the people: “Did you dream? Were any of you sitting with your buttocks firmly planted? Were any of you leaning against something? Did any of your limbs fall to the ground?” Had the ruling differed according to these circumstances, he would have questioned them. It is well known that all these things occur when such a large gathering waits at night. Women and children also used to pray behind him.

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀ’ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) reported:

“One night, the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) delayed the ʿIshā’ prayer. He did not come out until ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said, ‘The women and children have fallen asleep.’ Then the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) came out and said to those in the mosque, ‘No one else on earth is waiting for this prayer except you.’ This was before Islam had spread among the people.”

Al-Bukhārī included this hadith in the chapter “Women Going to the Mosque at Night and in the Predawn Darkness,” and in the chapter “Sleeping Before ʿIshā’ When Overcome by Sleep.” He also included it in the chapter “Children’s Ablution and Their Attendance at Congregational Prayer,” with the wording:

“No one else on earth offers this prayer except you.”

---

## Page 10799

This makes clear that ʿUmar’s words, “The women and children have fallen asleep,” referred to the people waiting for prayer in the mosque. It also shows that when someone waiting for prayer—such as someone waiting for the Friday prayer—falls asleep, whatever the nature of that sleep, his ablution is not invalidated. Sleep itself does not invalidate ablution; rather, what invalidates it is the occurrence of ritual impurity.

When someone sleeps in the usual manner people ordinarily choose—such as sleeping at night or taking a midday nap—he commonly passes wind without being aware of it. Since the underlying reason is hidden and cannot be known, its indicator takes its place: namely, the kind of sleep during which this ordinarily happens.

As for sleep about which one is uncertain whether any wind was passed, it does not invalidate ablution, because ritual purity is established with certainty and is not removed by doubt. There are several views on this issue, which this is not the place to discuss in detail. However, this is the view supported by the evidence. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah contains a text requiring ablution to be considered invalid after every kind of sleep.

For his saying,

“The eye is the drawstring of the anus; when the eyes sleep, the drawstring comes loose,”

has been reported in the Sunan collections on the authority of ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib and Muʿāwiyah

---

## Page 10800

—may Allah be pleased with them both—and several scholars have graded it weak. Even assuming it is authentic, all it says is:

“When the eyes sleep, the drawstring comes loose.”

This indicates that it is ordinary sleep that causes the drawstring to come loose. Yet the loosening itself does not invalidate ablution; rather, it is what comes out when it loosens that invalidates it. A person may relax until the drawstring comes loose without his ablution being invalidated.

As for the wording in the hadith of Safwān ibn ʿAssāl:

“We were commanded not to remove our leather socks when on a journey—or travelling—for three days and nights, except in a state of major ritual impurity, but not because of defecation, urination, or sleep.”

This does not state that sleep invalidates ablution. Rather, it states that someone wearing leather socks should not remove them for three days except because of major ritual impurity, and should not remove them because of defecation, urination, or sleep. It thus prohibits removing them for these reasons, and includes sleep that invalidates ablution. It does not state that every kind of sleep invalidates ablution. This is so even if the word “sleep” was spoken by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. How much more so if it was the narrator’s wording?

The Prophet, who conveyed the divine law, would have known that people sitting or standing, whether in prayer or otherwise, may become drowsy and fall asleep. Yet he did not instruct anyone to perform ablution in such cases.

As for ablution after what people ordinarily recognize as sleep, this concerns sleep during which passing wind is generally more likely. But sleep during which one may or may not pass wind does not invalidate ablution according to the principle held by the majority. They maintain that when one doubts whether ablution has been invalidated, it remains valid, on the basis of the established certainty of ritual purity.

## Page 10801

Section

He, glorified be He, has commanded us to perform both minor and major ritual purification, and dry ablution in place of either. He says:

“When you rise for prayer, wash.”

Thus He commanded ablution. He then says:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

Thus He commanded purification from major ritual impurity, just as He said concerning menstruation:

“Do not approach them until they become pure. Then, when they have purified themselves, approach them as Allah has commanded you.”

And He says in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ:

“Nor while in a state of major ritual impurity—except when passing through—until you have bathed.”

This makes clear that purification here means bathing. The Quran indicates that a person in a state of major ritual impurity is required only to bathe, and that once he has bathed, he may approach prayer. Someone bathing to remove major ritual impurity need not also intend to remove minor ritual impurity, as the majority of scholars hold.

The well-known position in Ahmad’s school, however, is that he must intend to remove minor ritual impurity. Likewise, according to the majority, he need not perform ablution, observe the prescribed order, or maintain continuity in washing. This is also the apparent position of Ahmad’s school.

It has also been said that minor ritual impurity is not removed without observing both order and continuity. Another view is that it is not removed until he performs ablution. This has been reported from Ahmad.

## Page 10802

And the Quran indicates that bathing suffices, and that after bathing to remove major ritual impurity, no other ritual impurity remains. Rather, minor ritual impurity is subsumed within major ritual impurity, just as the washing required for the former is part of that required for the latter, since the latter includes washing all four bodily areas.

This is supported by the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Umm ‘Atiyyah and the other women who washed his daughter:

“Wash her three times, or five, or more than that if you deem it necessary, with water and lote leaves. Begin with her right side and the parts of her body washed in ablution.”

Thus, he made washing the parts of the body washed in ablution part of the overall washing, but gave them precedence, just as he gave precedence to the right side. Likewise, those who described his bathing, such as ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, mentioned:

“He would perform ablution, then pour water over his hair, then over the rest of his body.”

He did not set out to wash the parts of the body washed in ablution twice, nor would he perform ablution after bathing. Thus, the Book and the Sunnah indicate that a person in a state of major ritual impurity and a menstruating woman need not wash the limbs of ablution separately or intend to perform ablution. Rather, they purify themselves and bathe as Allah Most High has commanded.

By His words:

“Purify yourselves,”

He meant bathing. This indicates that, in His words concerning menstruation:

“Until they become pure. Then, when they have purified themselves,”

He meant bathing, as held by the majority:

---

## Page 10803

Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad. It also indicates that the view that it means washing the private parts, as Dāwūd held, is weak.

Section

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

“If you are ill, on a journey, have relieved yourselves, or have touched women, and cannot find water, then perform dry ablution with clean earth.”

His words, “and cannot find water,” relate to His words, “on a journey,” not to illness. A sick person may perform dry ablution even when water is available, whereas a traveller may do so only when unable to find water.

He, glorified and exalted, mentions the two usual categories: those who would be harmed by using water and those who cannot find it. His words, “on a journey,” encompass both long and short journeys, as the majority hold.

His words, “If you are ill,” are like His words in the verse concerning fear:

“There is no blame upon you for laying aside your weapons if you are troubled by rain or are ill,”

and His words concerning ritual consecration:

“Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the scalp”

---

## Page 10804

and, concerning fasting:

“Whoever among you is ill or on a journey shall make up an equal number of other days.”

Allah Most High has set no specific limit regarding illness. The majority hold that fear of death is not a prerequisite: anyone whose illness would be aggravated, or whose recovery would be delayed, by ablution may perform dry ablution. The same applies to fasting and ritual consecration.

According to the majority, someone who would be harmed by using water because of the cold is treated like a sick person. However, Allah mentioned illness because it is a widespread cause of harm, unlike cold, which affects only some people in certain lands who cannot obtain warm water. Likewise, He mentioned the traveller who cannot find water, but not the resident, since water is rarely unavailable where people reside. Yet a man may be detained with only enough water to drink, just as a traveller may have only enough for himself and his animals to drink. According to the majority, such a person is considered unable to find water and may therefore perform dry ablution.

Section

His words:

“Or one of you has relieved himself, or you have touched women.”

He mentioned the foremost cause requiring ablution—relieving oneself—and the gravest cause requiring a full ritual bath—intercourse with women. He commanded each of the two, if he is

---

## Page 10805

ill or travelling and unable to find water, to perform dry ablution. This is the position of the majority of both the later and earlier generations.

Dry ablution for someone in a state of major ritual impurity is established in authentic and good hadiths, including the hadith of Ammār ibn Yāsir—may Allah be pleased with them both—recorded in the two Sahīh collections; the hadith of Imrān ibn Husayn—may Allah be pleased with him—recorded by al-Bukhārī; and the reports concerning Abū Dharr, Amr ibn al-Ās, and the man with a head wound—may Allah be pleased with them—recorded in the Sunan collections. Thus, there are two verses from the Book of Allah and five hadiths from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Ibn Mas‘ūd’s debate with Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī on this matter—may Allah be pleased with them both—is well known. There are many similar examples reported from the Companions. When you know these examples, you will appreciate the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah in relation to a man of great standing, giving effect to His words:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.”

This dispute must be referred only to Allah and the infallible Messenger who conveys Allah’s message, who does not speak from his own desire—it is nothing but revelation revealed—and who is the intermediary between Allah and His servants.

## Page 10806

Section

We discuss this in connection with His words:

“Or have touched women.”

What is meant is sexual intercourse, as Ibn Abbās—may Allah be pleased with them both—and other Arabs stated. This is also reported from Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—and others. This is the correct interpretation of the verse. Neither the Book nor the Sunnah establishes that touching women invalidates ablution. Muslims routinely touched their wives, yet not a single Muslim has transmitted that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered anyone to perform ablution because of touching women.

As for the view that the verse refers to contact short of intercourse and that this invalidates ablution, Ibn Umar and al-Hasan are reported to have explained it as “with the hand.” A number of the early generations held this view regarding touching with desire. Performing ablution after such touching is good and recommended, to quell desire, just as performing ablution when angry is recommended to quell anger. It is not, however, obligatory.

As for touching without desire, I know of no basis among the early generations for holding that it invalidates ablution. As for His words, exalted is He, “or have touched women,” the Quran does not mention ablution

---

## Page 10807

because of it. Rather, it mentions only tayammum (dry purification), after commanding a person in a state of minor ritual impurity who rises for prayer to perform ablution, and commanding a person in a state of major ritual impurity to bathe. It then mentions purification with clean earth, necessarily explaining both cases.

His words,

“Or one of you comes from relieving himself,”

explain tayammum in the former case. As for His words,

“Or have touched women,”

neither this nor the preceding expression was mentioned to explain purification with water, since the basic ruling on this was already known from His words, “When you rise for prayer, wash,” and His words, “If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

Thus, the verse states only that the person who has touched a woman should perform tayammum if he cannot find water. How, then, could this be a case of minor ritual impurity? Would He command someone who has touched a woman to perform tayammum when He has not commanded him to perform ablution? How could He command tayammum for someone whom He has not commanded to perform ablution? He commanded tayammum only for those whom He commanded to perform ablution or ritual bathing. Discussing comparable examples would take too long. Whoever reflects upon the verse will be certain that this is its intended meaning.

Section

The verse also indicates that a traveller may have intercourse with his wife even if he cannot find water, and that doing so is not disliked, as Allah has stated in the verse and as the hadiths indicate—the hadith of Abū Dharr and others.

## Page 10808

Section

His words,

“Then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to place you in hardship, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful,”

are evidence that tayammum is a means of purification just as water is.

It is likewise authentically established in the Sunnah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. When you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated this and graded it authentic. Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī also narrated it.

In the Sahīh, he is reported to have said:

“The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.”

He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—thus made earth a means of purification from minor and major ritual impurity. Similarly, he said in the hadith of Abū Saʿīd:

“When one of you comes to the mosque, let him turn his sandals over and inspect them. If there is dirt—or filth—on them, let him rub them on the earth, for earth is a means of purification for them.”

He also said in the hadith of Umm Salamah:

---

## Page 10809

“A woman’s trailing hem is purified by what it passes over afterward.”

This indicates that tayammum purifies, making the person who performs it pure, just as water makes the person using it for purification pure, if he is neither in a state of major nor minor ritual impurity.

Whoever says that a person who has performed tayammum remains in a state of major or minor ritual impurity has contradicted the Quran and Sunnah. Rather, that person has purified himself. The Prophet’s words in the hadith of ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās, may Allah be pleased with him,

“Did you lead your companions in prayer while in a state of major ritual impurity?”

are a question, meaning: “Did you do that?” ‘Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, informed him that he had not done so; rather, he had performed tayammum because he feared that the cold would kill him. The Prophet made no objection, laughed, and said nothing.

If it is said that this was a rebuke for his having prayed while in a state of major ritual impurity, then it indicates that praying in that state is impermissible. For he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not condemn what was objectionable. When ‘Amr informed him that he had prayed after performing tayammum, this indicated that he had not prayed while in a state of major ritual impurity. Thus, the hadith is evidence against those who invoke it to maintain that someone who has performed tayammum remains in a state of major or minor ritual impurity.

Allah says:

“And if you are in a state of major ritual impurity, then purify yourselves.”

Allah has therefore not permitted such a person to pray until he purifies himself. Someone who has performed tayammum has purified himself according to the explicit wording of the Quran and Sunnah. How, then, can he be in a state of major ritual impurity

---

## Page 10810

without having purified himself? Rather, this is a substitute form of purification. When he becomes able to use water, this purification ceases to be valid, and he must then purify himself with water. His earlier urination rendered him ritually impure, while clean earth rendered him pure until he finds water. If he finds water, he is ritually impure because of the earlier cause—not because his ritual impurity had persisted throughout.

As for someone who says, “Tayammum permits prayer but does not remove ritual impurity,” his disagreement is merely verbal.

If he says that it permits prayer despite major or minor ritual impurity, and that it does not purify, he contradicts the scriptural texts. Major ritual impurity prohibits prayer. It is therefore impossible for that which permits prayer and that which prohibits it to be fully operative together, since this would entail the coexistence of two opposites. Someone who has performed tayammum is not prohibited from praying. Thus, by agreement, the prohibition has been lifted, and prohibition is the ruling entailed by major ritual impurity. If this state is said to exist without its consequence—namely, prohibition—then the disagreement is merely verbal.

Section

The verse also indicates that someone who relieves himself is not obliged to wash his private parts with water. Water is required only for purification from ritual impurity in its appropriate manner; removing excrement and filth, however, does not specifically require water. This is what the scriptural texts indicate, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sometimes instructed that water be used for this and sometimes instructed that something other than water be used, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

## Page 10811

for the purpose here is to draw attention to what the verse indicates. His words,

“Or one of you comes from relieving himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum,”

explicitly establish that, when water is unavailable, a person may pray even after defecating without washing himself afterward. It is also established in the Sunnah that “three stones suffice him.”

As for cases involving an excuse, He says:

“When you rise to pray, wash…”

This includes everyone who rises to pray: someone who has relieved himself just as much as someone who has passed wind. If washing the two private parts with water were obligatory upon someone rising to pray, it would be obligatory just like washing the four bodily parts. Yet the Quran indicates that he is obliged to perform only the washing and wiping it mentions. It also indicates that both someone who performs ablution and someone who performs tayammum are ritually pure. As for the two private parts, the Sunnah establishes that cleansing them with stones is sufficient.

The words of the Most High,

“In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves,”

indicate that cleansing oneself with water after relieving oneself is recommended and loved by Allah, not obligatory. Other Muslims did not cleanse themselves with water, yet He did not censure them for this; rather, He approved their practice while singling out these men for praise. This indicates that what the others did was permissible, while what these men did was better, and that this is one of the ways in which Allah has favored some people over others.

## Page 10812

Section: Observing the Prescribed Order in Ablution and Other Acts of Worship and Contracts

The disagreement over this is well known. According to al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, it is obligatory; according to Mālik and Abū Hanīfah, it is not. Ahmad explicitly affirmed its obligation on several occasions. The earlier scholars—such as al-Qādī and those before him—reported no contrary position from him.

Abū Muhammad said: “I have seen no contrary report from him on this.” He added: “Abū al-Khattāb related another report from Ahmad stating that it is not obligatory.”

I say: This was inferred from his explicit statement concerning the handful of water used to rinse the nose. If this washing is delayed until after washing the feet, there are two explicit reports from Ahmad on the matter. In one of them, he said that if someone forgot both rinsing the mouth and rinsing the nose until after praying, he should rinse his mouth and nose and repeat the prayer, but not repeat the ablution. This is based on the report in the Sunan collections from al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib:

“He was brought water for ablution. He washed his hands three times, then washed his face three times, then washed his forearms three times, then rinsed his mouth and nose.”

---

## Page 10813

Scholars other than Abū al-Khattāb distinguished rinsing the mouth and nose from the other acts of ablution, arguing that observing the prescribed order is obligatory only for what is mentioned in the Quran, whereas these two are not mentioned there. Abū al-Khattāb and those who followed him considered this a weak distinction: had the nose and mouth not been part of the face, washing them would not have been obligatory.

Accordingly, the school’s jurists deduced that both are part of the face, as al-Khiraqī and others stated:

“The mouth and nose are part of the face.”

Moreover, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would begin washing his face by rinsing them, starting with its internal parts. He rinsed the mouth first because it is closer to the exterior than the nose. Hence the command to rinse the nose was more emphatic, and authentic hadiths expressly command it. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would then wash the rest of his face. Thus, if rinsing both is held to be obligatory despite the disagreement, they are like the other areas whose inclusion is disputed.

One example is the bare skin between the sideburn and the ear: Mālik and others say that it is not part of the face. There are three juristic views concerning the two hairless recesses flanking the forelock and the fine-haired areas between those recesses and the upper ends of the sideburns. One view regards both as part of the head; another regards both as part of the face. The correct view is that the two recesses are part of the head, while the fine-haired areas are part of the face. If someone forgets these areas, his case is therefore like that of someone who forgets to rinse the mouth and nose. Thus, Abū al-Khattāb’s treating these cases alike is the stronger position.

---

## Page 10814

On this basis, Ahmad’s explicit ruling concerned only someone who omitted this forgetfully. Thus, he was asked, “What if he forgot only to rinse his mouth?” He replied, “Rinsing the nose is, in my view, more emphatically required.” This concerns someone who forgot to do so and then prayed. He said, “He should rinse both and repeat the prayer.” He considered repeating the prayer more emphatically required when rinsing the nose had been omitted, because the authentic hadiths command it.

The same applies to the report traced back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. All those who described his ablution reported that he began by rinsing his mouth and nose. This report recounts a single occurrence, so one cannot be certain that he acted deliberately. Accordingly, there is no Prophetic precedent for deliberately postponing these two acts; rather, the precedent concerns forgetfulness. For the case of forgetfulness is established with certainty: even assuming there is doubt, the apparent likelihood is that he had forgotten. If it is permissible when done deliberately, it is all the more permissible when done forgetfully. Someone who forgets is therefore excused in either case, unlike someone who acts deliberately.

This is the third view: distinguishing between someone who deliberately reverses the prescribed order of ablution and someone excused by forgetfulness or ignorance. It is the strongest view, supported by the statements of the Companions and the majority of scholars. It also accords with the school’s principles in other matters and is Ahmad’s explicit position in the case from which Abū al-Khattāb derived his ruling by analogy.

One such case is departing from the prescribed order between slaughtering the sacrificial animal and shaving the head. Someone who does so out of ignorance is excused, without disagreement within the school. As for someone who does so knowingly and deliberately, two positions are reported from Ahmad.

---

## Page 10815

The Sunnah reports only that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would be asked about this and would reply:

“Do it; there is no harm.”

This was because they had performed the rites out of order without knowing; they had not deliberately contravened the Sunnah. The Quran, however, does prescribe an order, in His words:

“Do not shave your heads until the sacrificial offering reaches its place of slaughter.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“I have garlanded my sacrificial animal and matted my hair, so I shall neither leave the state of ihrām nor shave my head until I have slaughtered it.”

And His words,

“Then let them complete their prescribed rites, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House,”

provide stronger evidence for a prescribed order than His words:

“Indeed, Safā and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.”

It may, however, be said that they distinguished between the two on the grounds that the former is a single act of worship whose parts are interconnected, whereas the latter are separate acts of worship, like Hajj, ʿumrah, prayer, and zakat. This is how Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz distinguished between ablution and other acts of worship.

He said: All of that belongs to Hajj: the sacrificial offerings, slaughtering, shaving the head, and circumambulation. Hajj is a single act of worship. Thus, according to the majority of scholars, whenever someone has intercourse before the first release from ihrām, his Hajj is invalidated. Is this release attained as with sacrifice alone, or as with sacrifice and shaving? There are two reported positions.

Another example is someone who forgets some verses of a surah during the Ramadan night prayers. He need not repeat them or what follows them, even though, were he deliberately to reverse the order of a surah’s verses

---

## Page 10816

and recite its later verses before its earlier ones, this would be impermissible by consensus. The disagreement concerns only the order of the surahs. Ahmad stated this explicitly and related the practice of the people of Mecca. He was asked: “If the imam omits verses from a surah during Ramadan, do you think someone praying behind him should recite them?” He replied: “Yes, he should do so. In Mecca, they used to appoint a man to record whatever the imam omitted, whether letters or other portions. Then, on the night when the recitation of the Quran was completed, he would recite what had been omitted.”

Scholars of the school, such as Abū Muhammad, said: “He recommended this only so that the recitation of the entire Quran would be complete and the reward attained in full.”

Thus, the people of Mecca, Ahmad, and his followers considered that reciting only the forgotten verses completes the recitation of the Quran and its reward, even though the order has been disrupted here, since the surah had not been recited in full. A similar practice is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: he forgot a verse from a surah, then recited it partway through his recitation and returned to where he had left off. No one realized that he had forgotten anything except those who had memorized it.

Likewise, someone who forgets to wash a limb, or part of it, should wash only that part, without washing the subsequent parts again, which would mean washing them twice. There is no need for this.

This distinction accords with what has been transmitted from the Companions and the majority of scholars. For the Companions and others acted in this way, as Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAlī, Makhūl, al-Nakhaʿī,

---

## Page 10817

al-Zuhrī, and al-Awzāʿī concerning someone who forgot to wipe his head, then found moisture in his beard and used it to wipe his head: they did not instruct him to wash his feet again. Ibn al-Mundhir also adopted this view.

It has been reported from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd: “I do not mind which of my limbs I begin with.” Ahmad said: “What was meant was only beginning with the left before the right, since both are addressed together in the Quran.”

Ahmad then said: Jarīr narrated to me, from Qābūs, from his father:

“ʿAlī was asked: ‘One of us is in a hurry and washes one part before another. May he do so?’ He replied: ‘No; he must do it as Allah Most High has commanded.’”

This report that Ahmad related from ʿAlī indicates that observing the prescribed order is obligatory. What Ibn al-Mundhir related concerning forgetfulness indicates that this requirement is waived in cases of forgetfulness and that only the omitted act needs to be performed. This shows that the distinction was ʿAlī’s position, may Allah be pleased with him.

Those who dispensed with the requirement altogether cited the report that Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “There is nothing wrong with beginning with your feet before your hands.” However, Ahmad and others said: “We know of no basis for this.” They also transmitted reports supporting the obligation of observing the prescribed order

---

## Page 10818

from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAtāʾ, and al-Hasan. These were leading scholars of the Successor generation. The case of forgetfulness is certainly included. Thus, it is clear that this was the view of most, if not all, of the early generations.

What is objectionable is deliberately performing ablution out of its prescribed order. There is no doubt that this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Quran and the mass-transmitted Sunnah. Had this been permissible, it would have occurred on occasion, or its permissibility would have been made clear—as with the order of the words of remembrance, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best words after the Quran are four, and they are also found in the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest. It does not matter which of them you begin with.”

Further support for this, both in scriptural evidence and in the positions of the legal schools, is that whoever forgets a prayer must perform it upon remembering it, as explicitly stated in the text. Here, the requirement to observe the prescribed order is waived according to Ahmad’s school, without disagreement within it, and according to the school of Abū Hanīfah and others. It has, however, been related from Mālik that this requirement is not waived. Those taking this position drew an analogy with the prescribed order of purification.

---

## Page 10819

The Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it,”

explicitly establishes that he must perform it whenever he remembers it, and that nothing else is required of him.

The jurists of our school have accepted that the prescribed order of combined prayers is not waived through forgetfulness. Yet the general wording of the hadith indicates that it is waived. Thus, if the forgotten prayer was the first of the two combined prayers, he repeats that prayer alone, as the text requires. Whoever requires him to repeat the second has contradicted the text.

The same applies to others with valid excuses, such as a latecomer who joins the congregation during the second prayer: he performs it with them, then performs the first, just as when he catches only part of a prayer. Observing the prescribed order of his prayer in relation to its beginning is no more binding than observing the order of the latter part of a prayer in relation to its beginning. In such a case, the portion he has joined is discharged, and he makes up what he missed. This applies with even greater force to two separate prayers—especially since someone who catches only the tashahhud (seated testimony of faith) of the Maghrib prayer recites three tashahhuds, as in the well-known hadith of Ibn Masʿūd concerning the account of Masrūq and his narration.

This is a principle established by the revealed text and scholarly consensus, against which analogous cases are assessed: the requirement to observe the prescribed order is waived for the latecomer.

---

## Page 10820

In the early days of Islam, they did not observe this order: they would perform what they had missed and then pray with the imam. This, however, was abrogated. It is reported that Muʿādh was the first to adopt the new practice, whereupon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Muʿādh has established a practice for you, so follow him.”

The four imams agree that, in the two rakʿahs he makes up, he recites al-Fātihah and another surah. Likewise, if he joins the imam while the imam is prostrating, he prostrates with him, as established by the revealed text and the agreement of the imams. Thus, he has prostrated before standing in order to follow the imam, although this does not count toward a rakʿah. Yet doing this deliberately would not be permissible: if he were to pronounce the opening takbīr, prostrate, and then stand, his prayer would not be valid.

This nevertheless serves as evidence that the prescribed order must be observed within a single rakʿah. Even if, after the salām, he were to add a bow alone to that prostration, the two would not constitute a rakʿah. Rather, he must perform a rakʿah, with two prostrations following the bow, because he failed to observe the prescribed order and continuity.

Likewise, if he forgets to bow until he has recited the tashahhud and given the salām, there are two views within the school as to whether his prayer becomes invalid. The expressly stated position is that, if the interruption has not been lengthy, he builds upon what he has already performed. This is also the view of al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, and others.

A group of scholars held that the requirements of continuity and the prescribed order in prayer are waived

---

## Page 10821

in cases of forgetfulness. Thus, Makhūl and Muhammad ibn Aslam said concerning someone who forgets a prostration or a rakʿah: “He performs it whenever he remembers it and prostrates for forgetfulness.” Al-Awzāʿī said concerning a man who forgot a prostration in the Zuhr prayer and remembered it during the ʿAsr prayer: “He continues his prayer, then prostrates when he has finished.”

This view is supported by the hadiths concerning the prostrations of forgetfulness, which indicate that he completes the prayer and then prostrates for forgetfulness, even after a lengthy interruption.

As for someone who joins the prayer late, the prostration he performed with the imam was for the purpose of following the imam. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Abū Bakrah:

“May Allah increase your eagerness, but do not do that again.”

He is able to perform the rakʿah after the salām, so he has no excuse until … (1)

If he forgets an essential element of the first rakʿah and has already begun the second, there are two views concerning this. Mālik and Ahmad do not accept combining parts of the two rakʿahs. Rather, the rakʿah whose essential element was forgotten is disregarded, and the present one takes its place. There is disagreement, however, over whether this occurs upon beginning the recitation or upon bowing.

Al-Shāfiʿī says: Whatever he performed after the omitted bow is disregarded because he performed it out of its proper place—not that he performs its counterpart in the second rakʿah, so that it completes the first

## Page 10822

just as when he ends the prayer with the salām and then remembers, in which case the salām is disregarded.

Ahmad and Mālik say: He intended what he performed to belong to the second rakʿah, not the first. Once he has recited or bowed in the second rakʿah, he can count it as the first, since the requirement to maintain the order of the rakʿahs is waived when there is a valid excuse. There is therefore no reason to invalidate this rakʿah. His action would be out of its proper place only if this rakʿah were treated as the second; if it is treated as the first, he has performed the action in its proper place.

If it is said that he had already intended the second rakʿah and intended his prostration in it to belong to the second, then preserving the order within the parts of a single rakʿah—by not assigning some of its parts to another rakʿah—takes precedence over preserving the order between the two rakʿahs. Treating the first as the second is permissible when there is a valid excuse, as in the case of someone who joins the prayer late. But treating the prostration of the second rakʿah as completing the first has no parallel in the revealed law. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that the requirement to observe the prescribed order in ablution is waived because of forgetfulness, as is the requirement of continuity, according to Mālik’s view. The same applies to excuses other than forgetfulness, such as the water being far away, as reported from Ibn ʿUmar. If an interruption in the prayer itself is permissible because of a valid excuse, then this applies all the more to ablution. This is evidenced by the prayer in circumstances of fear described in Ibn ʿUmar’s hadith, and by the hadiths concerning the prostrations of forgetfulness.

---

## Page 10823

As for the hadith about the man who had an unwashed patch on the top of his foot, something like this would not be forgotten. This indicates that he left it unwashed through negligence.

Continuity is not obligatory when bathing to remove major ritual impurity, because of the hadith stating that he

“saw a spot on his body that water had not reached, so he squeezed water from his hair onto it.”

Our fellow jurists distinguish between this and ablution: since a prescribed order is not obligatory in ritual bathing, neither is continuity. Mālik, however, requires continuity in ablution even though he does not require a prescribed order.

In ritual bathing, the body is treated as a single part, and there is unanimous agreement that no prescribed order applies within a single body part. Deliberately interrupting ritual bathing is therefore like deliberately interrupting the washing of a single body part. Nevertheless, a distinction has been drawn between the two: bathing to remove major ritual impurity is like removing physical impurity, in that the purifying effect of the water does not extend beyond the area it touches. Ablution, by contrast, purifies the entire body, although only four body parts are washed. This, however, is open to question.

If someone in a state of major ritual impurity finds some, but not all, of the water he needs, he uses it. As for someone performing ablution, our fellow jurists hold two views. Those who permit this allow ablution to be performed in separate stages when there is a valid excuse, and hold that washing some parts achieves partial purification.

The same applies to someone who has wiped over his leather socks and then removes them: may he merely wipe his feet, or must he repeat his ablution? There are two views, transmitted in two reports.

It has been said that the basis for this disagreement is continuity. It has also been said that the basis is that

---

## Page 10824

ablution is not invalidated. Thus, if ritual impurity returns to a man, it returns to all his limbs. Whether this applies when there is a valid excuse is disputed, as noted above.

A prescribed order may also be a condition that is not waived through ignorance or forgetfulness, as in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever slaughters before the prayer has merely slaughtered a sheep for meat.”

For the Eid sacrifice to be valid, the prayer must therefore precede its slaughter. Abū Burdah ibn Niyār, may Allah be pleased with him, was unaware of this, yet the Prophet did not excuse his ignorance; rather, he instructed him to slaughter another animal.

This contrasts with those who, during Hajj, slaughtered before throwing the pebbles, or shaved their heads before performing the preceding rites. To them he said:

“Do so; there is no blame.”

These are two rulings established by the Sunnah: an Eid sacrifice slaughtered before the prayer is not valid, whereas a pilgrimage offering slaughtered before throwing the pebbles out of ignorance is valid. The difference between them—and Allah knows best—is that the pilgrimage offering had become a ritual offering through being driven to the Sacred Precinct, garlanded, and marked with an incision. It had thus reached its appointed place and time. If its slaughter was brought forward out of ignorance, it did not cease to be a pilgrimage offering.

The Eid sacrifice, however, is indistinguishable before the prayer from a sheep slaughtered for meat. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever slaughters before the prayer has merely slaughtered a sheep for meat, which he has provided for his family.”

It becomes a ritual sacrifice only after the prayer, as Allah Most High says:

“So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.”

And He says:

“Indeed, my prayer and my sacrifice”

Performing it before this time is therefore like performing a prayer before its appointed time.

---

## Page 10825

This, then, is the time for the Eid sacrifice: it begins after the prayer has been performed, as the Messenger explained in authentic hadiths. This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others. Only al-Shāfiʿī and those of Ahmad’s followers who agreed with him, such as al-Khiraqī, reckoned its beginning by the time needed to perform the prayer.

According to one of the two views concerning the Eid sacrifice, it is a condition that one slaughter after the imam has slaughtered. This is Mālik’s position and one of the two views within Ahmad’s school, as reported by Abū Bakr. Its proof is Jābir’s hadith in the Sahīh. It has also been said that Allah’s words:

“Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger”

were revealed concerning this matter. Likewise, there are two views within Ahmad’s school concerning departure from ʿArafah before the imam, one being that a sacrificial offering is required. Those who require it regard this as comparable to the obligation of someone praying behind an imam to follow him in prayer.

Section

The explicit statement he cited concerning reciting what one has forgotten indicates that the requirement to follow the prescribed order in recitation is waived in cases of forgetfulness. Ahmad and his followers have stated that al-Fātihah must be recited without interruption. Concerning someone who interrupts it because of forgetfulness, they say—the wording is Abū Muhammad’s—“If that—that is, the interruption—is prolonged, he must begin its recitation anew, unless the silence is

---

## Page 10826

required, as when someone praying behind an imam begins reciting al-Fātihah, then hears the imam’s recitation and falls silent to listen. When the imam pauses, he completes his recitation, and it suffices. Ahmad indicated this. Likewise, if the silence is due to forgetfulness or afflictions, or to mistakenly switching to another passage, his recitation is not invalidated. When he remembers, he recites what remains of it. If, after remembering it, he persists in what he was doing, he invalidates his recitation and must begin it anew.”

He said: “If he brings forward a verse of it out of its proper place, he invalidates his recitation. If this was a mistake, he returns to the point of the error and completes it.”

Thus, they did not waive the prescribed order on account of an excuse, although they waived uninterrupted recitation, since the requirement of uninterrupted recitation is less stringent. If someone recites part of a surah today and another part tomorrow, that is permissible; but reciting its verses in reverse order is not. Regarding the prescribed order, a distinction is made between a self-contained passage that may properly be recited on its own and one that depends on another passage.

For example, if someone says:

“The path of those You have blessed,”

this does not convey a complete meaning unless he says:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed.”

But if he says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

and then says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,”

this does convey a complete meaning. Yet no one makes such an error: no one begins al-Fātihah in this way, whether deliberately or mistakenly. Rather, mistakes occur in passages whose meaning requires the prescribed order. This, then, distinguishes what they mentioned concerning something forgotten from al-Fātihah from something forgotten during a complete recitation of the Quran.

---

## Page 10827

Section

A further indication that the prescribed order is waived when observing it would require repetition through no negligence on the person’s part is that tayammum (dry ablution) is valid with a single strike of the hands on the ground. This is established by the authentic hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir—may Allah be pleased with them both—and is Ahmad’s position, without dispute. It is reported in both Sahīh collections through Abū Mūsā and through Ibn Abzā. In Ibn Abzā’s narration:

“Doing this would have sufficed you.” He struck the ground with his palms and blew on them, then wiped his face and hands with them.

Likewise, Muslim’s version of Abū Mūsā’s narration reads:

“Doing this would have sufficed you.” He struck the ground with his hands, shook them off, then wiped his face and hands.

Al-Bukhārī’s version reads:

“And he wiped his face and hands once.”

The jurists of the school differed over how this is to be done. One view is that he observes the prescribed order, wiping his face with the inner surfaces of his fingers and the backs of his hands with his palms. Another view is that this is not obligatory; rather, he wipes his face and the backs of his hands with both hands.

---

## Page 10828

On either view, he does not postpone wiping his palms until after wiping his face. Rather, he wipes them either before his face or while wiping his face and the backs of his hands. Hence Ibn ʿAqīl said:

“I find that tayammum with a single strike dispenses with an order required in ablution: the face is wiped after the inner surfaces of the hands.”

Both Sahīh collections record the hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, transmitted through Abū Mūsā—may Allah be pleased with them both:

“‘It is enough for you to do this with your hands.’ Then he struck the ground once with his hands, then passed his left hand over his right and wiped the backs of his hands and his face.”

Al-Bukhārī’s wording is:

“He struck the ground once with his palms, then shook them off. Then, using his hands, he wiped the back of his hand with his left—or the back of his left hand with his palm—then wiped his face with both hands.”

This explicitly shows that he did not wipe his palms after his face. There is no disagreement within Ahmad’s school that this is not obligatory.

As for the backs of the hands, al-Bukhārī’s narration explicitly states “that he passed his hand over the back of the hand before the face.” The words in the other narration, “and the backs of his hands,” indicate that he wiped the back of each hand with the palm of the other. That narration also says: “Then he passed his left hand over his right and wiped the backs of his hands before his face.”

Abū Muhammad said: “The obligation to wipe the palms is discharged by passing each one over the back of

---

## Page 10829

the other hand.” This, however, only discharges the obligation to wipe the palm itself. As for the inner surfaces of the fingers, according to his account, the obligation to wipe them is discharged when wiping the face.

In any event, dust reaches the inner surfaces of both hands when one strikes the ground with them and when one uses them to wipe the face and the backs of the hands. If one also wipes each hand with the other, this occurs three times. Were the prescribed order obligatory, one would have to wipe their inner surfaces after the face. This is not possible if one holds that a single strike suffices. Doing so would entail wiping them repeatedly. That requirement is therefore waived, for repetition is not prescribed in tayammum, unlike ablution. In ablution, even if one washes one’s hands at the outset and scoops up water with them for the face, one then washes them up to the elbows after washing the face, while also using them to scoop up water. Thus, they are washed repeatedly, because repetition is generally recommended in ablution, which is purification with water.

However, if one does not wash one’s hands after washing the face, the matter calls for consideration, since one scoops up water with them. The jurists have said: “If one intends to scoop up water, the water does not become used; if one intends to wash one’s hands in it, it becomes used; and if one has neither intention, there are two views.”

The correct view is that the water does not become used even if one intends to wash one’s hands in it, since this practice is established in the Sunnah. This implies that washing them with the intention of scooping up water does not purify them; rather, another washing is necessary.

---

## Page 10830

The stronger view, however, is that this is not obligatory. Rather, washing them with the intention of scooping up water suffices, without having to wash them again, as in tayammum. Moreover, one washes one’s forearms with one’s hands, thereby washing the inner surfaces of the hands.

It would also be reasonable to say that washing them at the outset and while washing the face remains sufficient to discharge the obligation regarding them, just as has been said of tayammum. For He says concerning ablution:

“Wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows,”

just as He says concerning tayammum:

“Wipe your faces and your hands with it.”

Thus, in the verse concerning ablution, He mentions the hands after the face.

However, the report found in al-Bukhārī alone makes clear that he wiped the backs of his hands before his face. The other reports are general in wording and imply that, when he performed the wiping, he did not wipe his palms after his face. The same therefore applies to the backs of his hands: rather, he wiped their backs together with their inner surfaces, since wiping the hands as a whole is closer to observing the prescribed order. Wiping the parts of a single limb together is preferable to wiping them separately.

Moreover, the palms would then be wiped together with the backs of the hands. Counting this wiping is preferable to counting their wiping along with the face. What some of our fellow jurists have stated—that one should use the fingers for the face and the inner surfaces of the palms for the backs of the hands—is contrary to what the hadiths describe.

---

## Page 10831

Nor is there anything in Ahmad’s words to support this. It is difficult, if not impossible, and is an innovation with no basis in Islamic law. The inner surfaces of the fingers can scarcely cover the whole face. They only resorted to this in order to reserve some dust for the backs of the hands after wiping the face.

They may be answered as follows:

Just as the palms need not be wiped after the face—a point on which there is no disagreement—the same applies to the backs of the hands. For even if they wipe the backs of the hands with the palms, using the inner surfaces of the fingers, the palms are wiped along with the face; wiping with the hands comes before wiping the face, as Ibn ‘Aqīl said.

For this reason, al-Majd preferred the view that observing the prescribed order is not obligatory in tayammum. Rather, the backs of the hands may be wiped before the face, as the authentic hadith indicates. The authentic hadith also indicates that the face and the backs of the hands are wiped with that same dust, and that wiping the backs of the hands with whatever dust remains on the hands suffices.

All the wordings of the hadith describe wiping the face with the hands and wiping one hand with the other. He did not reserve part of the inner surface of the hand for the face and another part for the hands. Rather, he used the inner surfaces of both hands to wipe his face and his hands, wiping one hand with the other.

Al-Qādī and those who agreed with him, following the jurists of al-Shāfi‘ī’s school, answered that when someone performs tayammum because of a wound on a limb, he must perform it at the point when that limb would have to be washed. He thus interrupts the stages of ablution with tayammum. This is an innovated practice involving immense harm and hardship that is not

---

## Page 10832

sanctioned by Islamic law. This and similar practices go too far in requiring a prescribed order where Allah and His Messenger have not required it. Those who deny that this order is obligatory allow it to be reversed without an excuse. The best course is the middle one, and Allah’s religion lies between excess and neglect. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Does tayammum take the place of ablution in the matters mentioned, or not?

He answered:

Tayammum takes the place of purification with water. Whatever otherwise prohibited acts become permissible through ritual bathing and ablution also become permissible through tayammum.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A man is in a state of major ritual impurity while in an orchard. He has only cold water available and fears that using it will harm him. The bathhouse is so far away that, by the time he reaches it and bathes, the prayer time will have ended. If he performs tayammum for his major ritual impurity, performs ablution, and prays within the prescribed time, must he repeat the prayer? Does he incur sin by doing so? Or does he incur sin if he performs tayammum? Does tayammum take the place of water, such that he may perform tayammum for a voluntary prayer and then offer an obligatory prayer with it, or offer two obligatory prayers at two different times with a single tayammum?

---

## Page 10833

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Every Muslim must offer the five daily prayers at their prescribed times. No one may ever delay a prayer beyond its time, whether with or without an excuse.

An excuse does, however, permit two things: omitting what one is unable to perform and combining two prayers. Whatever obligations of prayer a person is unable to fulfil cease to be binding upon him. Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And He Most High says:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

“We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

And in the verse concerning purification, He says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you,” to the end of the verse.

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

A sick person therefore prays as his condition allows, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

Whatever he cannot do—whether standing, sitting, or bowing and prostrating fully—is no longer required of him. He does whatever he can. If he can purify himself with water, he does so. If he cannot, because water is unavailable or because he fears harm from using it, he performs tayammum and prays. By scholarly consensus, he does not have to repeat the prayer because of his omission of standing or sitting. Likewise, by their consensus, he does not have to repeat the prayer if he prayed with tayammum. Even if there is impurity on his body

---

## Page 10834

that he cannot remove, he prays in that state and, according to most scholars, likewise need not repeat the prayer. If he can find only an impure garment, some scholars say that he should pray unclothed; others say that he should pray and then repeat the prayer; and others say that he should pray in the impure garment without repeating the prayer. This last view is the soundest scholarly opinion.

Likewise, a traveler who cannot use water prays with tayammum. Some say that the prayer must be repeated when one is not traveling; others say that it must be repeated when traveling; and others say that it need not be repeated either when traveling or when not traveling. This last view is the soundest scholarly opinion.

The correct scholarly view, then, is that anyone who has done what he was commanded to do to the best of his ability need not repeat the prayer. Only someone who has omitted an obligation that he is capable of fulfilling must repeat it, such as someone who omitted it through forgetfulness or sleep. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must pray it when he remembers it. There is no expiation for it other than that.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—also instructed someone who had performed ablution but left a small patch of his foot untouched by water to repeat both the ablution and the prayer.

As for what a person omits because he does not know it is obligatory—for example, someone who prayed without stillness, unaware that it was obligatory—the scholars have differed over whether he must repeat the prayer after its prescribed time has ended. There are two well-known opinions on this, both found within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The correct view is that such a person need not repeat the prayer, for it is authentically reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to the Bedouin who erred in

---

## Page 10835

his prayer:

“Go and pray, for you have not prayed”—twice or three times. The man said, “By Him who sent you with the truth, I cannot do any better than this, so teach me how to perform my prayer adequately.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then taught him to pray with stillness. He did not command him to repeat the prayers he had performed before that time, despite his saying, “By Him who sent you with the truth, I cannot do any better than this.” He did, however, command him to repeat that particular prayer, because its prescribed time had not yet ended, and he was therefore commanded to perform it within its time. As for the prayers whose prescribed times had ended, he did not command him to repeat them, even though he had omitted some of their obligatory elements, because he had not known that those elements were obligatory for him.

Likewise, he did not command ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—to make up the prayers he had omitted because of major ritual impurity, since he had not known that it was permissible to pray with tayammum.

Similarly, the woman suffering from irregular vaginal bleeding said to him, “I suffer severe, abnormal bleeding that prevents me from fasting and praying.” He commanded her to perform ablution for each prayer, but did not command her to make up what she had omitted.

Likewise, those who ate during Ramadan until they could distinguish white cords from black cords ate after dawn had broken, yet he did not command them to repeat their fasts. These people had been unaware of what was obligatory, so he did not command them to make up what they had omitted while in a state of

---

## Page 10836

ignorance, just as a disbeliever is not commanded to make up what he omitted during his unbelief and pre-Islamic ignorance. This differs from someone who knew that an act was obligatory but omitted it out of forgetfulness: he commanded such a person to perform it upon remembering.

He likewise commanded the sleeper to pray upon awakening, for while asleep he was not commanded to pray. Thus, according to the majority of scholars—including al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and Mālik according to one of the two reports from him—someone who awakens shortly before sunrise performs ablution and takes a full ritual bath, even if the sun rises in the meantime.

This differs from someone who is awake with ample time remaining—for example, someone who has been sleeping in an orchard or village where the water is harmfully cold, and the bathhouse is so far away that going there would cause the prayer’s prescribed time to expire. He must perform tayammum and pray within the prescribed time, rather than delay the prayer until its time has ended.

The same applies if he is in a city but cannot enter the bathhouse because it has not yet opened, is too far away, or he lacks the money to pay the bathhouse attendant, or for some similar reason. He must pray after performing tayammum, since praying with tayammum is obligatory when one cannot use water, either because it is unavailable or because one fears harm from using it. None of these people is required to repeat the prayer. In many situations involving harm, Muslims agree that no repetition is required, as in the case of the sick and the traveller. Scholars have differed concerning some kinds of harm. The correct view is that no one who prays to the best of his ability, as commanded, is required to repeat the prayer.

---

## Page 10837

Among the disputed cases, then, are those of someone who has no water while not travelling, and someone who performs tayammum for fear of the cold. The same applies to anyone else who omits an obligatory act because of an uncommon excuse that does not persist. According to al-Shāfi‘ī and one of the two reports from Ahmad, such a person must repeat the prayer. According to Mālik, most scholars, and the other report from Ahmad, he need not repeat it. If someone lets the prayer’s prescribed time expire by delaying a night prayer until daytime, or a daytime prayer until night, he thereby sins.

As the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in an authentic hadith:

“Whoever misses the ‘Asr prayer, it is as though he has been deprived of his family and wealth.”

Some scholars have permitted delaying prayer in certain circumstances, such as during sword combat. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah and one of the two reports from Ahmad. Most scholars, however, hold that prayer may not be delayed beyond its prescribed time under any circumstances. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad according to the apparent position of his school. Nevertheless, most scholars permit combining two prayers for a valid excuse, just as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) combined Zuhr and ‘Asr at ‘Arafah, and Maghrib and ‘Ishā’ at Muzdalifah. Combining prayers at these two places is established by mass-transmitted reports of the Sunnah and scholarly consensus.

Authentic reports also establish that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would combine prayers when pressing on with his journey, and that in Medina he prayed eight rak‘ahs together—Zuhr and ‘Asr—and seven—Maghrib and ‘Ishā’. His purpose was to spare his community hardship, in accordance with the words of Allah Most High:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

---

## Page 10838

For this reason, Imam Ahmad and other scholars, including a group of Mālik’s followers, held that two prayers may be combined when performing them separately entails hardship. Thus, a sick person may combine them; this is also the position of Mālik and a group of al-Shāfi‘ī’s followers. Combining Maghrib and ‘Ishā’ because of rain is permissible according to the majority, including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

Ahmad said: “He may combine prayers when he has a task to attend to.” Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā said: “If he has an excuse that permits him to miss Friday and congregational prayers, he may combine prayers.”

The position of the jurists of the Hijaz and the jurists of the hadith tradition—including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Thawr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others—is that combining two prayers is permissible in principle, but letting their prescribed times expire by delaying a daytime prayer until night or a night prayer until daytime is not permissible. A group of the jurists of Kufa, including Abū Hanīfah and others, hold that prayers may not be combined except at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah. They also hold that if a person is unable to perform a prayer within its prescribed time, he postpones it beyond that time.

The view of those who instruct people to combine two prayers without letting their prescribed time expire is stronger than that of those who instruct them to let the time expire rather than combine prayers. For the Quran and Sunnah indicate that Allah has commanded that prayer be performed at its prescribed time and that prayers be carefully observed. As Allah Most High says:

“Guard strictly your prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

This verse was revealed

---

## Page 10839

to abrogate the allowance for delaying prayer as on the day of the Trench. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Offer prayer at its prescribed time.”

The Quran and Sunnah indicate that there are “five” prayer times under normal circumstances, but “three” when there is a valid excuse. Thus, when someone with a valid excuse combines two prayers—Zuhr and ‘Asr, or Maghrib and ‘Ishā’—he has performed each prayer within its prescribed time, not after its time has expired. For this reason, according to most scholars, he need not specifically intend to combine prayers or to shorten them. This is the position of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and Ahmad in his well-known explicit statements, and it is the view preferred by Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz.

For this same reason, the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, hold that if a woman’s menstruation ends near the end of the day, she must perform both Zuhr and ‘Asr; and if it ends near the end of the night, she must perform both Maghrib and ‘Ishā’. This has been transmitted from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf, Abū Hurayrah, and Ibn ‘Abbās. This is because the two prayers share a common time when there is a valid excuse. Thus, if her menstruation ends near the end of the day, the time for Zuhr still remains, so she performs it before ‘Asr. If her menstruation ends near the end of the night, the time for Maghrib still remains in circumstances involving a valid excuse, so she performs it before ‘Ishā’. For this reason, Allah sometimes mentions five prayer times and sometimes three

---

## Page 10840

as in His words:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night”—to the end of the verse. The latter refers to the time for Maghrib and ‘Ishā’.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Establish prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of the night, and the recitation at dawn.”

The sun’s decline means its passing the zenith, while the darkness of the night means the gathering of its darkness, which occurs after the twilight has disappeared. Allah thus commanded prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of night, prescribing Zuhr, ‘Asr, Maghrib, and ‘Ishā’ within that period. This indicates that the whole of this period is a time for prayer: from the sun’s decline until sunset is a time for prayer, and from sunset until the darkness of night is a time for prayer.

He also says:

“And the recitation at dawn.”

This is because Fajr is distinguished by its lengthy recitation. For this reason, it consists of two units of prayer both when resident and when travelling: it is neither shortened nor combined with another prayer. The lengthy recitation compensates for the smaller number of units.

Section

As for the view that dry ablution must be performed for each prayer and within each prayer’s time, and that an obligatory prayer may not be offered with dry ablution performed for a voluntary prayer, its reasoning is that dry ablution is a form of purification permitted out of necessity, and a ruling prescribed out of necessity is limited to the extent of that necessity. Thus, dry ablution may not be performed before the prayer time begins, nor does it remain valid after that time ends. It permits prayer but does not remove the state of ritual impurity. This is because, when a person becomes able to use water, he must use it without any new occurrence of ritual impurity. It is therefore clear that the state of ritual impurity had remained, and that permission to pray was granted only out of necessity.

---

## Page 10841

Thus, he is permitted to perform only what he intended. This is the well-known position in the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

Another view holds that dry ablution takes the place of water without qualification: it permits whatever purification with water permits. It may be performed before the prayer time begins, just as ablution with water may be performed beforehand, and it remains valid after that time ends, just as purification with water does. If someone performs dry ablution for a voluntary prayer, he may offer an obligatory prayer with it, just as someone who performs ablution with water for a voluntary prayer may offer an obligatory prayer with it. This is the view of many scholars, and it is the position of Abū Hanīfa and of Ahmad according to the second report from him.

Ahmad said, “This is what analogy dictates.” This view is correct and is supported by the Quran, the Sunnah, and sound reasoning, for Allah has made dry ablution a means of purification just as He has made water a means of purification. Allah Most High says:

“Then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High thus tells us that He intends to purify us with earth just as He purifies us with water.

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“We have been favoured over other people in five respects: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the spoils of war have been made lawful for us, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; and the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.” In another wording: “Whenever the time for prayer comes upon any man of my nation, he has his place of prayer and his means of purification at hand

---

## Page 10842

and each prophet was sent only to his own people, whereas I have been sent to all mankind.” In Sahīh Muslim, Hudhayfa reports that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“We have been favoured over other people in three respects: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the earth has been made a place of prayer for us; and its soil has been made a means of purification for us.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus made clear that Allah has made the earth a means of purification for his nation, just as He has made water a means of purification.

Abū Dharr reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a Muslim’s means of purification, even if he finds no water for ten years. But when you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

Al-Tirmidhī said, “This is a good and authentic hadith.” Thus, he stated that Allah has made clean earth a Muslim’s means of purification, even if he finds no water for ten years. Whoever says that earth does not purify a person from ritual impurity has therefore contradicted the Quran and the Sunnah. Since it purifies a person from ritual impurity, that impurity cannot remain when Allah has purified Muslims of it through dry ablution.

Dry ablution therefore removes ritual impurity and purifies the person who performs it. However, this removal is temporary, lasting until the person can use water. Since dry ablution substitutes for water, it purifies so long as water remains unavailable. Similarly, the finder of a lost article owns it so long as its owner has not come to him. Its possessor’s ownership is temporary, lasting until the owner appears, for he

---

## Page 10843
