stood in for its owner. When its owner comes, it passes out of the finder’s ownership and returns to its owner. What is established by a scriptural text or consensus does not require an analogous case against which to measure it. An analogous case is sought only for matters that we can know solely through analogy and comparison; these need to be assessed against a comparable case. As for what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed, we must follow what has been sent down to us from our Lord, without seeking an analogous case for it—although sound analogy does accord with the text. As Ahmad said, “Analogy requires treating earth like water.”

According to this correct view, a person may perform dry ablution before the prayer time begins if he wishes, and pray with it until he enters a state of ritual impurity or becomes able to use water. If he performs dry ablution for a voluntary prayer, he may use it for an obligatory prayer. He may also use a single dry ablution for two obligatory prayers and to make up missed prayers. Those who hold the other view have cited reports transmitted from some of the Companions, but these are weak and not established. Even if they were established, none would constitute proof.

If someone says, “This is purification allowed out of necessity, so its use must be limited to what is needed,” the reply is: “Yes, but a person needs to remain continually in a state of purity. He therefore purifies himself before the prayer time begins, for he needs an increase in reward.”

For this reason, Muslims agree that one may offer voluntary prayers with dry ablution. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed dry ablution to return a greeting while not travelling, and said:

“I disliked remembering Allah except in a state of purity.”

This shows that dry ablution is sometimes recommended and sometimes obligatory. That is, a person may perform dry ablution at a time when he is not obliged to do so, even though it is a prerequisite for prayer. And dry ablution

---

## Page 10844

before the prayer time begins is recommended, just as ablution before the prayer time begins is recommended. The soundest scholarly view is that one may perform dry ablution for any prayer one fears missing, such as the funeral prayer, the Eid prayer, and others. Praying with dry ablution is better than missing the prayer, just as offering voluntary prayer with dry ablution is better than missing it. Thus, someone who regularly offers prayers at night may perform dry ablution for them if he enters a state of major ritual impurity and the water is so cold that using it would harm him. Performing dry ablution and then offering voluntary prayers and reciting the Quran is better than missing these acts of worship.

As for the statement, “This ruling is restricted to necessity and must therefore be limited to what that necessity requires”: if this means that dry ablution is performed only when water cannot be used, that is accepted. But if it means that dry ablution is permissible only when it is obligatory, that is mistaken. This contradicts both the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims. Rather, dry ablution may be performed for obligatory acts and for recommended acts, such as voluntary prayer, recommended Quran recitation, and recommended touching of a copy of the Quran.

Allah has made it a means of purification for Muslims when water is unavailable. No one may therefore restrict for Muslims what Allah has made easy for them. He has intended to remove hardship from the Muslim community, so no one may introduce hardship into this matter, as some people have done, imposing well-known difficulties. Hence, the correct view is that dry ablution may be performed with a single strike for both the face and the hands.

---

## Page 10845

and no particular order is required. Rather, if he wipes his face with his palms, this suffices for both his face and his palms. He then wipes the backs of his hands, without needing to wipe his palms twice. This is what the Sunnah indicates. These issues are discussed in detail elsewhere. Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

If a man cannot find water, or cannot use it because of illness, or fears harm from severe cold or the like, may he perform dry ablution or not?

He replied:

Dry ablution is permissible when water is unavailable and when one fears becoming ill through using it, as Allah Most High indicated by mentioning the sick person and the person who cannot find water. Anyone whom water would harm by worsening his condition, because of a wound or illness, or who fears harm from the cold or the like, should perform dry ablution and pray, whether he is in a state of major or minor ritual impurity. If he may pray, he may also circumambulate the Kaaba, recite the Quran, touch a copy of the Quran, and remain in the mosque.

If he prays, he need not repeat the prayer, whether he is at home or travelling, according to the sounder of the two scholarly views. For the correct view is that anyone who does what he has been commanded to do to the best of his ability, without

---

## Page 10846

negligence or transgression on his part need not repeat the act, whether it is prayer, fasting, or Hajj. Allah has not required a person to perform the same prayer twice, fast two months in one year, or perform Hajj twice, unless there has been negligence or transgression on his part.

If he forgets a prayer, he must perform it when he remembers it. The same applies if he forgets any of its obligatory requirements, such as purification, bowing, or prostration.

If, however, he is unable to fulfil an obligation—for example, if he prays naked because he has nothing to cover himself with, prays without reciting because he cannot speak, or cannot bow and prostrate fully because of illness or the like—he need not repeat the prayer. There is no distinction between an unusual excuse and a common one, or between one that persists and one that does not. The Muslims agree that a traveller who cannot find water should pray after performing dry ablution and need not repeat the prayer, and that a naked person who cannot find anything to cover himself with should pray and need not repeat the prayer.

They also agree that a sick person should pray as his condition allows, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.”

He need not repeat the prayer.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A man wakes in a state of major ritual impurity and has no money to enter the bathhouse, nor can he bathe at home because of the cold. May he perform dry ablution and pray

---

## Page 10847

and recite the Quran, or not? If he does so, must he repeat the prayer, or not? If he has something he can pledge as security for the bathhouse fee, must he do so, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. A man may do so if he cannot find water or fears harm from using it, even if he is in a state of major ritual impurity. If he fears that bathing in cold water will harm him, and he cannot bathe in warm water at home, in a bathhouse, or elsewhere, he may perform dry ablution. According to the correct view, he need not repeat the prayer.

If he can enter the bathhouse for a fee, he must do so, provided he can afford the fee without substantial hardship, just as he must purchase water for purification. If he can leave the tābiya and the mīzāb as security with the bathhouse keeper and pay him within a day or thereabouts, he should do so. But if paying the bathhouse fee would cause harm, such as leaving him short of what he needs to support his dependants or repay his debts, he should pray after performing dry ablution. And Allah knows best.

He was also asked:

A man needed to perform a ritual bath, but at that time he did not have the money to enter the bathhouse, and he could not use cold water because it was so intensely cold. He therefore performed dry ablution and offered the obligatory prayer. He has an assigned duty at the congregational mosque, and he recited the Quran in fulfilment of it. Afterwards, he entered the bathhouse. Has he sinned, or not?

---

## Page 10848

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. He has not sinned by doing so; rather, he has done what he was commanded to do. If someone fears that using cold water will cause him a headache, a cold, or some other illness, and he cannot bathe in warm water, he should perform dry ablution—even if he is in a state of major ritual impurity—and pray. This is the view of the overwhelming majority of Muslim scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others.

Even if he regularly offers prayers at night and enters a state of major ritual impurity while the water is so cold that using it would harm him, he should perform dry ablution, offer his regular voluntary prayers, and recite the Quran both within and outside prayer. He should not miss his regular devotions because he is unable to bathe with water.

Must he repeat the obligatory prayer? There are two views:

The first is that he need not repeat it. This is the view of Mālik and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

The second is that he must repeat it. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and the other position reported from Ahmad. This applies when he is not travelling. As for a traveller, there is even stronger reason for him not to repeat it; this is one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two views.

Anyone permitted to pray after performing dry ablution is, with even greater reason, permitted to recite the Quran and remain in the mosque. The correct view is that he need not repeat the prayer, nor need anyone who has prayed according to

---

## Page 10849

his ability. This applies whether the major ritual impurity arose from something lawful or unlawful. However, someone who commits an unlawful act bears both major ritual impurity and the defilement of sin. If he repents and purifies himself with water, Allah loves him, for “Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves.”

If he purifies himself but does not repent, he has purified himself of major ritual impurity, but not of the defilement of sin, which only repentance can remove.

If he has nothing with which to pay the bathhouse keeper, he may undoubtedly perform dry ablution and pray. If he is not someone whom the bathhouse keeper allows time to pay, finds nothing to leave with him as security, and the keeper does not accept what he offers, must he enter on a deferred-payment basis? There are two views on this, both held within Ahmad’s school.

The more evident view is that, where this accords with the bathhouse keeper’s customary indication, he may bathe in the bathhouse as usual. If the bathhouse keeper prevents him from entering out of personal dislike or the like, although the keeper would suffer no harm and would receive his due, he may enter without the keeper’s consent and pay him his fee.

But if he does not have the fee, and the keeper refuses him entry because he has not paid what is due immediately and is not someone the keeper knows well enough to allow him time to pay, he may not enter without the keeper’s consent.

If the bathhouse keeper willingly allows him to take water in a vessel but does not willingly allow him to purify himself in the bathhouse entrance passages, he may do what the keeper willingly permits. He may not do what the keeper does not willingly permit unless he pays fair compensation.

He is only required to buy cold and hot water and pay the bathhouse keeper

---

## Page 10850

the admission fee if the water is offered at the usual price or at a surcharge of a kind people do not ordinarily accept in their dealings, provided he can afford it. If he needs that money for his own maintenance, that of his dependants, or repayment of a debt whose payment is being demanded, spending it on these necessities takes precedence over spending it on water. Likewise, if he needs the water for himself or his animals to drink, he should use it for that purpose and perform dry ablution. If the surcharge above the usual price does not substantially diminish his wealth, there are two views within the school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and among other scholars as to whether he must pay it. Most scholars hold that he is not obliged to do so. Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

He was asked:

A woman has intercourse with her husband but cannot enter the bathhouse because she lacks the admission fee or for some other reason. May she perform dry ablution? Is it disliked for her husband to have intercourse with her under these circumstances? Likewise, if the time for prayer begins when a woman has not yet performed the ritual bath, and she fears that entering the bathhouse will cause her to miss the prayer’s prescribed time, may she pray after performing dry ablution, or should she pray in the bathhouse?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If someone in a state of major ritual impurity, whether a man or a woman,

---

## Page 10851

has no water or fears harm from using it, then, if he cannot enter the bathhouse because he lacks the admission fee or for some other reason, he should pray after performing dry ablution. It is not disliked for a man to have intercourse with his wife in these circumstances. Rather, he may do so, just as he may have intercourse with her while travelling, with both then praying after performing dry ablution. If the man or woman can perform the ritual bath and then pray outside the bathhouse, they should do so.

If that is not possible—for example, if he does not wake at the beginning of dawn, and searching for water would cause the prescribed time to expire, or if finding firewood to heat the water or going to the bathhouse would cause him to miss the prescribed time—then, according to the majority of scholars, he should pray after performing dry ablution. However, some later scholars of the schools of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad said that he should set about obtaining the means of purification even if the prescribed time expires. They said the same about occupying himself with sewing clothing, learning the signs indicating the direction of prayer, and similar matters.

This view is mistaken. Its logical implication is that a traveller should delay prayer until after its prescribed time so that he can pray with ablution, and that a person without clothing should delay prayer until after its prescribed time so that he can pray clothed. This contradicts the consensus of the Muslims. Rather, a person must pray within the prescribed time as best he can, and whatever obligatory elements of prayer he is unable to fulfil are waived.

But if he wakes near the end of the prescribed time, or if he sets about drawing water from

---

## Page 10852

the well the prescribed time would expire, or if going to the bathhouse for the ritual bath would cause the prescribed time to expire, then, according to the majority of scholars, he should perform the ritual bath. Mālik—may Allah have mercy on him—says: Rather, he should pray after performing dry ablution, so as to observe the prescribed time.

The majority say: If he wakes near the end of the prescribed time, it is then that he becomes obliged to pray. Thus, in his case, purification and the prayer time are reckoned from the moment he wakes, and his allotted time is the period in which he can perform the prayer. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its time.”

For someone who is asleep, therefore, the time in which he is commanded to pray is when he wakes, not before that; and for someone who has forgotten, it is when he remembers. And Allah knows best.

As for a woman or man who can go to the bathhouse but, upon entering, cannot leave until the prescribed time has elapsed—whether because they are being compelled to remain, as in the case of a slave boy whose master will not let him leave to pray, or a woman accompanied by her children who cannot leave until she has washed them, or similar circumstances—such people must do one of the following: perform the ritual bath and pray inside the bathhouse within the prescribed time; pray outside the bathhouse after the prescribed time has elapsed; or pray outside the bathhouse after performing dry ablution.

Each of these views is upheld in the fatwas of a group of scholars. The stronger view, however, is that they should pray outside the bathhouse after performing dry ablution, because praying in the bathhouse is forbidden, while allowing the prescribed time to elapse without praying is an even graver matter. There is no way to avoid both of these prohibitions except by praying

---

## Page 10853

after performing dry ablution, within the prescribed time and outside the bathhouse. This is comparable to someone who, if he performs the ritual bath, can only pray in an impure place within the prescribed time or in a pure place after it has elapsed; alternatively, he can perform dry ablution and pray in a pure place within the prescribed time. This last option is preferable, because both of the other options are forbidden.

The jurists differed over whether someone confined in an impure place who prays there must repeat the prayer. There are two views, the sounder being that he need not repeat it. Indeed, the correct view, held by most scholars, is that anyone who has prayed within the prescribed time as commanded, to the best of his ability, need not repeat the prayer, whether his excuse is unusual or commonplace. Allah has not obliged a person to perform a particular prayer twice unless he has failed to fulfil an obligation or committed a forbidden act.

If, however, he has fulfilled his obligation to the best of his ability, Allah has not commanded him to do it twice. Nor has Allah commanded anyone to perform a prayer and then repeat it. Rather, whenever He commands someone to repeat a prayer, He had not commanded its initial performance in that manner. An example is someone who forgetfully prays without ablution: he was not commanded to perform that prayer as he did; his belief that he was commanded to do so was mistaken. Allah only commanded him to pray in a state of ritual purity. Thus, if he prays without ritual purification, he must repeat the prayer, just as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the man who performed ablution but left a fingernail-sized area of his foot untouched by water to repeat both his ablution and his prayer. Likewise, he commanded the man who prayed incorrectly to repeat his prayer. And likewise, he commanded

---

## Page 10854

the man praying alone behind the row to repeat his prayer. As for someone unable to attain ritual purity, cover himself as required, face the qiblah, avoid impurity, bow and prostrate fully, or recite al-Fātihah—and others unable to fulfil some of the prayer’s obligations—he does what he can and need not repeat the prayer. As Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

He was asked:

If a woman lives far from the bathhouse, enters a state of major ritual impurity, and fears the cold if she bathes at home, may she perform dry ablution and pray? If her husband wishes to have intercourse and she fears the cold for both him and herself, may he perform dry ablution? Or should he bathe if he is able, while she performs dry ablution? Or should he refrain from intercourse?

If he has intercourse with her and she wishes to go to the bathhouse to purify herself, should she perform dry ablution and combine the two prayers, or pray in the bathhouse after performing the ritual bath?

If her menstruation has ended but she has not performed the ritual bath, may she perform dry ablution and have intercourse with her husband, or not? Does dry ablution for major ritual impurity require ablution

---

## Page 10855

or not? If it does, should ablution come before dry ablution, or vice versa? Must dry ablution be performed anew for every prayer, or may several prayers be offered with a single dry ablution?

If a woman’s menstruation ends toward the end of the day—or the night—and she is unable to perform the ritual bath because of the cold or some other reason, should she perform dry ablution and pray? Must she make up the prayers of the day—or night—in which her menstruation ended?

If someone sustains a wound or fracture and bandages it, should he wipe over the bandage, or should the injured person perform dry ablution instead of ablution with water? He may be unable to let water flow over some limbs because of the wound or fracture. Should he refrain from intercourse in this condition, or may he have intercourse and perform dry ablution, even if he knows that treatment will take a long time and he will therefore continue performing dry ablution for a prolonged period? May a woman likewise refuse her husband intercourse if she is unable to perform the ritual bath, or should she comply with his wishes and perform dry ablution?

If someone finds that the bathhouse is so far away that the prayer time will have elapsed by the time he reaches it, should he perform dry ablution, or go there even if the prayer time elapses? If someone fears missing the congregational prayer if he purifies himself with water, may he perform dry ablution in order to join the congregation, or not?

If someone is with companions who wish to combine prayers, is it better for him to combine prayers with them so as to pray in congregation, or to pray alone at the prescribed time? He may himself be their imam: which is better for him—combining prayers, or praying alone at the prescribed time for each prayer?

If someone practises a trade alongside other craftsmen, and praying at the prescribed time causes him hardship and leaves the other craftsmen idle, may he combine the two prayers? Likewise, if someone is engaged in ploughing and cultivation and finds it difficult to seek water, may he perform dry ablution and pray?

And someone who performs dry ablution—

---

## Page 10856

may he recite the Quran outside prayer and offer his customary night prayers? May a woman who is in a state of major ritual impurity or menstruating recite over her young child? If someone cannot find earth, may he perform dry ablution using a carpet or mat if there is dust on it?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

Anyone who enters a state of major ritual impurity through a wet dream or intercourse, whether lawful or unlawful, must perform the ritual bath and pray. If bathing is impossible because water is unavailable or using it would cause harm—for example, he is ill and bathing would aggravate his illness, or the weather is cold and he fears that bathing would cause a headache, a cold, or catarrh—then he should perform dry ablution and pray. This applies to men and women alike. One must not delay prayer beyond its prescribed time.

A woman may not refuse her husband intercourse; rather, he may have intercourse with her. If she can perform the ritual bath, she must do so; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution. The same applies to the man: if he can perform the ritual bath, he must do so; otherwise, he should perform dry ablution. He may have intercourse with her before entering the bathhouse. If she can bathe and pray outside the bathhouse, she should do so. If she fears missing the prayer, she should screen herself from view in the bathhouse and pray, without letting the prayer time elapse.

Combining two prayers with complete purification using water is better than offering them separately with dry ablution. Likewise, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—instructed the woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to combine two prayers with a single ritual bath, and this was deemed better than offering them separately with ablution.

---

## Page 10857

Moreover, combining two prayers is prescribed to meet a worldly need, so it is all the more appropriate when it serves to perfect the prayer. One who combines two prayers is praying within the prescribed time. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—combined the noon and afternoon prayers at Arafah during the time of the noon prayer, so that his standing at Arafah would be complete and uninterrupted. Otherwise, he could have dismounted to pray. Since he combined the two prayers to perfect the standing at Arafah, combining them to perfect the prayer is all the more appropriate.

He also combined prayers in Medina because of rain, although he himself—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was not harmed by the rain. Rather, the prayers were combined to enable people to pray in congregation. Combining prayers to secure congregational prayer is better than offering them separately and alone. Combining two prayers is also better than praying in a bathhouse, for the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—forbade prayer in camel pens and bathhouses, whereas combining prayers is prescribed.

Indeed, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its time.”

Yet when he slept through the prayer, he moved elsewhere, saying:

“This is a valley in which Satan was present with us.”

Thus, he delayed the prayer beyond the time at which he had been commanded to offer it because Satan had been present in that place. Prayer in such a place is disliked but permissible; nevertheless, moving elsewhere is recommended. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others explicitly stated this.

Bathhouses and camel pens are dwelling places of devils; hence, he prohibited prayer there. Combining prayers, however, is prescribed when it serves an overriding benefit. Thus, if someone combines the prayers to avoid praying in the haunts of

---

## Page 10858

devils, he has done well. If a woman cannot combine the prayers after purifying herself with water, she should combine them after performing dry ablution. Praying with dry ablution within the prescribed time is better than offering the prayers separately or praying in places where prayer is prohibited. If a man or woman can perform both ablution with water and dry ablution, they should do so. If they perform dry ablution alone, however, it suffices according to one of the two opinions transmitted from the scholars.

The position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik is that purification with water and dry ablution—the original means and its substitute—are not combined; rather, one uses either one or the other. The position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, however, is that one should wash as much of the body with water as possible and perform dry ablution for the remainder. When performing both ablution with water and dry ablution, either may come first, though beginning with ablution with water is better.

According to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions, one may offer several prayers with a single dry ablution, just as one may do so with a single ablution with water or a single ritual bath. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him, based on the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. When you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

When a woman’s menstruation ends, she should take a ritual bath if she can; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution and pray. If her menstruation ends in the latter part of the day, she should offer the noon and afternoon prayers. If it ends in the latter part of the night, she should offer the sunset and night prayers. No one is required to repeat prayers offered with dry ablution.

If a wound is uncovered and can be wiped with water, doing so is better than dry ablution.

---

## Page 10859

And likewise, if the wound is bandaged, or a bone is broken and a splint has been placed over it, wiping over it with water is better than dry ablution. If someone who is ill, wounded, or suffering from a broken bone enters a state of major ritual impurity through intercourse or otherwise, and water would harm him, he should perform dry ablution and pray. Alternatively, he should wipe over the splint and wash the rest of his body, if he can, and pray.

A woman may not refuse her husband intercourse; rather, he may have intercourse with her. If she can take a ritual bath, she should do so; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution and pray. When her menstruation ends, he must not have intercourse with her until she has taken a ritual bath. If she cannot do so, she should perform dry ablution, and her husband may then have intercourse with her. The man who has intercourse should perform dry ablution in the same circumstances in which he would do so for prayer.

If the time for prayer begins—for example, at dawn—and taking a ritual bath would prevent him from praying until after sunrise because the water is far away, the bathhouse is closed, or he is poor and cannot afford the bathhouse fee, he should perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time. He must not delay the prayer until its time has passed.

If, however, he wakes up with insufficient time remaining to take a ritual bath, and water is available, then according to most scholars he should bathe and pray after sunrise. For him, the prayer time begins when he wakes up, unlike someone who is already awake, for whom it begins at dawn.

Prayer must be offered within its prescribed time. No one whatsoever may delay it beyond that time, whether with an excuse or without one. Rather, one must pray within the prescribed time to the best of one’s ability.

---

## Page 10860

so a sick person should pray within the prescribed time as his condition permits, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Imrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

He should therefore pray sitting within the prescribed time, rather than standing after it has ended. Likewise, those without clothing, such as people who have been shipwrecked, should pray unclothed within the prescribed time, rather than delay the prayer until after its time so that they can pray clothed.

Similarly, someone who is unsure of the direction of prayer should pray within the prescribed time, using his own judgment or following another’s judgment. He must not delay the prayer until after its time so that he can pray with certainty about the direction. Someone with an impurity on his body or clothing that he cannot remove before the prayer time ends should pray with it within the prescribed time. He must not let the prayer time pass so that he can pray free of impurity.

Likewise, someone confined in an impure place, a bathhouse, or any other place where prayer is forbidden, who cannot leave before the prayer time ends, must pray there within the prescribed time. He must not let the prayer time pass so that he can pray elsewhere.

Offering prayer within its prescribed time is obligatory to the extent that circumstances and one’s ability permit, even if the prayer falls short of its complete form. Even someone in danger must offer the prayer of fear within the prescribed time as best he can. He must not let its time pass so that he can pray in safety afterward. Even during combat, he must pray while fighting, rather than let the prayer time pass so that he can pray without fighting. An obligatory prayer offered within its prescribed time, even if deficient, is better than letting its time pass and then offering it, even in its complete form;

---

## Page 10861

indeed, a prayer offered after deliberately letting its time lapse is not accepted from the person who offers it, nor is he absolved of the sin of unlawfully letting its time lapse, even if he makes it up. On this the Muslims are agreed.

Section

If someone fears missing the funeral prayer, the Eid prayer, or the Friday prayer, there is disagreement over whether he may perform dry ablution. The more evident view is that he should offer the prayer with dry ablution rather than miss it. Likewise, if he can offer the obligatory congregational prayer only with dry ablution, he should do so.

According to one of the two reports from Ahmad, dry ablution is permissible for the funeral prayer, although his position consistently allows repeating that prayer after performing ablution with water. Thus, in his school, the underlying reason is not the impossibility of repeating the prayer. Abū Hanīfah, by contrast, based this permission specifically on the impossibility of repeating it, and distinguished between the funeral prayer and the Eid and Friday prayers. Ahmad does not base his ruling on that reason. How could he, when the Friday prayer is not repeated, but the noon prayer is offered instead? The noon prayer is not equivalent to the Friday prayer. Likewise, if someone can offer the obligatory Friday prayer only with dry ablution, he should do so.

Where combining two prayers is prescribed, the prayer is offered within its time; this does not amount to letting its time lapse. According to most scholars, an intention to shorten or combine prayers is not required. This is the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfah, and one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school. Indeed, Ahmad’s own words indicate this, and it is the position explicitly reported from him.

---

## Page 10862

The other view is adopted by some of Ahmad’s followers and is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

Combining two prayers is permissible for a valid excuse. Thus, a traveller pressing on with his journey may combine the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers. If travellers are overcome by drowsiness and find it difficult to wait for the night prayer, they may combine it with the sunset prayer. Even if the imam himself stays awake, it is better for him to lead them in the two prayers combined than to pray alone without combining them.

If a farmer fears that seeking water will expose his property to theft or interrupt work that he needs to do, he should pray with dry ablution. If he can combine the two prayers with ablution using water, that is better than offering them separately. The same applies to all others whose valid excuses permit them to perform dry ablution: if they can combine the two prayers after purifying themselves with water, that is better than offering them separately with dry ablution.

For those with an excuse such as rain or a strong, cold wind, as well as those suffering from urinary incontinence and women experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, offering the two prayers combined in a state of complete purification is better than offering them separately in a state of incomplete purification.

A sick person may also combine two prayers, especially when combining them allows him to pray more fully, whether through complete purification or through being able to stand. Even if the two prayers would be the same either way, he may combine them if offering them separately would worsen his illness.

---

## Page 10863

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Combining prayers is permissible because of an occupation.” Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā explained: “An occupation that excuses a person from attending Friday and congregational prayers.”

Shaykh Muwaffaq al-Dīn ibn Qudāma al-Maqdisī clarified who these people are: “They include a sick person; someone who fears that a relative may die; someone resisting the urge to urinate or defecate; someone whose food has been served and who needs to eat; someone who fears being seized by a ruler, or pursued by a creditor when he has nothing with which to pay him; a traveller who fears missing his caravan; someone who fears harm to his property or hopes to find it; someone who fears being overcome by drowsiness and thus missing the prayer time; and someone who fears severe cold. The same applies on a dark night when there is mud. Such people are excused even if they miss Friday and congregational prayers.” This is how Ibn Qudāma related it in his *Mukhtasar al-Hidāya*. They may therefore combine the two prayers in accordance with the statements of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā.

If craftsmen and farmers find it difficult to pray within the time allotted to each prayer—for example, because water is far away when they need to pray, and going to it and purifying themselves would interrupt work they need to do—they may pray during the shared time, combining the two prayers. Better still, they should delay the noon prayer until close to the afternoon prayer, combining it with the afternoon prayer and offering them together, even if this means combining them at the end of the noon prayer’s time and the beginning of the afternoon prayer’s time. When water is far away, it is also permissible to perform dry ablution and pray within the time allotted to each prayer. Combining the prayers with purification using water, however, is better. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

---

## Page 10864

Section

Anyone permitted to pray after dry ablution, whether in a state of major or minor ritual impurity, may also recite the Quran outside prayer, touch a copy of the Quran, offer voluntary and obligatory prayers after dry ablution, recite the Quran for healing and protection, and so forth. Prayer is greater than recitation, so anyone who may pray after dry ablution may all the more readily recite after it. The rules governing recitation outside prayer are less restrictive than those governing recitation within prayer, since someone in a state of minor ritual impurity may recite outside prayer.

Whatever one may do after purification with water, whether through ablution or a full ritual bath, one may also do after dry ablution when water is unavailable or one fears harm from using it. If someone in a state of major ritual impurity can perform ablution but cannot take a ritual bath, he may perform ablution and substitute dry ablution for the bath. If he performs dry ablution without performing ablution, there are two views:

One holds that this suffices in place of the ritual bath. This is the view of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa.

The other holds that it does not suffice. This is the view of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

It is permissible to perform dry ablution using the earth beneath a mat in one’s home. Likewise, if dust clings to an object, it is permissible to perform dry ablution using that adhering dust.

As for recitation of the Quran by someone in a state of major ritual impurity or by a menstruating woman, the scholars hold three views:

---

## Page 10865

One view holds that it is permissible for both. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and the well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

Another view holds that it is not permissible for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, but is permissible for a menstruating woman, either without restriction or when she fears forgetting what she has memorized. This is Mālik’s position, and a view within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere.

Regarding a menstruating woman’s recitation of the Quran, nothing has been established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, apart from the hadith narrated by Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh, from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar:

“Neither a menstruating woman nor someone in a state of major ritual impurity should recite anything from the Quran.”

It was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others. This hadith is weak by agreement of the scholars versed in hadith. The hadiths Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh narrates from transmitters of the Hijaz are weak, unlike his narrations from Syrian transmitters. No trustworthy transmitter narrated this from Nāfiʿ.

It is well known that women menstruated during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, yet he did not prohibit them from reciting the Quran, just as he did not prohibit them from remembering Allah and supplicating. Rather, he instructed menstruating women to come out on Eid and join the Muslims in proclaiming Allah’s greatness.

He also instructed a menstruating woman to perform all the pilgrimage rites except circumambulation of the House: she recites the talbiya while menstruating, and likewise at Muzdalifa, Minā, and the other pilgrimage sites.

As for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, he did not command him to attend Eid, to pray, or to perform any of the pilgrimage rites, because such a person can purify himself and therefore has no excuse for

---

## Page 10866

neglecting purification. A menstruating woman, by contrast, remains in a state of ritual impurity and cannot purify herself while it persists. For this reason, the scholars have stated that someone in a state of major ritual impurity may not stay at ʿArafa, Muzdalifa, or Minā until he has purified himself, even though ritual purity is not a condition for doing so.

The point, however, is that the Lawgiver has instructed menstruating women, whether by way of obligation or recommendation, to remember Allah and supplicate to Him, whereas this is disliked for someone in a state of major ritual impurity. It is therefore clear that, because of her excuse, a menstruating woman is granted concessions that are not granted to someone in a state of major ritual impurity, even if her waiting period is more stringent. The same applies to reciting the Quran: the Lawgiver did not prohibit her from doing so, even if it is said that he prohibited someone in a state of major ritual impurity.

For someone in a state of major ritual impurity can purify himself and recite, unlike a menstruating woman, who remains menstruating for days. Preventing her from reciting the Quran would deprive her of an act of worship she needs while she is unable to purify herself. Recitation is not like prayer: prayer requires purification from both major and minor ritual impurity, whereas recitation is permissible in a state of minor ritual impurity, as established by the revealed texts and the agreement of the imams. Prayer also requires facing the qibla, wearing clothing, and avoiding physical impurity, whereas recitation requires none of these. Indeed:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would rest his head in the lap of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, while she was menstruating.”

This is an authentic hadith. In Sahīh Muslim it is also reported:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the Prophet

---

## Page 10867

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘I am sending down to you a Book that water cannot wash away; you will recite it asleep and awake.’” Thus, recitation is permissible while standing, sitting, walking, lying down, or riding.

He was asked:

A man suffering from inflammation of the eyes enters a state of major ritual impurity. He cannot wash himself with either warm or cold water, but he can perform ablution. What should he do?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If he has inflammation of the eyes, he should wash whatever parts of his body he can. As for the parts that would be harmed by water—such as the eye and the surrounding area—the scholars hold two views:

The first is that he must perform dry ablution. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The second is that he is not required to perform dry ablution. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik. They all agree, however, that washing the greater part of the body, where washing is possible, is obligatory. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man has intercourse with his wife while in good health. May he delay purifying himself until later in the morning, or should he perform dry ablution and pray? Give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

---

## Page 10868

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. He may not delay the prayer until its prescribed time has ended. If he can perform the ritual bath with cold or hot water, he must do so and pray within the prescribed time. Otherwise, he must perform dry ablution, for dry ablution out of fear of the cold is permissible by agreement of the imams. If he prays after performing dry ablution, he need not repeat the prayer. However, once he is able to perform the ritual bath, he must do so. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A woman suffers from an eye condition and is burdened by excess body fat. She is unable to use the bathhouse because of her condition, and her husband will not let her purify herself, yet she wishes to pray. May she wash the healthy parts of her body and perform dry ablution for her head?

He answered:

Yes. If she cannot perform the ritual bath with either cold or hot water, she must pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution, according to the vast majority of scholars. However, the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that she must wash whatever she can and perform dry ablution for the remainder. The position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik is that if she washes the greater part of her body, she need not perform dry ablution; but if she can wash only the smaller part, she should perform dry ablution and is not required to wash.

---

## Page 10869

He was asked:

A man was travelling with a group and leading them in prayer. He then experienced a wet dream on a bitterly cold day and feared that the cold would kill him, so he performed dry ablution and led them in prayer. Must he repeat the prayer? Must those who prayed behind him repeat it?

He answered:

This question comprises three issues:

The first:

His dry ablution is permissible, his prayer is valid, and he is not required to perform the ritual bath under these circumstances. The imams agree on this. A hadith concerning this is reported in the Sunan collections:

“ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs did this during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. While travelling, he performed dry ablution and led his companions in prayer, and this was mentioned to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

The same practice is also known to have been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second:

May he lead those who have performed ablution with water? The majority hold that he may lead them, as ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs and Ibn ʿAbbās did. This is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and the sounder of the two positions in the school of Abū Hanīfa. Abū Muhammad’s position is that he may not lead them.

---

## Page 10870

The third:

Concerning repetition of the prayer: there is unanimous agreement that one praying behind the imam need not repeat it, provided his prayer is valid. As for the imam, or anyone else who prays after performing dry ablution for fear of the cold, several views have been expressed.

One view is that he must repeat the prayer in all cases, as al-Shāfiʿī holds. Another is that he must repeat it only when not travelling, but not when travelling. This is one position attributed to al-Shāfiʿī and one narration from Ahmad.

A further view is that he need not repeat it in either case. This is the position of Mālik and of Ahmad according to the other narration. This is the correct view, because he has done what he was able to do and therefore need not repeat the prayer. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not instruct ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs to repeat it. Nor is there any established evidence in Islamic law that distinguishes, in this matter, between customary and unusual excuses. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man entered a state of major ritual impurity but was unable to use water because of severe cold, or because of fear and the censure he might face. Is he permitted to perform dry ablution, pray, recite the Quran, touch the Quran, and lead others in voluntary night prayer? Must he repeat the prayer? For how long may he continue to perform dry ablution?

He answered:

If he fears that bathing with water in the cold will make him ill; or fears that bathing will expose him to an accusation of something of which he is innocent, causing him harm; or fears harm from an enemy or wild beast between him and the water if he approaches it—then he may perform dry ablution for major or minor ritual impurity and pray.

---

## Page 10871

As for repeating the prayer:

The scholars have differed concerning someone who performs dry ablution for fear of the cold: must he repeat the prayer both when travelling and when not travelling, in neither case, or only when not travelling? These are three opinions. The view most consistent with the Quran and Sunnah is that he need not repeat it in either case. Whoever is permitted to pray is also permitted to recite the Quran and touch a copy of it. According to the majority of scholars, someone who has performed dry ablution may lead someone who has performed ritual bathing in prayer. This is the position of the four imams; Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, however, disagreed. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning dry ablution: if someone has a wound on his hand and begins performing ablution, washing his face, must he perform dry ablution when he reaches the washing of his arms? Or should he complete his ablution and then perform dry ablution afterward?

If the wound is bandaged, must he remove the dressing and wash all the sound skin, or should he wash the exposed areas and leave the dressing in place?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. There is disagreement concerning this issue, with two opinions in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

The correct view is that he may delay dry ablution until he has finished his ablution. Indeed, this is what he should do if one adopts the view that he must combine ablution with dry ablution. The position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik is that he does not need to perform dry ablution, whereas the position of

---

## Page 10872

al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad is that he must combine the two. If he applies a splint over the wound, he should wipe over it, whether it was applied while he was in a state of ablution or not. The same applies if he binds it with a bandage; he does not need to perform dry ablution in that case. This is the most correct scholarly opinion. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning a man in a state of major ritual impurity who is locked inside a house with a tiled floor and no earth available, and does not know when he will be able to leave: should he refrain from praying until water and earth become available, or not?

He answered:

If he is unable to use water or perform dry ablution with earth, he should pray without either ablution with water or dry ablution, according to the majority of scholars. This is the more correct of the two opinions. Must he repeat the prayer?

There are two opinions. The stronger is that he need not repeat it, for Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

The servant has not been commanded to pray twice. When he prays, he must perform the obligatory recitation. Allah knows best.

---

## Page 10873

He was asked:

Concerning a man who went to sleep in a state of major ritual impurity and did not awaken until shortly before sunrise: he feared bathing with cold water in cold weather, but if he heated the water, the prayer time would end. May he delay the prayer until he can bathe, or should he perform dry ablution and pray?

He answered:

Scholars hold two opinions on this issue. The majority, including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, require him to seek water, even if he prays after sunrise. Mālik requires him to perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time, because observing the prescribed time takes precedence over the other obligations of prayer. The evidence for this is that, if he awakens within the prescribed time and knows that he will not find water until after it ends, then, by the consensus of the Muslims, he must perform dry ablution and pray within that time, rather than bathe and pray after it has ended.

Those holding the first opinion distinguish this case and similar cases from the situation in the question on the grounds that the obligation to pray applies to him only when he awakens, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it.”

Since he is only commanded to perform it after awakening, he must perform it in accordance with what he is able to do

---

## Page 10874

by bathing in the usual manner. Thus, praying after sunrise is, in his case, praying at the time Allah has commanded. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning a man who entered a state of major ritual impurity and awoke after dawn had broken: he intended to bathe but feared that the sun would rise, so he performed ablution and prayed, then bathed after the prayer. Is his prayer valid or not?

He answered:

If he enters a state of major ritual impurity, he must bathe and pray within the prescribed time; he may not delay bathing. If he awakens only at sunrise, most scholars say that he should bathe and pray after sunrise, and must not pray while in a state of major ritual impurity. Some, however, say that he should pray within the prescribed time after performing both ablution and dry ablution. But the first opinion is more correct. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning someone in a state of major ritual impurity who, while not travelling, awakens shortly before the prescribed prayer time ends: should he perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time, or bathe and pray after the time has ended?

---

## Page 10875

He answered, may Allah have mercy on him:

According to most scholars, he should bathe and should not pray after performing dry ablution in such a case. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

If the prayer time begins while someone is in a state of major ritual impurity, and he fears that performing ritual purification will cause him to miss the prescribed time, is he permitted to perform dry ablution or not?

He answered:

If the prayer time begins while he is awake, but water is far away and he fears that seeking it will cause him to miss the prayer, or if it is cold and he fears that heating the water or going to the bathhouse will cause him to miss the prayer, then he should pray after performing dry ablution, according to the school of Ahmad and the majority of scholars.

If, however, he awakens near the end of the prescribed time and fears that the sun will rise while he is purifying himself, then in this case he should pray after sunrise, having performed ablution. There is disagreement on this among the majority of scholars, as in one of the two positions reported from Mālik. In this case, he was only commanded to pray upon awakening. Whoever sleeps through a prayer should perform it upon awakening; that is its prescribed time for him.

---

## Page 10876

He was asked:

Some people travelled from one village to another to attend the Friday prayer, but found that the prayer had already begun. Some of them had not performed ablution, and if one of them went to perform it, he would miss the prayer. May he perform dry ablution?

He answered:

There is disagreement on this issue. The stronger view is that if they can only attend the Friday prayer by performing dry ablution, they should perform dry ablution and pray. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A traveller reaches water when little time remains for the prayer. If he occupies himself with obtaining it, the prescribed time will expire. May he pray after performing dry ablution?

He answered:

If a traveller reaches water when little time remains for the prayer, he should pray after performing dry ablution, according to the majority of scholars. The same applies if there is a well, but he cannot make a rope to draw water from it before the prescribed time expires, or if water can be reached by digging, but the digging cannot be completed before the prescribed time expires. In either case, he should pray after performing dry ablution.

---

## Page 10877

Some jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad have said that he should perform a ritual bath and pray after the prescribed time has ended, since he is occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite for prayer. This view is weak, because a Muslim is commanded to pray within the prescribed time to the best of his ability. If a traveller knows that he will not find water until the time has elapsed, he must, by agreement of the leading scholars, pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution. He may not delay the prayer until he reaches water when so little time remains that he cannot complete both the ritual bath and the prayer before the time expires. Indeed, if he does so, he is sinful by unanimous agreement.

Thus, if he reaches water when little time remains, his aim is simply to pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution. He is not commanded to use the water when doing so would cause him to miss that time. This differs from the case of someone who wakes near the end of the prescribed time with water available: he is commanded to perform a ritual bath and pray, because his prayer time begins when he wakes, not at dawn. This is unlike someone who was awake at dawn or when the sun passed its zenith, whether resident or travelling, for his prayer time begins at that point.

He was asked about dry ablution:

May a person use it to perform the regular Sunnah prayers and the obligatory prayer, and continue to rely on it until he breaks his state of ritual purity, or not?

---

## Page 10878

He replied:

Yes. According to the better-supported of the two scholarly views, he may pray with dry ablution just as he prays with ablution using water. He may perform both obligatory and voluntary prayers with it, and may perform dry ablution before the prayer time begins. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and one of the two views reported from Ahmad. Dry ablution is invalidated only by what invalidates ablution using water, or by becoming able to use water. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

For someone holding back urine, which is better: to pray while retaining his ablution and holding back urine, or to relieve himself and then perform dry ablution because no water is available?

He replied:

Praying with dry ablution without holding back urine is better than praying with ablution using water while holding it back. Prayer while holding back urine is disliked and has been forbidden; there are two reported views concerning its validity. As for praying with dry ablution, it is valid and involves nothing disliked, by agreement. Allah knows best.

## Page 10879

Chapter: Removing Impurity

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

As for removing impurity with something other than water, there are three views within Ahmad’s school:

The first is that it is not permissible, as al-Shāfiʿī held. This is one of the two views within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

The second is that it is permissible, as Abū Hanīfah held. This is the other view within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

The third view within Ahmad’s school is that it is permissible when needed, as when a cat’s mouth becomes pure through its own saliva, or children’s mouths become pure through theirs, and similar cases.

The Sunnah contains instructions to use water, as in the Prophet’s words to Asmā’:

“Scrape it off, then rub it with your fingertips

---

## Page 10880

then wash it with water.” He also said concerning the vessels of the Magians:

“Wash them, then wash them with water.”

And in the hadith about the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque, he said:

“Pour a bucketful of water over his urine.”

Thus, he commanded that impurity be removed with water in particular cases; he did not issue a general command that every impurity must be removed with water.

He also permitted its removal without water in several instances. These include cleansing oneself with stones after relieving oneself, and his words concerning sandals:

“Then let him rub them on the earth, for the earth purifies them.”

They also include his words concerning the trailing hem of a garment:

“What it passes over afterward purifies it.”

Another instance is that dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—yet the people did not wash those places.

Another is his statement concerning cats:

“They are among those who move about among you, male and female.”

Cats ordinarily eat mice, yet there was no water channel to which they would go to purify their mouths with water. Rather, their saliva purified them.

Another instance is that wine which transforms of its own accord becomes pure, by the agreement of the Muslims. Accordingly, the stronger view in this matter is that whenever impurity is removed, by whatever means, its ruling as impure ceases to apply. For a ruling established on account of a cause ceases when that cause ceases. However, food and drink may not be used to remove impurity without a need, because doing so wastes wealth, just as they may not be used to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself.

---

## Page 10881

Among those who maintain that impurity can only be removed with water, some say that this is a purely devotional requirement. That is not so. The Lawgiver commanded the use of water in particular cases because it was the only practicable means: using beverages from which Muslims benefit to remove impurity would waste them, while removing it with solid materials was impracticable—as in washing garments, vessels, and the ground with water. It is well known that even if they had possessed rosewater, vinegar, or similar substances, he would not have ordered them to waste them, let alone when they had none.

Others say that water possesses a fineness that other liquids lack, so they cannot be treated as equivalent to it. That is not so either. Vinegar, rosewater, and other liquids remove impurity from vessels as effectively as water, or even more effectively. Transformation is more effective at eliminating impurity than washing with water, since washing with water may leave some of the impurity’s colour, which is then excused. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Water is sufficient for you, and its remaining trace will not harm you.”

Substances other than water can remove the taste, colour, and smell.

Others say that analogical reasoning would dictate that impurity cannot be removed with water, because the water itself becomes impure upon contact. However, a concession was granted to use water because of need. They thus regard removal with water as an instance of juristic preference upon which no analogy may be based. Both premises are invalid. Removing impurity with water does not run contrary to analogical reasoning. Rather, analogical reasoning dictates that when a ruling is established on account of a cause, it ceases when that cause ceases.

Their claim that water becomes impure upon contact is disputed, and those who concede it distinguish between incoming water

---

## Page 10882

and water into which impurity is introduced, or between flowing and standing water.

Even if it were said that this runs contrary to analogical reasoning, the correct view is that a case contrary to analogy may itself serve as the basis for an analogy when its underlying cause is known. What matters in analogical reasoning is the shared basis and the relevant distinctions.

Drawing an analogy between removing physical impurity and purification from ritual impurity is unsound. Purification from ritual impurity belongs to the category of commanded acts; hence its obligation is not waived through forgetfulness or ignorance, and the majority of scholars stipulate intention for it. Removing physical impurity, however, belongs to the category of abstaining from prohibited things: its purpose is to avoid impurity. It therefore requires neither a person’s action nor their intention. Indeed, if the impurity is removed by rain falling from the sky, the intended purpose is achieved, as maintained by the imams of the four schools and others.

The view of those followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad who stipulate intention for removing physical impurity is anomalous and contradicts the preceding consensus, besides contradicting the imams of the schools. Such a view was advanced only because they found themselves cornered in debate: their opponent on the question of intention drew an analogy between purification from ritual impurity and removing physical impurity, so they disputed the ruling in the case used as the basis of the analogy. This is groundless.

Accordingly, the sounder of the two scholarly views is that someone who prays with impurity present, unaware of it or having forgotten it, need not repeat the prayer. This is the position of Mālik and of Ahmad according to the stronger of the two reports from him. For the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—removed his sandals during prayer because of the impurity that was

---

## Page 10883

on them, and he did not restart the prayer. Likewise, in the other hadith, when he found impurity on his garment, he instructed them to wash it and did not repeat the prayer. This is because, where the purpose is to avoid something prohibited, a person incurs no sin if he does it forgetfully or by mistake, as indicated by the Quran and the Sunnah.

Allah Most High says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”

And He Most High says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

Allah Most High said, “I have done so.” Muslim narrated this in his Sahīh.

Accordingly, the strongest scholarly view is that prohibited acts committed forgetfully or by mistake during prayer, fasting, or Hajj do not invalidate the worship—for example, speaking forgetfully during prayer, eating forgetfully while fasting, or applying perfume forgetfully during Hajj. The same applies when someone forgetfully performs the act to which his oath relates. These questions involve disagreement and distinctions that are beyond the scope of this discussion.

The purpose here is simply to point out that removing physical impurity falls under refraining from what is prohibited. Thus, whenever the impurity is removed, by whatever means, the intended purpose is achieved. However, if it is removed through a person’s action and intention, he is rewarded for that. If it disappears without his action or intention, the harm is eliminated, but he receives neither reward nor punishment.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About the transformation of impure matter, such as ash from impure dung and impure manure

---

## Page 10884

that is exposed to wind and sun and turns into soil. Is it permissible to pray on it or not?

He replied:

As for the transformation of impure matter, such as ash from impure dung and impure manure that turns into soil, this issue has already been discussed. We have mentioned that there are two views concerning it within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

One is that it is pure. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah, the literalists, and others. We have also mentioned that this is the stronger view.

As for ground affected by impurity, some followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad hold that it becomes pure even if they do not accept purification through transformation. Thus, considering this issue together with “the issue of transformation,” there are three views. The correct view is that purity is achieved in all these cases, as explained previously.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

As for mud in the streets, its ruling rests on a fundamental question: if the ground is affected by impurity, which then disappears through wind, sunlight, or the like, does the ground become pure?

---

## Page 10885

The jurists hold two views on this, both of which are found within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

One view is that the ground becomes pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and others. However, according to Abū Hanīfah, one may pray on it but may not use it for dry ablution. The correct view is that one may both pray on it and use it for dry ablution. This is the sound position, for it is established in an authentic hadith from Ibn ʿUmar:

“Dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the people would not sprinkle water over any of that.”

It is well known that, had the impurity remained, washing the affected area would have been obligatory. This does not contradict the authentic report that:

“He ordered them to pour a bucketful of water over the urine of the Bedouin who had urinated in the mosque.”

Pouring water hastens the purification of the ground, which is an intended objective. By contrast, if water is not poured over it, the impurity remains until it undergoes transformation.

Furthermore, it is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When one of you comes to the mosque, let him inspect his sandals. If he finds any filth on them, let him rub them against the earth, for the earth purifies them.”

It is also reported in the Sunan collections:

“He was asked about a woman who drags the hem of her garment over a filthy place and then over a clean place. He replied, ‘What comes after it purifies it.’”

Ahmad explicitly endorsed acting upon this second hadith. In one of the two reports from him, he also explicitly endorsed acting upon the first hadith. This is likewise the position of those among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and others who accept it. Thus, if the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

---

## Page 10886

has made earth a means of purifying the soles of sandals and the hems of garments, and has called it a purifier, then it is all the more fitting that it should purify itself. Thus, when an impurity is transformed within the earth and becomes earth, it is no longer impure.

The scholars have also disagreed about cases in which the essential nature of an impurity is transformed. They agree that wine becomes pure if, by Allah’s action and without its owner intending it, it turns into vinegar. When its owner deliberately turns it into vinegar, however, they disagree and draw various distinctions. The correct view is that, if he deliberately turns it into vinegar, it does not become pure under any circumstances, as is established from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him. This is because the Prophet’s prohibition of turning wine into vinegar is authentically established, and because keeping it is a sin, whereas purity is a blessing, and sin cannot be a cause of blessing.

They have also disagreed about an impurity that becomes salt in a saltworks, turns into ash, or—as with carrion, blood, and pus—becomes earth, such as the soil of a graveyard. There are two views on this within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. The first is that it is pure, which is also the position of Abū Hanīfah and the Zāhirīs. The second is that it is impure, which is the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

The correct view is that all of this is pure if no trace of the impurity remains—neither its taste, its colour, nor its smell. For Allah has permitted wholesome things and forbidden foul things, and this depends on the properties and essential natures of the substances themselves.

---

## Page 10887

Thus, when the substance is salt or vinegar, it falls among the wholesome things that Allah has permitted, not among the foul things that He has forbidden. Likewise, earth, ash, and similar substances do not fall within the scriptural texts prohibiting such things. When the evidence for prohibition does not encompass them, either in wording or in meaning, it is not permissible to declare them impure or forbidden; they are therefore pure. If this applies to substances other than earth, then earth is all the more entitled to this ruling.

Accordingly, if no trace of impurity is apparent in street mud, it is pure. If, however, it is known with certainty that impurity is present in it, a small amount of such mud is excused.

For a Companion—may Allah be pleased with them all—would wade through mud, then enter the mosque and pray without washing his feet. This is known to have been the practice of Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—and other Companions, as mentioned previously. Mālik related this practice from them without qualification, and stated that even if faeces were dispersed throughout the mud, this would be excused. Other scholars, including followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad and others, likewise stated that a small amount of street mud is excused even when its impurity is known with certainty. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 10888

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about wine:

“If it turns into vinegar without his knowledge, may he consume it or sell it? And if he knows that it has turned into vinegar, may he consume some of it or sell it?”

He replied:

As for deliberately turning wine into vinegar, there is disagreement. Some hold that this is permissible, as is reported from Abū Hanīfa. Others hold that it is not permissible, but that if it is turned into vinegar, it becomes pure, as is reported from Mālik. Another view permits doing so by moving it from sunlight into shade, uncovering it, or similar means, without adding anything to it. This is one opinion within the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad.

Others hold that deliberately turning it into vinegar is impermissible under any circumstances. This is the position of some followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and it is the correct view. For it is established that the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—

“was asked about wine belonging to orphans, and he ordered that it be poured away. He was told, ‘They are poor,’ and he replied, ‘Allah will enrich them out of His bounty.’”

Since he ordered that it be poured away and forbade turning it into vinegar, he must be obeyed in what he commanded and prohibited. Wine must therefore be poured away, not turned into vinegar. This was despite their being orphans and despite that wine having been made before the prohibition, so they had committed no sin.

---

## Page 10889

If it is said, “This was abrogated, for it occurred in the early days of Islam. They were commanded to do this, just as they were commanded to break the vessels and tear open the containers, so that they would abstain from wine,” the reply is:

This is mistaken on several grounds.

First, a command of Allah and His Messenger can only be abrogated by a command of Allah and His Messenger, and no subsequent text has been transmitted that abrogates this command.

Second, the Rightly Guided Caliphs acted upon this after the Prophet’s death. It is authentically reported that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said:

“Do not consume vinegar made from wine unless Allah Himself initiated its souring. There is no blame upon a Muslim who buys vinegar from non-Muslims under Muslim protection.”

Here ‘Umar prohibits vinegar made from wine that someone deliberately soured, while permitting that whose souring Allah initiated. He also permits buying wine vinegar from the People of the Book, because they do not deliberately sour their wine; rather, it turns into vinegar without their choosing. ‘Umar’s statement provides evidence against all those opinions.

Third, the Companions were the most obedient of people to Allah and His Messenger. Thus, when wine was forbidden to them, they poured it away. If, despite this obedience, they were forbidden to turn it into vinegar and commanded to pour it away, then later generations have even greater reason to be subject to that command, since they are less obedient to Allah and His Messenger than the Companions were. This is illustrated by the fact that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb made the punishment imposed on people more severe for drinking

---

## Page 10890

wine, even going so far as to exile people for it, because the people of his time were less careful to avoid it than the Companions had been during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. What, then, of an age in which neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, is present? Undoubtedly, its people are less careful to avoid forbidden things. How, then, could this avenue to sin be closed to those pious people yet opened to others who are less pious than they were?

As for the reported saying:

“The best of your vinegar is vinegar made from your wine,”

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say these words. Whoever attributes them to him is mistaken. Nevertheless, the statement itself is true, since wine vinegar contains no water. What is meant, however, is vinegar whose transformation Allah Himself initiated. Moreover, any wine made from grapes without water is like wine vinegar.

Scholars have described the process of making vinegar: something that sours the grapes is added at the outset, so that they do not first turn into wine.

For this reason, they disagreed over the wine produced by a vinegar maker: must it be poured away? There are two opinions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The stronger of the two is that it must be poured away like any other wine, for Islamic law accords no wine protected status. If any wine deserved such protection, it would have been the wine purchased for orphans before the prohibition. Allah has commanded that wine be avoided, so it is impermissible to keep it, and no wine should be present in a Muslim’s home at all. Doubt arose only concerning its conversion into vinegar, because some scholars believed that this made it fit for use, just as tanning does an impure hide.

Some of them said: “Keeping it is impermissible, whether for conversion into vinegar or for any other purpose. But

---

## Page 10891

if it turns into vinegar, how can it be impure?” Others said: “If something is added to it, that substance first becomes impure, and then makes the vinegar impure in turn. This differs from the case where nothing is added, for then nothing causes it to become impure.”

Those who uphold the stronger opinion said:

The vinegar maker’s deliberate intention to turn it into vinegar is what renders it impure. He has been forbidden to keep it and commanded to pour it away; thus, by deliberately undertaking its conversion into vinegar, he has committed a forbidden act. At most, converting it into vinegar is comparable to slaughtering an animal. Something forbidden does not become lawful through a prohibited act, for disobedience cannot be a means of obtaining blessing and mercy.

An animal is forbidden to eat before slaughter and becomes permissible only through slaughter. Accordingly, if someone slaughters it in a prohibited manner—for example, by cutting somewhere other than the throat or the hollow at its base despite being able to slaughter it there, by acting without intending its ritual slaughter, or by instructing an idolater or a Magian to slaughter it, or something similar—it does not become permissible. Likewise, game killed by someone in ihrām (pilgrimage consecration) is not deemed validly slaughtered.
