Thus, the very same thing may be pure and lawful in one circumstance, yet forbidden and impure in another.

Sometimes this depends on who performs the act, as in the distinction between a person belonging to the People of the Book and an idolater. Sometimes it depends on the act itself, as in the distinction between slaughtering with a sharp instrument and slaughtering by other means. Sometimes it depends on the subject of the act and other considerations, as in the distinction between manumission and other acts. Sometimes it depends on the intention of the person acting, as in the distinction between intending to slaughter an animal ritually and merely intending to kill it. Indeed, according to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, if someone not in ihrām slaughters game, it is permissible for someone not in ihrām, but not for someone in ihrām. Thus, it is lawful and pure for the former

---

## Page 10892

but forbidden and impure for the latter. Turning wine into vinegar is a similar case: since doing so is prohibited, deliberately undertaking it does not make the resulting vinegar lawful or pure, just as slaughtering an animal in a manner not prescribed by Islamic law does not make its meat lawful and pure.

What we have related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb is the authoritative basis in this matter: whenever it is known that the owner deliberately set out to turn the wine into vinegar, it must not be purchased from him. If that is not known, it may be purchased from him, because the owner of wine is ordinarily unwilling to turn it into vinegar. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 10893

He was asked:

If an impurity, such as a mouse or a similar creature, falls into oil and dies in it, does the oil become impure?

If it is held to become impure, may more liquid be added to it until its volume reaches two qullahs? If such an increase in volume is permissible, may the pure liquid be poured onto the impure liquid, or the reverse, or is there no difference? If increasing its volume is not permissible and the oil is deemed impure, is there any way they may benefit from it, such as using it as lamp fuel or washing it—if it is held that washing purifies it? If small quantities of impure water become pure by adding more water, do other liquids likewise become pure by adding more liquid?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

The fundamental question here concerns liquids into which an impurity falls: do they become impure even when their volume is large, exceeding two qullahs? Or are they like water, which, regardless of quantity, becomes impure only if its properties change? Or does a large quantity—such as one reaching two qullahs—become impure only if its properties change?

Three positions are reported from Ahmad on this matter:

The first is that such liquids become impure even in large quantities. This is also the view of al-Shāfi‘ī and others.

The second is that they are like water, whether aqueous or non-aqueous.

---

## Page 10894

and this is the view of a number of earlier and later scholars, including Ibn Mas‘ūd, Ibn ‘Abbās, al-Zuhrī, Abū Thawr, and others.

This was Abū Thawr’s position, as transmitted from him by al-Marwadhī. When it was related to Ahmad, he said: “Abū Thawr likened it to water.” Al-Khallāl recorded this in his al-Jāmi‘, on the authority of al-Marwadhī. Likewise, the followers of Abū Hanīfah stated that, in their view, liquids have the same ruling as water. Their position concerning liquids in this regard is well known: if the liquid extends over an area such that movement at one end does not cause movement at the other, it does not become impure, just as they hold concerning water. Abū Thawr, by contrast, applies the two-qullah threshold, like al-Shāfi‘ī.

The position that liquids are like water is also mentioned as one view within Mālik’s school. His followers transmitted two reports from him concerning a small amount of impurity falling into a large quantity of food. It is also reported from Abū Nāfi‘, of the Mālikī school, concerning the large oil jars used in Syria, that a mouse dying in one does not render the oil impure. He said: “Oil is not like water.”

Ibn al-Mājishūn said that if a dead animal falls into oil or another liquid, without changing its properties, and the quantity is large, it does not become impure—unlike when the animal dies in it. He thus distinguished between its dying in the liquid and its falling into it after death.

The position of Ibn Hazm and other adherents of the literalist school is that liquids do not become impure when an impurity falls into them, except for clarified butter into which a mouse falls, just as they hold that water does not become impure unless someone urinates in it.

The third position distinguishes between an aqueous liquid, such as wine vinegar, and a non-aqueous liquid, such as grape vinegar: the former is treated like water, but not the latter.

---

## Page 10895

In summary, scholars hold three views concerning liquids:

The first is that they are like water.

The second is that there are stronger grounds for holding that they do not become impure than there are for water, because they serve as food and condiments, so destroying them entails harm. Moreover, they transform impurity more effectively than water does, or differ more markedly from it than water does.

The third is that water has a stronger claim than these liquids to remaining pure, because it is purifying.

We have discussed this issue at length elsewhere and presented the argument of those who hold that these liquids become impure. They cite the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter. But if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

This was reported by Abū Dāwūd and others. We have explained the weakness of this hadith. Al-Bukhārī, al-Tirmidhī, Abū Hātim al-Rāzī, al-Dāraqutnī, and others criticized it and showed that Ma‘mar had erred in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī.

Abū Dāwūd said:

“Chapter on a Mouse Falling into Clarified Butter. Musaddad narrated to us: Sufyān narrated to us: al-Zuhrī narrated to us, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, that a mouse fell into some clarified butter. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was informed, and he said: ‘Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the butter.’

He also said: Ahmad ibn Sālih and al-Husayn ibn ‘Alī narrated to us—the wording is al-Husayn’s—

---

## Page 10896

they both said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq narrated to us, saying: Ma‘mar informed us, from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, who said:

‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “If a mouse falls into clarified butter, then if it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”’

Al-Hasan said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq said: ‘Ma‘mar would sometimes transmit it from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’

Abū Dāwūd said: Ahmad ibn Sālih said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq said: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mardawayh informed us, from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with a report like the hadith transmitted by al-Zuhrī from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib.”

Abū ‘Īsā al-Tirmidhī said in his Jāmi‘:

“Chapter on Reports Concerning a Mouse Dying in Clarified Butter.”

Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān and Abū ‘Ammār narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah:

“A mouse fell into some clarified butter and died. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it, and he said: ‘Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the butter.’”

Abū ‘Īsā said: This hadith is good and authentic. This hadith has also been transmitted from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, stating that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it, without mentioning Maymūnah in the chain. The hadith transmitted by Ibn ‘Abbās from Maymūnah is more authentic.

---

## Page 10897

Ma‘mar also transmitted a similar report from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but this version is not reliably preserved. He said: “I heard Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl say: ‘Ma‘mar’s report on this matter, from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is erroneous.’ He said: ‘The authentic report is that transmitted by al-Zuhrī from ‘Ubayd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah.’”

I say:

This report of Ma‘mar, which al-Bukhārī judged erroneous and al-Tirmidhī described as not reliably preserved, is the one containing the words: “If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it,” as transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and others. It was likewise transmitted by Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, in his Musnad, and by others. ‘Abd al-Razzāq mentioned that Ma‘mar sometimes transmitted it through the other chain. Thus, he was inconsistent in its chain of transmission, just as he was inconsistent in its wording. He also differed from the trustworthy masters of hadith, who transmitted it with wording other than his. Ma‘mar was known to make mistakes, whereas al-Zuhrī was not. For this reason, al-Bukhārī cited statements by al-Zuhrī that demonstrated Ma‘mar’s error in this hadith.

Al-Bukhārī said in his Sahīh:

“Chapter: When a Mouse Falls into Solid or Melted Clarified Butter.”

Al-Humaydī narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Al-Zuhrī narrated to us, saying: ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Utbah informed me that he heard Ibn ‘Abbās narrating from Maymūnah:

“A mouse fell into some clarified butter

---

## Page 10898

and died. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it, and he said: ‘Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the rest.’”

Sufyān was told: “But Ma‘mar narrates it from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah.” He replied: “I only ever heard al-Zuhrī narrate it from ‘Ubayd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. I heard it from him repeatedly.”

‘Abdān narrated to us: ‘Abd Allāh—that is, Ibn al-Mubārak—narrated to us, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, that he was asked about an animal—a mouse or some other creature—that dies in oil or clarified butter, whether solid or not. He said:

“We have been informed that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave instructions concerning a mouse that had died in clarified butter: he ordered that what was close to it be discarded, and then he ate some of it.”

This was from the report of ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh. Al-Bukhārī then narrated it through Mālik, just as he had narrated it through Ibn ‘Uyaynah.

The transmitters narrated this hadith from al-Zuhrī with the same chain and wording as Ibn ‘Uyaynah’s version. Ma‘mar, however, was inconsistent in both its chain and its wording. On one occasion, he narrated it from Ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, including the words:

“If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

It was also reported from him:

“If it is liquid, use it as lamp fuel.”

The reports transmitted from Ma‘mar were also inconsistent. Some scholars thought that Ma‘mar’s hadith was reliably preserved and therefore acted upon it. Among those who upheld it was Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī, in his compilation of al-Zuhrī’s hadiths. Ahmad likewise relied on it when he issued a fatwa distinguishing between solid

---

## Page 10899

and liquid. Ahmad would sometimes rely on hadiths that later proved to him to be defective, as when he relied on the saying:

“A vow involving disobedience is not valid, and its expiation is the same as for an oath.”

Later, when its defect became clear to him, he relied on other evidence. Al-Bukhārī, al-Tirmidhī and others, however, identified the defect in Ma‘mar’s hadith and explained his error. Their judgment is correct.

Here al-Bukhārī cited Ibn ‘Uyaynah as saying: “I heard it from al-Zuhrī repeatedly; he narrated it only from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh.” Its wording contains only the instruction:

“Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the rest.”

Mālik and others narrated it likewise. Al-Bukhārī also cited Yūnus’s report that al-Zuhrī was asked about an animal dying in clarified butter, whether solid or otherwise. He gave his ruling by citing the report:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave instructions concerning a mouse that had died in clarified butter, ordering that what was close to it be discarded.”

This, then, was al-Zuhrī’s ruling concerning both solid and liquid clarified butter. How could he have narrated a distinction between them in this hadith when he cites that very hadith as evidence that both types have the same ruling, narrating it by meaning? Al-Zuhrī had the strongest memory of anyone in his time, so much so that it is said that no error or lapse of memory in any hadith is known of him, even though no one in his time possessed more hadiths than he did.

It is also said that he preserved for the Muslim community ninety teachings of the Sunnah which no one else transmitted. Sulaymān ibn ‘Abd al-Malik wrote down a book from his recitation from memory, then asked him to repeat it a year later, and he did not miss a single letter. Thus, even if the only question concerning this hadith were whether al-Zuhrī or Ma‘mar had forgotten, attributing the lapse to Ma‘mar would be more appropriate, by the unanimous agreement of the scholars

---

## Page 10900

who specialize in hadith narrators, quite apart from the abundant evidence of Ma‘mar’s lapse of memory. Hadith experts agree that Ma‘mar frequently erred when narrating from al-Zuhrī. Regarding the report Muhammad ibn Ja‘far Ghundar narrated to him from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhrī, from Sālim, from his father—that Ghaylān ibn Salamah embraced Islam while married to eight women—Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“This is how Ma‘mar narrated it in Basra. He narrated it to them in Basra from memory, whereas in Yemen he narrated it correctly from al-Zuhrī.”

Abū Hātim al-Rāzī said: “The reports Ma‘mar ibn Rāshid narrated in Basra contain errors, though he is an acceptable hadith narrator.”

Most of those who narrated this hadith from Ma‘mar, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah were Basrans, such as ‘Abd al-Wāhid ibn Ziyād and ‘Abd al-A‘lā ibn ‘Abd al-A‘lā al-Shāmī. The inconsistency in the wording is evident. One narrator says:

“If it is melted or liquid, it must not be eaten.”

Another says:

“If it is liquid, do not make use of it, and burn it in lamps.”

Another says:

“Do not go near it.”

Yet another says:

“He ordered that it be removed, together with what surrounded it, and discarded.”

Thus, he gave an unqualified answer without mentioning any distinction.

This shows that he did not narrate it from a written text with precisely preserved wording. Rather, he narrated it according to what he thought it meant, and so erred. Even assuming that this wording is authentic, namely his statement:

“And if

---

## Page 10901

it is liquid, do not go near it,” this would only indicate that a small quantity into which an impurity has fallen becomes impure, as with the clarified butter asked about. It is well known that the questioner did not have more than two large jarfuls (qullahs) of clarified butter into which a mouse had fallen, such that one could invoke the maxim:

“Failure to seek further particulars about a reported situation, when different possibilities exist, gives the statement the force of a general ruling.”

Rather, the clarified butter that the people of Medina kept in their containers was generally small in quantity. Thus, even if the hadith were authentic, it would indicate only that a small quantity becomes impure. As for large quantities of liquids into which an impurity falls, neither an authentic nor a weak text, nor scholarly consensus, nor valid analogical reasoning establishes that they become impure.

Those who deem such liquids impure rely chiefly on the assumption that, when an impurity falls into water or another liquid, it spreads throughout it and renders all of it impure. The invalidity of this has already been established, as has the fact that no Muslim has applied it consistently, for doing so would entail declaring the sea impure. Rather, those who adopted this unsound principle made exceptions: some exempted a body of liquid in which movement at one end does not cause movement at the other; some, with respect to certain impurities, exempted quantities that cannot be drained away; and others exempted quantities exceeding two qullahs.

Some justified these exceptions by the hardship involved in declaring such quantities impure; others, by the impurity’s not reaching the entire large quantity; and others, by the impossibility of purification. These same reasons apply to large quantities of oils. An enormous storage jar may contain vast quantities of oil, which people cannot protect from things falling into it. Houses and shops are full of things that cannot be protected in this way, such as sugar and other goods. Declaring these impure would therefore entail very great difficulty and hardship.

---

## Page 10902

For this reason, no report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his Companions declares large quantities impure. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, expressed differing views on declaring large quantities impure. As for small quantities, he believed Maʿmar’s hadith to be authentic and therefore acted upon it. Others, however, discovered a defect undermining its authenticity; had he known of it, he would not have adopted that ruling. There are similar instances: he would act upon a hadith, then abandon it when its weakness became apparent to him. Conversely, he might refrain from acting upon a hadith before its authenticity became clear, then act upon it once its authenticity was established. Such is the way of people of knowledge and religious devotion, may Allah be pleased with them. Because he believed this hadith to be authentic, he gave it precedence over the reports he had encountered from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Sālih ibn Ahmad reported in his Masāʾil, on the authority of his father, Ahmad ibn Hanbal:

My father narrated to us: Ismāʿīl narrated to us: ʿUmārah ibn Abī Hafsah narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about a mouse that had died in clarified butter. He said, “Remove the mouse and the clarified butter surrounding it.”

I said, “Our master, but there were traces of it throughout the clarified butter!”

He replied, “May you bite your father’s private parts! It left those traces in the clarified butter only while it was alive. It died only where it was found.”

My father narrated to us: Wakīʿ narrated to us: al-Nadr ibn ʿArabī narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, who said:

A man came to Ibn ʿAbbās and asked him about a jar of oil into which a rat had fallen. Ibn ʿAbbās said, “Remove it and the oil surrounding it, throw that away, and eat the rest.”

I said, “Had it not moved throughout the jar?”

He replied, “It moved about while it was alive, then came to rest where it died.”

Al-Khallāl also reported from Sālih, who said:

My father narrated to us: Wakīʿ narrated to us: Sufyān narrated to us, from Humrān ibn Aʿyan, from Abū Harb ibn Abī

---

## Page 10903

al-Aswad al-Du’alī, who said:

Ibn Masʿūd was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied, “Only the flesh and blood of a dead animal are forbidden.”

I say: These, then, are the rulings of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Zuhrī, even though Ibn ʿAbbās himself transmitted Maymūnah’s hadith. Moreover, the wording transmitted by Maʿmar in the weak hadith, “Do not go near it,” is generally not acted upon by the early and later authorities among the Companions, the Successors and the imams. Most of them permit using it as lamp fuel, and many permit selling it or purifying it. This is contrary to the wording, “Do not go near it.”

Those who defend this view argue that the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,” distinguishes water from clothing, the body, vessels and similar things that become impure. The implication of a statement is not universal in scope: this does not entail that everything other than water becomes impure. Air, for example, does not become impure, yet it is not water.

Likewise, his statement, “Water does not enter a state of major ritual impurity,” distinguishes it from the body, which does enter that state. It does not entail that everything other than water enters a state of major ritual impurity. Rather, water was specifically mentioned in both instances because its ruling needed clarification. One of his wives had bathed, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to perform ablution with the water she had left. She told him that she had been in a state of major ritual impurity, and he said, “Water does not enter a state of major ritual impurity.” Yet neither clothing nor the ground enters that state. Water was specifically mentioned to distinguish it from the body, not from everything else.

Similarly, they asked him, “May we perform ablution with water from the well of Budāʿah, a well into which people throw

---

## Page 10904

menstrual refuse, dog flesh and foul-smelling matter?” He replied, “Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure.” He thus denied that it was impure because this needed clarification, just as he denied that it entered a state of major ritual impurity because that needed clarification. Allah, Glorified is He, has permitted wholesome things for us and forbidden foul things. Impurities are among foul things, so when water is altered by an impurity, using it becomes forbidden, because that constitutes using something foul.

This rests on a fundamental question: when an impurity falls into a large quantity of water, does analogical reasoning require that the water be deemed impure because the lawful has mixed with the unlawful, unless evidence establishes its purity? Or does analogical reasoning require that it remain pure until the foul impurity whose use is forbidden becomes perceptible in it?

The jurists among Ahmad’s followers and others hold two views on this principle. The first holds that impurity is the default ruling. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah’s followers and those among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad who agree with them, on the grounds that mixing the lawful with the unlawful makes both forbidden.

Abū Hanīfah’s followers then applied this principle consistently to water in which movement at one end causes movement at the other. They said, “The impurity reaches wherever the movement reaches.” They could not extend this principle to quantities greater than that, since doing so would require deeming the sea impure, whereas nothing renders the sea impure, according to explicit scriptural evidence and scholarly consensus. Nor did they apply this principle consistently in cases where

---

## Page 10905

the water is deep but has a small surface area. Moreover, once water becomes impure, their analogical reasoning requires that it cannot be purified by drawing water out. Impure wells would therefore have to be filled in. Bishr al-Marīsī applied this analogy consistently.

Abū Hanīfah and his followers, however, held that purification by drawing out water was permissible on the basis of juristic preference: either by emptying the entire well if the animal was large or had decomposed, or by drawing out some of its water if the animal was small, using a specified number of bucketfuls. Thus, they could not apply that analogy consistently.

Likewise, the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad held that water exceeding two qullahs (large jars) in volume remains pure, because such quantities occur in open country and in pools that cannot be protected from impurities. They therefore treated its purity as a concession granted out of need, contrary to analogical reasoning. Similarly, those among Ahmad’s followers who held that urine and moist excrement render water impure only when it is possible to drain it did not apply the analogy consistently. Since water that cannot be drained cannot be purified, they treated the impossibility of purification as a barrier to its becoming impure.

These and other statements by those who uphold this principle show that none of the jurists applied it consistently. Rather, all of them departed from its analogical implications by way of concession, permitting the use of water mixed with impurities because of a particular need.

The second view is that of those who hold that analogical reasoning requires that water should not be deemed impure until

---

## Page 10906

it changes, as held by some of the jurists of the Hijaz and Iraq, the jurists of hadith, and others, including Mālik and his followers and those among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad who agreed with them. This is the approach adopted by Judge Abū Yaʿlā ibn Judge Abī Khāzim, even though he held that a small quantity of water becomes impure through contact with an impurity.

Ibn ʿAqīl, Ibn al-Munā, Ibn al-Muzaffar, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Nasr, and other followers of Ahmad defended the view that water becomes impure only if it changes, in accordance with the opinion transmitted from Ahmad that agrees with the scholars of Medina. This was also the view of Abū al-Mahāsin al-Rūyānī and other followers of al-Shāfiʿī.

Al-Ghazālī said: “I wish al-Shāfiʿī’s position on water had been the same as Mālik’s.”

The statements of Ahmad and others accord with this view. Ahmad was asked on what basis water is deemed impure when an impurity falls into it and changes its taste or colour, given that the hadith reported on this subject, which states:

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure except that which changes its colour, taste, or smell,”

is weak. He replied that Allah has forbidden carrion, blood, and pork. Thus, if the taste of blood, carrion, or pork becomes apparent in the water, anyone using that water is using these foul substances. Had he considered analogical reasoning to require an unrestricted prohibition, he would not have confined the prohibition to cases involving the use of the impurity itself.

In short, this view is correct. Allah has forbidden foul substances such as blood, carrion, pork, and the like. When these fall into water or another substance and are entirely absorbed into it, no blood, carrion, or pork remains

---

## Page 10907

at all.

Likewise, when wine is entirely absorbed into another liquid, someone who drinks that liquid is not drinking wine. When wine changes by itself into vinegar, it becomes pure by scholarly consensus. This argument is even stronger according to those who hold that an impure substance becomes pure when transformed into a different substance. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and the Zāhirīs, and one of the two positions within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. For an impure substance’s transformation into salt, ash, or the like is no different from its transformation into water. There is no distinction between its becoming ash, salt, earth, water, air, or something similar. Allah Most High has permitted wholesome things for us.

These oils, milks, sweet and sour drinks, and other such things are wholesome, while the foul substance has been entirely absorbed and transformed within them. How, then, can something wholesome that Allah Most High has permitted become forbidden? Who has said that it becomes forbidden when a foul substance mixes with it, is entirely absorbed into it, and is transformed? There is no evidence for this in the Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly consensus, or analogical reasoning.

Thus, in the hadith concerning the well of Budāʿah, when it was mentioned to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that menstrual cloths, dog flesh, and putrid matter were thrown into it, he said:

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

In the hadith concerning the two qullahs, he said:

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not carry impurity.”

Another wording states:

“Nothing renders it impure.”

This was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others.

His words, “It does not carry impurity,” explain that water becomes impure by carrying impurity—that is, by having impurity borne within it. This makes clear that water does not become impure when the impurity has been transformed.

---

## Page 10908

Section

Once the underlying principle of this issue is understood, a ruling established on the basis of a cause ceases when that cause ceases. Thus, since wine’s intoxicating potency is what makes it forbidden and impure, it becomes pure when that potency disappears through Allah’s action—not when it is deliberately removed by human intervention, according to the correct view. As Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Do not consume vinegar made from wine unless Allah Himself began the wine’s souring.”

There is no blame on a Muslim for purchasing wine vinegar from the People of the Book unless he knows that they deliberately caused the wine to sour. This is because keeping wine is forbidden. Whoever keeps it with the intention of turning it into vinegar has committed a forbidden act, and a forbidden act cannot be a means of making something lawful and permissible. But whoever keeps it to drink and use as wine does not intend to turn it into vinegar. If Allah turns it into vinegar, this is a punishment that brings about the opposite of what he intended. Thus, no harmful consequence results from its being lawful and pure.

As for other impure substances, it is permissible to cause them to break down deliberately, since doing so is not forbidden. Likewise, someone who drinks them is not subject to a prescribed legal punishment, because there is no fear that approaching them will lead people into what is forbidden, as there is with approaching wine. For this reason, the majority of scholars permit the tanning of

---

## Page 10909

the hides of dead animals. They also permit the transformation of impure matter by fire or other means.

Water becomes impure for two reasons: one is agreed upon, while the other is disputed. The agreed-upon reason is a change caused by impurity. Whenever such a change is what makes water impure, it becomes pure once that change disappears, just as a garment smeared with blood becomes pure again when washed.

The second reason is small quantity. When an impurity falls into a small quantity of water, scholars hold two views as to whether it becomes impure. According to al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad in one report from him, water amounting to less than two qullahs becomes impure. In the well-known report from Ahmad, however, urine and liquid excrement are exceptions: any body of water that can be drained is deemed impure if either falls into it.

According to Abū Hanīfah, any water reached by the motion becomes impure. The scholars of Medina, and Ahmad in a third report, hold that it does not become impure even if it amounts to less than two qullahs. Some Shāfiʿī scholars preferred this first view, corresponding to one of the transmitted reports. Some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers defended this report, just as many of Ahmad’s followers defended the first. However, a group of Mālik’s followers said that a small quantity of water becomes impure through a small quantity of impurity, without setting the threshold at two qullahs. Most scholars of Medina stated their position without qualification: they do not deem anything impure unless it undergoes a change.

Those who treat water and other liquids alike—as in one of the two reports from Ahmad—and adopt this view, which is also reported from Ahmad, apply the same ruling to other liquids, as al-Zuhrī and others did. Thus, they do not deem any liquid impure

---

## Page 10910

unless it undergoes a change, as al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Sahīh. According to the well-known report from Ahmad, however, the threshold of two qullahs applies to water, and likewise to other liquids if they are treated in the same way.

We therefore say: If an impurity falls into a small quantity of liquid, and a large quantity of liquid is then poured into it, the whole becomes pure, provided it has not undergone a change. If a small quantity of water, less than two qullahs, is poured into it, bringing the total to a large quantity exceeding two qullahs, there are two views within Ahmad’s school. The first, which is also al-Shāfiʿī’s position concerning water, is that the whole is pure.

The second view is that it does not become pure unless the quantity added is itself large. Purification by adding a greater quantity requires pouring the pure liquid onto the impure liquid. If, however, the impure liquid is poured into a large quantity of pure liquid, this is like pouring impure water into a large quantity of pure water: this too purifies it, provided it has not undergone a change. If the small quantity that has come into contact with impurity is poured into another small quantity that has not, and the combined quantity is large, exceeding two qullahs, this is like combining two small quantities of water. The two views mentioned above apply here as well.

The position we have stated—that other liquids are like water and have an even stronger claim than water not to be deemed impure—is the one most clearly supported by the evidence of Islamic law. Indeed, even if a small quantity of water were deemed impure, it would not necessarily follow that drinks and foods should be deemed impure. For this reason, Mālik ordered the pouring away of whatever had been lapped from by

---

## Page 10911

a dog when the liquid was a small quantity of water, as stated in the hadith. Yet he did not order food or drink from which a dog had lapped to be poured away, and he considered discarding food and drink for such a reason a grave matter. This is because water ordinarily costs nothing, unlike Muslims’ food and drink. Declaring these impure entails hardship, difficulty, and distress that are plain to everyone. As explained earlier, all jurists take the removal of hardship into account in this matter. If they do not deem large quantities of water impure in order to avert hardship, how can they deem comparable quantities of food and drink impure, when the hardship in this case is greater? Perhaps most large quantities of liquid are scarcely ever free of some impurity.

If it is said, “Water removes impurity from other things, so it should be all the more able to keep impurity from itself, unlike other liquids,” the answer is that this can be addressed in several ways.

First: Water removes impurity from other things only because it carries it away from the affected place, and the impurity goes with it, leaving none behind. When impurity falls into water, however, the water remains pure because the impurity undergoes transformation within it, not because the water has removed it from itself.

For this reason, the followers of Abū Hanīfah say that other liquids are like water both in removing impurity and in being rendered impure. That being so, it does not follow from water’s removing impurity when it carries that impurity away that it removes impurity when the impurity remains within it.

Water containing impurity is comparable to the wash-water that drains away from the place being washed.

---

## Page 10912

and that wash-water is impure before the affected place becomes pure. Once the place has become pure, there are three views concerning the wash-water: is it pure, purifying, or impure?

Abū Hanīfah considered this point and held that water becomes impure when impurity falls into it, even though it removes impurity from other things, for the reason we have explained.

If, then, the revealed texts and the majority view establish that water in large quantities does not become impure merely because impurity falls into it—as indicated by the Prophet’s statements, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,”

and,

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not bear impurity”—

then, if water is purifying and other things are purified with it, we know that it does not become impure through contact. For if such contact rendered it impure, it would become impure upon contact whenever impurity was poured into it. Thus, impurity falling into water does not render it impure. However, if the actual substance of the impurity remains, it renders the water unlawful; if it undergoes transformation, it ceases to exist.

This shows that impurity undergoing transformation within water through contact with it does not render the water impure, even though the impurity has not been removed as it is removed from the affected place. Anyone who says that water repels impurity from itself just as it removes it from other things contradicts what is observable. This same principle applies to all other liquids, whether beverages or otherwise.

Second: At most, this argument entails that impurity can be removed with a liquid. This is one of the two positions within the schools of Ahmad and Mālik, as well as the position of Abū Hanīfah and others. Ahmad regarded it as a necessary consequence of the position of anyone who says that a liquid does not become impure

---

## Page 10913

through contact with impurity, and said that, on this view, it must also be possible to remove impurity with it. This is because, if it repels impurity from itself, it also repels it from other things, as they have argued concerning water. According to this position, it therefore follows that impurity may be removed with any pure liquid capable of removing its substance and eliminating its traces. This is what analogical reasoning requires, and we therefore accept it on this assumption.

If, on the other hand, repelling impurity from itself does not entail repelling it from other things, because transformation is more effective than removal, then anyone who holds that impurity may be removed with liquids other than water must accord those liquids the same ruling as water. Thus, if the correct ruling concerning water is that it becomes impure only when its properties change—whether regardless of quantity or when present in large quantities—then the same is the correct ruling concerning other liquids.

In short, water and other liquids can be treated alike under either assumption. This is what the revealed texts and analogical reasoning require, both regarding the removal of impurities and regarding their contact with liquids, whether water or otherwise. Whoever reflects on the fundamental principles established by the revealed texts and agreed upon, and on the considerations recognized by the Sacred Law in its rulings, will see that this is the most correct position. Deeming water and other liquids impure without any change in their properties is far removed from the apparent meanings of the texts and from analogical reasoning. Likewise, maintaining that the ruling of impurity remains attached to affected places after the impurity has been removed with a liquid or something else is far removed from those fundamental principles and the requirements of analogy. Whoever is a jurist well versed in the grounds of the rulings of the Sacred Law and sets aside personal bias

---

## Page 10914

will recognize this. However, if using such substances causes harm, such use is prohibited, just as slaughtering horses used in jihad, camels used for pilgrimage, cattle used for ploughing, and similar animals is prohibited because they are needed, not because they are unclean. As an authentic report concerning the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) relates:

“During one of his journeys with his Companions, their provisions ran out. They asked his permission to slaughter their riding camels, and he gave them permission. Then ʿUmar came and asked him to gather the provisions and supplicate to Allah to bless them, so that the riding camels could be spared. He did so.”

His prohibition against slaughtering their riding camels was therefore due to their need for them as mounts, not because camels are forbidden to eat. Likewise, using needed food and drink to remove impurity is prohibited, just as it is prohibited to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself with things whose protected status must be respected: food for humans and jinn, and fodder for the animals of humans and jinn. This is not because these substances cannot be used for cleansing, but because of their protected status. The same reasoning thus applies to liquids as to solids.

The third argument:

Other liquids are more effective than water at transforming impurity into their own substance, while water is more readily altered by impurities than other liquids are. If water does not become impure when impurity falls into it because that impurity is transformed into its own substance, then this applies all the more to other liquids.

The fourth argument:

If the impurity imparts no taste, colour, or smell to water or another liquid, we do not concede that the water or liquid can be deemed impure at all, as in the case of wine that has undergone transformation, or

---

## Page 10915

an even stronger case. This reasoning is applied consistently to all forms of transformation. The majority hold that impure substances become pure through transformation. This is the well-known position of the Hanafīs and Zāhirīs, one of the two opinions within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and a position within the school of al-Shāfi'ī.

The fifth argument:

The ability to resist impurity, which other liquids share with water, is not exclusive to water. Rather, the same ruling applies to soil and other substances.

Scholars have differed over whether ground becomes pure when impurity that has fallen upon it disappears through sunlight, wind, or transformation. There are two opinions.

The first is that it becomes pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and one of the two opinions within the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad. It is the correct opinion according to the evidence.

It is authentically reported that Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“Dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), yet they would not sprinkle water on any of those places.”

The Sunan collections also report that he said:

“When any of you comes to the mosque, let him inspect his sandals. If there is any filth on them, let him rub them against the soil, for soil purifies them.”

The Companions, such as ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others, would wade through mud and then enter to lead the people in prayer without washing their feet.

Still stronger evidence is his statement (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) concerning the trailing hems of women's garments when they come into contact with clean ground after unclean ground:

“The latter counteracts the former.”

And his statement: “It is purified by

---

## Page 10916

what comes after it.” This is one of the two opinions within the school of Ahmad and others. Ahmad explicitly stated it in the transmission recorded by Ismā'īl ibn Sa'īd al-Shālanjī, on which Ibrāhīm ibn Ya'qūb al-Jawzajānī wrote a commentary. It is among the most distinguished collections of legal questions.

This is because trailing hems repeatedly come into contact with impurity, making them comparable to the underside of leather footwear and the area cleansed after relieving oneself. Since the Lawgiver has allowed solid substances to remove impurity from other things out of necessity—as when cleansing oneself with stones—and has made solid substances purifying, it follows that this property is not exclusive to water. If solid substances are not rendered impure by impurities transformed into them, this applies all the more to liquids, since they bring about transformation more thoroughly and rapidly. A detailed treatment of these questions and related matters belongs elsewhere.

As for those who hold that oil becomes impure through what falls into it, there are two opinions within the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad concerning whether it may be used as lamp fuel. The stronger opinion permits this, as has been reported from a number of the Companions. There are also two views within the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad concerning whether it becomes pure through washing.

The first is that it becomes pure through washing. This was the view preferred by Ibn Shurayh, Abū al-Khattāb, Ibn Sha'bān, and others. It is the well-known position within the school of al-Shāfi'ī and others.

The second is that it does not become pure through washing, and this is the position held by most of them. This disagreement also applies to

---

## Page 10917

oil whose properties have been altered by impurity, for it is undoubtedly impure. The same disagreement concerns whether it may be used as lamp fuel and whether it may be purified by washing. As for selling it, the well-known position is that it may not be sold to either a Muslim or a disbeliever. This is the well-known position within the school of al-Shāfi'ī and others. It is also reported from Ahmad that it may be sold to a disbeliever provided he is informed of its impurity, as has been related from Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī.

A view permitting its sale has also been derived from Ahmad’s positions. Some scholars, including Abū al-Khattāb and others, derived this from the permissibility of using it as lamp fuel. This reasoning is weak, because Ahmad and other leading scholars distinguished between the two matters. Others derived the permissibility of selling it from the possibility of purifying it: if it can be purified, it is comparable to an impure garment or vessel, whose sale is permissible by agreement.

Likewise, the scholars of al-Shāfi'ī’s school have two views on whether it may be sold if they hold that it can be purified. Some of them held that it may be sold without qualification. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

As for liquids—such as oil, clarified butter and other fats, as well as vinegar, milk and the like—if an impurity, such as a dead mouse or something similarly impure, falls into them, the scholars hold two opinions on the matter.

---

## Page 10918

The first view is that these liquids are subject to the same ruling as water. This is the view of al-Zuhrī and other early scholars, and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. In some passages, it is also cited as a position reported from Mālik. This is also the underlying principle of Abū Hanīfah’s view, since he reasoned about water by analogy with other liquids.

The second view is that liquids become impure when an impurity falls into them, unlike water, for which a distinction is made between small and large quantities. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and the other position reported from Mālik and Ahmad.

There is also a third view, reported from Ahmad, which distinguishes between aqueous liquids and other liquids: date vinegar is treated like water, whereas grape vinegar is not.

According to the first view, if the quantity of oil is large—for example, two qullahs in volume—it does not become impure unless its properties change. Ahmad explicitly stated this concerning a dog that lapped from a large quantity of oil, saying, “It does not become impure.”

If the quantity of liquid is small, the ruling depends on the previously mentioned disagreement concerning a small quantity of water. Those who hold that a small quantity becomes impure only if its properties change apply the same ruling to oil and other liquids. This was the ruling given by al-Zuhrī when he was asked about a mouse or another animal dying in clarified butter or other fats. He said:

“It should be removed, along with what is near it, and the rest may be eaten, whether the quantity is small or large, and whether it is solid or liquid.”

Al-Bukhārī related this from him in his Sahīh for a reason we shall explain, Allah willing.

---

## Page 10919

Those who hold that a small quantity of liquid becomes impure when an impurity falls into it also hold that it is like water: it can be purified by adding a sufficiently large quantity to it, just as water can. Thus, if a large quantity of oil is poured into it, the whole becomes pure.

The stronger view is that liquids, like water, do not become impure merely through such contact. Indeed, there is even greater reason not to regard them as impure than there is with water. This is because Allah has made wholesome things lawful for us and forbidden foul things. Foods and drinks—including fats, milk, oil, vinegars, and liquid foods—are among the wholesome things Allah has made lawful for us. If none of the characteristics of the foul substance appears in them—neither its taste, colour, nor smell—and none of its constituent parts remains apparent, they retain their wholesome character. They may not, therefore, be classified as forbidden, foul things when their characteristics remain those of wholesome things, not foul ones. The distinction between wholesome and foul things rests on the characteristics that distinguish them. It is because of those characteristics that one is forbidden and the other permitted.

If a drop of blood or wine falls into such a storage jar and undergoes transformation, while the milk retains its characteristics and the oil retains its characteristics, there is no basis for declaring it forbidden. That drop has been absorbed and transformed, and it no longer retains any legally relevant identity to which the rulings concerning blood or wine could apply.

There is greater reason to regard these liquids as pure than water because the Lawgiver has permitted water to be poured away and used up in circumstances where He has not permitted other liquids to be used up. One example is cleansing oneself after relieving oneself: water is used for this, but not these other liquids. The same applies to removing all other impurities with water.

---

## Page 10920

As for using other liquids for this purpose, that is not permissible, whether or not they are held to remove the impurity. This is why some scholars have said that water is to be poured away if a dog laps from it, whereas the contents of vessels holding food and drink are not.

Moreover, water is more readily altered by impurity than salt is, and impurity undergoes a greater transformation in substances other than water than it does in water. Thus, other liquids are less susceptible than water to becoming impure, both physically and according to Islamic law. Wherever water does not become impure, there is even greater reason for other liquids not to become impure.

Furthermore, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He said:

“Discard it and the butter surrounding it, and eat your butter.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave them a general, unqualified answer: they were to discard the mouse and the butter surrounding it, and eat their butter. He did not ask them whether it was liquid or solid. When a reported case admits more than one possibility, not asking for further details gives the answer the force of a general statement. Moreover, clarified butter in the Hijāz is usually liquid; indeed, it has been said that it is always liquid. The quantity of clarified butter also usually falls short of two qullahs, yet he did not ask whether the quantity was small or large.

If it is objected that the following wording has been transmitted in the hadith:

“If it is solid, discard it and the butter surrounding it, and eat your butter; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

This was reported by Abū Dāwūd and others.

---

## Page 10921

The reply is:

This addition is what those who distinguished between liquid and solid clarified butter relied upon. They believed it to be authentically established as a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In doing so, they exercised scholarly judgment and spoke according to the extent of their knowledge and judgment. Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī declared al-Zuhrī’s hadith weak and this addition authentic. Others, however, have found that this addition entered the hadith by mistake and is not a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

This is what has become clear to us and to others. We are certain that this addition is not a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We therefore ceased issuing fatwas based on it, having previously done so, for returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood. Al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī, may Allah have mercy on them both, and other leading hadith scholars have shown us that it is erroneous and that Maʿmar made a mistake in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī. Maʿmar frequently made mistakes, and the reliable narrators among al-Zuhrī’s students, such as Mālik, Yūnus and Ibn ʿUyaynah, differed with him on this. His own transmission of this hadith was inconsistent in both its chain and its wording. He transmitted it from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, whereas it is actually from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Maymūnah. In some versions transmitted from him, the wording is:

“If it is liquid, use it as fuel for lamps.”

In others:

“Do not go near it.”

Al-Bukhārī demonstrated his mistake in this by recording in his Sahīh, through Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī himself, that he was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied:

“If it is

---

## Page 10922

solid or liquid, in a small or large quantity, the mouse and whatever is near it should be discarded, and the rest may be eaten. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter, and he said:

‘Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter.’”

Thus al-Zuhrī, the central transmitter of this hadith, ruled that, whether the clarified butter is liquid or solid, the mouse and whatever is near it should be discarded, and the rest may be eaten. He cited this hadith as evidence, in the form transmitted from him by the majority of his students. It is therefore clear that whoever attributed to him a distinction between the two kinds was mistaken.

Moreover, the distinction between solidity and liquidity cannot be precisely delimited. With many foods, it is unclear whether they should be classified as solid or liquid. The Lawgiver distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful only by a clear distinction that leaves no ambiguity. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah would not let a people go astray after He has guided them until He has made clear to them what they must avoid.”

Forbidden things are among what they must avoid, so He must explain these things to them in a way that clearly distinguishes them from what is lawful. Allah Most High also says:

“He has explained in detail to you what He has forbidden you.”

Furthermore, if wine—which is the mother of all evils—becomes lawful by the agreement of the Muslims when it turns into vinegar of its own accord, then other impure substances have even greater reason to become pure through transformation. If a drop of wine were to fall into a Muslim’s vinegar without his choosing, and then undergo transformation, there would be even greater reason to regard it as pure.

If it is said:

“Wine became impure through transformation, so it becomes pure through transformation, unlike other substances. Moreover, when wine is deliberately turned into vinegar, it does not become pure.”

---

## Page 10923

The answer to the first objection is:

All impure substances became impure through transformation. A person eats food and drinks liquids that are pure; they then turn into blood, urine and excrement, becoming impure.

Likewise, an animal is pure while alive. When it dies, waste substances are retained within it, and its condition after death differs from its condition during life, so it becomes impure. This is why, according to the majority of scholars, its hide becomes pure through tanning, whether tanning is considered equivalent to life or to lawful slaughter. These are two well-known scholarly views, and the Sunnah indicates that tanning is equivalent to lawful slaughter.

As for wine deliberately turned into vinegar, the reason is that keeping wine is forbidden, whether it is kept for the purpose of making vinegar or otherwise. Purity is a blessing, and a blessing cannot be acquired through a forbidden act.

He was also asked:

A man travels in winter, gets wet from rain and dampness, and touches the animals’ foreparts, their saddles and other things that a traveller can scarcely avoid. He stays at places contaminated with impurity and spreads his bedding over them, along with other familiar circumstances of travel. Is this overlooked? And if it is overlooked, then, upon returning to his hometown, is he

---

## Page 10924

required to wash whatever has touched his clothes, bedding and furs? These are tied to those reins. The animals’ equipment is not free of impurities, and sometimes the reins are wet with urine or other moisture. He holds them in his hand and then touches his clothes with that hand, which may be sweaty in summer. Is all of this overlooked? If it is overlooked while travelling, is it also overlooked when he is at home, or must the things mentioned be washed? Many people do not wash them, and only a few take care to do so. Did the Companions wash such things, or did they overlook them? Would washing them be contrary to the Sunnah? The aim is to follow the Companions and their practice.

What about a man who, when a butcher with some grease on him touches his clothing or hand, washes whatever the butcher has touched? Is he right to do this, or is this obsessive misgiving?

Likewise, what about a man beside whom a butcher prays in the mosque, who says, “The place where this butcher is praying is not pure, because butchers do not take precautions against impurity on their bodies and clothes”? If a butcher shakes his hand, he washes it. Similarly, if an itinerant meat seller touches him, he washes whatever the seller has touched. Is he mistaken? What is the ruling on this, and what was the practice of the Companions?

What about a man who eats strips of meat, when those who prepare them customarily do not wash the meat? Is eating them forbidden or disliked, because butchers slaughter with a knife

---

## Page 10925

and use it to skin the animal without washing it? If this is overlooked with regard to eating, is it also overlooked when a man eats some of this food and some gets on his clothes and body, but he does not wash it off? What we seek to know is how such conduct would have been regarded had it occurred or been practised in the Companions’ presence. Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He answered:

Horses’ reins and tethers are pure by agreement of the imams, for horses themselves are pure by agreement. As for donkeys, however, there is disagreement: are they pure, impure, or of uncertain status? The correct view, beyond doubt, is that their hair is pure. We have already explained that a dog’s hair is pure, so a donkey’s hair is all the more deserving of this ruling. The uncertainty concerns only a donkey’s saliva: should it be treated like a dog’s saliva or a horse’s?

As for their reins and saddlecloths, they are deemed pure. At most, they may be soiled by the animals’ urine and dung. Scholars disagree about the urine of mules and donkeys. Some consider it pure, while others consider it impure. The latter are the majority, and this is the position of the four imams. But are small amounts of it overlooked? There are two views, both reported from Ahmad. Thus, if small amounts of their urine and dung are overlooked, whatever gets on the reins and other things is overlooked. This applies when the presence of impurity is certain.

When there is doubt, however, the basic presumption is purity, and taking precautions in such a case is obsessive misgiving. For if something gets on a man that may be pure or may be

---

## Page 10926

impure, the correct view is that neither avoiding it nor taking precautions is recommended. For ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—was passing beneath a waterspout with a companion when some water dripped from it onto his companion.

His companion asked, “Owner of the waterspout, is your water pure or impure?”

ʿUmar said, “Owner of the waterspout, do not tell him, for he is not obliged to know.”

According to the view that small amounts are overlooked, if someone spreads bedding over the dung of donkeys or similar animals in caravanserais or elsewhere, a small amount of such contamination is overlooked. As for horse dung, the correct view is that it is pure, so there is no need for it to be overlooked. Nor is he required to take any of these measures upon entering a town. Whether his hand is moist from water or otherwise, contact with the reins does him no harm. Washing the reins is an innovation; no such practice has been reported from the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them. Rather, they used to ride these animals, and Allah reminded them of this blessing in His words, Most High:

“And horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had a mule which he used to ride.”

It is also reported of him:

“He rode a donkey.”

There is no report that he instructed those who tended the animals to take precautions against such things.

Section

A butcher’s clothing and body are deemed pure, even if there is grease on them. Washing one’s hands because of this is an obsessive misgiving and an innovation. The place he occupies in the mosque or elsewhere is also pure.

---

## Page 10927

and the most that happens to a butcher is that he occasionally gets blood on himself. Touching him when there is no blood on him does no harm. Even if a small amount of blood gets onto the person touching him, it is overlooked, for small amounts of blood are excused. Any impurity on a butcher does not come from grease, for grease is pure and contains no impurity, while small amounts of blood are overlooked. Washing one’s hand after shaking hands with a butcher or an itinerant meat seller is an obsessive misgiving and excessive scrupulousness contrary to the Sunnah.

Al-Bukhārī mentioned that Umar ibn al-Khattāb performed ablution using water from a Christian woman’s jar. Moreover:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to kiss al-Hasan’s penis. He also prayed while carrying Umāmah, his daughter’s daughter: when he prostrated, he put her down, and when he stood up, he carried her.”

There are many similar reports demonstrating the latitude allowed in this matter.

Section

Eating roasted meat and strips of meat is permissible, whether the meat has been washed or not. Indeed, washing the meat of a slaughtered animal is an innovation. Throughout the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—would take meat, cook it and eat it without washing it. They would see streaks of blood in the cooking pot. This is because Allah only forbade them blood that flows out—that is, blood that is poured out and shed. He did not forbid the blood remaining in the veins. He did, however, forbid them to trace out the veins, as the Jews do, on account of whose wrongdoing

---

## Page 10928

Allah forbade them good things that had previously been lawful to them, and because they turned many away from Allah’s path.

The butcher’s knife, which he uses for slaughtering and skinning, does not need washing. Washing slaughtering knives is an innovation, as is washing swords. The early generations would simply wipe them. Hence, according to one of the two scholarly opinions, polished objects such as swords and mirrors may be wiped rather than washed if impurity gets onto them. This concerns impurities that are not excused. Anything established to be free of impurity requires neither washing nor wiping, while a small amount is excused. Whatever is excused may undoubtedly be carried, and one may walk with it.

Anything that may be eaten may also be touched during prayer or at other times. Yet not everything that may be touched during prayer or at other times may be eaten. Harmful poisons, for instance, may not be eaten, even if one has touched them, although they are pure and may be touched during prayer. This is because Allah Most High has forbidden us foul things and permitted us wholesome things: what is foul is harmful, and what is wholesome is beneficial. Whatever harms the outside of the body on contact causes far greater harm when eaten and mixed into the body. Yet not everything that harms the body when mixed into it is harmful through direct contact or touch.

For this reason, concerning what is excused when carried on one’s person—such as blood from wounds and boils, sheep’s blood adhering to a knife, and the like—it has been said that, if it falls into water or another liquid, it renders it impure. It is excused only in liquids, as noted earlier: Allah forbade only blood that flows out. Indeed, there were

---

## Page 10929

Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who would put a finger inside their nose, get blood on their fingers, and continue praying. Likewise, their hands would touch boils and wounds, yet it has not been reported that they avoided touching liquids until they had washed their hands. It is also established that they would put meat into a pot, leaving streaks of blood in the water. I know of no disagreement among the scholars that this is excused; they agree that it does not render the liquid impure. What difference, then, is there between blood being in the broth of a pot or another liquid and its being on a knife or something else? And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man has sixty qintārs of oil, by the Damascene measure, in a single well, and a mouse falls into it. Does this render it impure or not? Is it permissible to sell or use it? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. According to one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, this does not render it impure; rather, it may be sold and used, provided it has undergone no change. According to one of the two positions reported from him, liquids have the same ruling as water: if the liquid reaches two qullahs in volume, it does not become impure unless it changes. However, the impurity and whatever surrounds it must be discarded. The view that liquids have the same ruling as water has been adopted by a group

---

## Page 10930

of scholars, including al-Zuhrī and al-Bukhārī, the compiler of the Sahīh. This has also been cited as a position reported from Mālik. It is likewise the position of Abū Hanīfah, who treated water and other liquids alike both when they come into contact with impurity and when they are used to remove impurity. Regarding the removal of impurity, this is also a position reported from Ahmad. However, Abū Hanīfah held that mere contact renders them impure, whereas the majority of the leading scholars disagreed: they did not consider mere contact to render a large quantity impure, though they differed over a small quantity.

Some jurists considered the evidence to indicate that when something impure falls into something pure, it renders it impure. Others said that it does so only when its effect becomes apparent. If, however, it is wholly absorbed into the other substance and transformed, there are no grounds for declaring that substance impure. This is comparable to wine turning into vinegar without deliberate human action: it is then pure and lawful by agreement of the leading scholars. His position regarding water, however, is well known. There is evidence supporting this, which we have set out at length elsewhere.

There is no evidence that it is impure, either in the Book of Allah or in the Sunnah of His Messenger. The principal argument of those who declared it impure is their reliance on a hadith narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “He was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter and replied: ‘If it is solid, discard the mouse and whatever surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter. But if it is liquid, do not

---

## Page 10931

go near it.’” Even if this hadith established anything, it would establish only the impurity of the clarified butter into which the mouse fell. How, then, can it serve as proof when the hadith is weak—indeed, invalid? Ma‘mar made an error in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī, an error well known to the foremost hadith critics, as al-Tirmidhī related from al-Bukhārī.

Those jurists who believed that it met the conditions for an authentic hadith were unaware of its hidden defect, which establishes its invalidity. Knowledge of hidden defects is among the specialized fields mastered by the leading hadith scholars. Thus, in his Sahīh, al-Bukhārī explained what demonstrates the unsoundness of this version, and that the authentic hadith supports the purity of the clarified butter more strongly than its impurity. He said:

“Chapter: When a Mouse Falls into Solid or Melted Clarified Butter

‘Abdān narrated to us, saying: ‘Abd Allāh—meaning Ibn al-Mubārak—narrated to us, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, that he was asked about an animal—a mouse or otherwise—that dies in oil or clarified butter, whether solid or liquid. He said:

‘It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave instructions concerning a mouse that had died in clarified butter. He ordered that whatever was near it be discarded, after which the clarified butter was eaten.’

In the hadith transmitted by ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, it is stated:

‘The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied: “Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat the clarified butter.”’”

Thus, al-Bukhārī related from Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī—the most knowledgeable person in the Muslim community concerning the Sunnah in his time—that he ruled that when a mouse dies in oil or clarified butter, whether solid or liquid, it and whatever is near it should be discarded.

---

## Page 10932

and cited as evidence the hadith he narrated from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He said: ‘Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat the clarified butter.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say, “If it is liquid, do not go near it.” Rather, this wording is invalid. Al-Bukhārī, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned this to show that anyone who attributed to al-Zuhrī the narration of this distinction in the hadith had misreported him. Al-Zuhrī gave a general ruling covering both solid and melted clarified butter, citing this very hadith as evidence. This is especially significant since clarified butter in the Hijāz is more often melted than solid. Indeed, it has been said that it is never solid in the Hijāz at all.

The Prophet’s unrestricted answer, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, without any distinction, therefore entails general applicability, since the question is understood as being repeated in the answer. It is as though he said: “If a mouse falls into clarified butter, discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter.” Not asking for further details about a reported situation, despite the possibility of differing circumstances, has the force of a statement expressed in general terms. This applies if clarified butter in the Hijāz can be either solid or melted. If, however, solid clarified butter is rare or nonexistent there, then the hadith explicitly establishes that when a mouse falls into melted clarified butter, it and whatever surrounds it are to be discarded, and the clarified butter may be eaten.

This was the ruling al-Zuhrī gave, for his position is that water, whether in a small or large quantity, does not become impure unless it undergoes a change. Near the beginning of his Sahīh, al-Bukhārī mentioned that water and other liquids are treated alike. We have discussed this issue, its supporting evidence, and the scholars’ statements concerning it at length

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Are Frankish cheese and broadcloth disliked? Has any imam whose opinion is authoritative declared them impure, given that the cheese is coated with pig fat, as is the broadcloth?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

Those who regard cheese imported from Frankish lands as disliked have mentioned two reasons:

First, pig fat is placed between the cheeses when they are transported aboard ships.

Second, they do not slaughter the animals from which the rennet is obtained in the prescribed manner. Rather, they strike the cattle on the head and do not slaughter them in the prescribed manner.

As for the first reason, at most this renders the surface of the cheese impure. Once the surface is scraped off or washed, the cheese becomes pure. For the following is established in the Sahīh: “The Prophet

---

## Page 10937

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was asked about a mouse that had fallen into ghee, and said: ‘Throw it away, along with the ghee around it, and eat your ghee.’” If contact with a mouse does not render all the ghee impure, how could contact with impure fat render the inside of the cheese impure? Moreover, removing its outer layer is required only when it is certain that impurity has touched it. Mere doubt does not require this.

As for the second reason, it is known that they do not leave all the livestock they wound without proper slaughter. Indeed, it has been said that they do this only to cattle. It has also been said that they do this until the animal falls, then slaughter it properly. Such a practice does not make their slaughtered animals unlawful. Rather, when the unlawful is mixed with the lawful among a number too large to count—as when a man's sister is indistinguishable among the inhabitants of a town, or carrion and usurped property are mixed among the possessions of its people—this does not make everything in the town unlawful, just as when a sister is confused with an unrelated woman, or a properly slaughtered animal with one that died without proper slaughter. Thus, what has been mentioned does not make their slaughtered animals unlawful when the circumstances of their slaughter are unknown.

Even supposing that the cheese is made with rennet from an animal that died without proper slaughter, scholars hold two well-known views on this matter:

The first is that it is permissible and pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him.

The second is that it is unlawful and impure, as held by Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad according to

the other report. There is a well-known disagreement concerning the milk and rennet of an animal that died without proper slaughter: are they pure or impure? The item itself is pure, and whenever its impurity is doubtful, the presumption is purity. Even if we were certain that some items of a particular kind were impure while others were not, we would not judge every item of that kind impure, nor would we judge impure an item whose contamination remained doubtful.

However, if someone is certain that the cloth is impure, or wishes to dispel doubt, washing it purifies it. It is merely wool that has come into contact with impure grease. Urine and blood affect cotton and linen garments more severely and cling to them more tenaciously. Yet the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to a woman whose garment had been stained with menstrual blood:
