He—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

To proceed:

We were gathered to deepen our understanding of the religion and examine the grounds of the rulings prescribed by the Sharia—clarifying their scope, establishing them, setting out their foundations, and elaborating their details. The discussion turned to explaining the ruling on semen from humans and other ritually pure animals, and on the dung of livestock lawful to eat: are these pure or impure? Our companions wished to have the discussion recorded, allowing for some additions or omissions, so I wrote the following for them. I say—and there is no power nor might except through Allah:

This discussion is built around a foundational principle and two sections.

As for the foundational principle:

---

## Page 10940

know that the fundamental rule concerning all existing things, however varied their kinds and characteristics, is that they are unrestrictedly lawful for human beings and ritually pure: people are not forbidden to use, handle, or touch them. This is a comprehensive statement, a general principle, and a valuable proposition of immense benefit and far-reaching blessing. Those versed in the Sharia turn to it in countless matters of conduct and situations arising in people’s lives. It is supported by ten proofs from the Sharia that I presently recall. These are:

The Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and following the path of the believers—all brought together in His words, Exalted is He:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

And His words:

“Your ally is none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe.”

Then come the methods of analogy and reflection, and the approaches of reasoned judgment and discernment.

The first category: the Book

This comprises several verses. The first is His saying, Exalted is He:

“It is He who created for you all that is on the earth.”

This addresses all people, since the passage begins with His words:

“O mankind, worship your Lord.”

The reasoning is that He declares that He created everything on earth for people, relating these things to them through the preposition li- (“for”). This preposition expresses a relationship: it indicates that the thing so related is assigned to the one to whom it is related, and that the latter is entitled to it in whatever manner is appropriate. This meaning applies throughout its uses, as when people say, “The wealth belongs to Zayd,” or “The saddle is for the riding animal,” and similar expressions. It follows, then, that people have been granted possession of, and enabled to make use of, everything on earth

---

## Page 10941

as a grace and blessing from Allah. Certain things are excepted from this—namely, foul things—because they harm people in their worldly life or their life to come. Everything else therefore remains permissible by virtue of the verse.

The second verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“Why should you not eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned, when He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you, except that to which you are compelled by necessity?”

The verse provides evidence in two ways. First, He rebuked and reproached them for refraining from eating that over which Allah’s name had been mentioned, before declaring it lawful by its specific name. Had things not been unrestrictedly permissible, they would not have incurred blame or reproach, for neither would have been warranted if their ruling were unknown or if they were forbidden.

The second way is that He said:

“He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you.”

Explaining in detail means making clear. He thus states that He has made the forbidden things clear. Whatever He has not declared forbidden is therefore not forbidden, and whatever is not forbidden is lawful, since there is nothing other than lawful or forbidden.

The third verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

Since everything on earth has been subjected to us, we may benefit from it, as explained above.

---

## Page 10942

The fourth verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“Say: I find nothing in what has been revealed to me that is forbidden for anyone to eat, unless it be carrion or blood poured out,”

to the end of the verse. Whatever he finds no prohibition against is not forbidden, and whatever is not forbidden is lawful. Similar to this verse is His saying:

“He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine,”

to the end of the verse. The particle “only” restricts the former to the latter; thus, forbidden things must be confined to those mentioned. The Book also establishes this comprehensive principle in other passages.

The second category: The Sunnah

Two hadiths come to mind here.

The first hadith: In the two Sahīh collections, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Muslim who incurs the greatest guilt is one who asks about something that has not been forbidden, and it is then forbidden because of his question.”

This indicates that things become forbidden only through a specific prohibition, as shown by his words, “has not been forbidden.” It also indicates that a prohibition may arise because of a question, thereby making clear that, without it, those things are not forbidden. This is the point being established.

The second hadith: Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan that Salmān al-Fārisī said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about clarified butter, cheese, and furs. He said: ‘What is lawful is what Allah has declared lawful in His Book, and what is forbidden is what Allah has forbidden in His Book. Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.’”

This provides evidence in two ways:

---

## Page 10943

The first is that he gave a ruling permitting it without restriction. The second is his saying:

“Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.”

This explicitly states that no sin is incurred regarding what He has remained silent about. His calling this a pardon is apparently—and Allah knows best—because declaring something lawful means authorizing its consumption through a specific pronouncement, while declaring it forbidden means prohibiting its consumption in the same way. As for what He has remained silent about, He has neither authorized it through a pronouncement specific to it nor prohibited it. One therefore returns to the foundational principle: there is no punishment until messengers have been sent. If something carries no punishment, it is not forbidden. The Sunnah contains much evidence for this principle.

The third category: Following the way of the believers and the testimony of Allah’s witnesses on His earth—those upright people who enjoin right and forbid wrong, who are protected from collectively agreeing upon error, and whom it is obligatory to follow.

I know of no disagreement among the scholars of earlier generations that whatever has not been prohibited by evidence is unrestricted and not barred. Many who have written on the principles of jurisprudence and its practical rulings have explicitly stated this. I believe that some of them have reported consensus on this, either with certainty or with a conviction approaching certainty.

If it is asked: How can there be consensus on this, when you know that people have differed concerning things before the coming of the messengers and the revelation of the Books? Is the basic rule concerning them prohibition or permissibility? Or is their ruling unknown? Or do they have no ruling at all? Moreover, the presumption that an existing state continues is an accepted form of evidence, and some of those who have written on the principles of

---

## Page 10944

jurisprudence, both among our scholars and others, have held that the ruling applicable to things before the coming of revealed law is presumed to continue afterward, and that whoever holds prohibition to be the basic rule concerning things maintains that ruling until evidence establishes their permissibility?

I say: This is a later view whose basis has not been transmitted from any early scholar of recognized standing. It has been established that, after the coming of the messengers, such things are unrestricted. The ruling derived from that original presumption has been superseded by the revealed evidence I have mentioned. I do not deny that someone who has not fully grasped the sources of rulings, and who lacks discernment where confusion may arise, might extend what applied before revealed law to what comes afterward. Yet this is a grave error which, if pointed out to him, he would recognize. Like an error in arithmetic, it neither breaches the sanctity of consensus nor undermines the established paths of adherence.

People have indeed differed over whether the situation envisaged in that question is possible or impossible, since the earth has never been without a prophet sent by Allah, Adam himself having been a prophet to whom Allah spoke. This corresponds to their disagreement over whether lands can be without a revealed law, although the correct view, in our judgment, is that this is possible. Some have framed the question in terms of someone born on an island, alongside other such discussions. All this makes clear that the question has no practical application: it is purely theoretical, with no bearing on practice, like discussions of the origin of languages and similar matters. Moreover, the incontrovertible truth is

---

## Page 10945

that before revealed law there is neither a declaration of permissibility nor a declaration of prohibition. Since there was no prohibition, that absence is presumed to continue and remain in effect; thus the position remains the same now. The point is that these things entail neither sin nor punishment.

As for reasoning from similarities and parallels, and exercising independent judgment concerning comprehensive principles, there are many arguments, some of which we shall indicate.

First:

Allah, glorified be He, created these things and placed enjoyment and benefit for human beings in them; some may even become indispensable to them. He, glorified be He, is Generous, Glorious, Munificent, Merciful, Self-Sufficient, and the One upon whom all depend. Knowing this leads to the knowledge that He does not punish or torment a person merely for enjoying these things. This is the point to be established.

Second:

They provide benefit free from harm, and are therefore permissible, like everything else whose permissibility is expressly stated. Revelation indicates that the ruling is attached to this characteristic, in His words:

“He makes lawful for them what is good and forbids them what is foul.”

Thus, everything beneficial is good, and everything harmful is foul. There is also the evident appropriateness, apparent to anyone possessed of reason, of associating benefit with permissibility and harm with prohibition. There is, moreover, their correlation: prohibition accompanies harm, being present in carrion, blood, pork, creatures with fangs or talons, wine, and other things harmful to people, and absent in livestock, milk, and other such things.

Third:

These things either have a ruling or they do not.

---

## Page 10946

and the former is correct, while the latter is false by consensus. If these things have a ruling, then obligation, reprehensibility, and recommendation are all known to be entirely inapplicable; only permissibility remains. Prohibition is invalid because there is no evidence for it, whether explicit or inferred. Thus, only permissibility remains, which is the point to be established.

Having established this principle, we say: the default ruling concerning physical substances is ritual purity, for three reasons.

First:

A ritually pure substance is one that a person may come into contact with, touch directly, and carry during prayer. An impure substance is the opposite. Most of the preceding evidence encompasses every way of benefiting from things: eating, drinking, wearing, touching, and so forth. Thus, ritual purity is shown to be included within permissibility, which is the point to be established. The other two arguments are supplementary.

Second:

If it is established that the default ruling is that these things may be eaten and drunk, then their coming into contact and mingling with people is all the more deserving of being deemed permissible by default. This is because food mingles and blends with the body, which grows from it, so that it becomes the body's substance and constituent material. If it is foul, the body becomes foul and consequently deserves the Fire. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every body nourished by ill-gotten gains is more deserving of the Fire.”

Paradise is pure, and none but the pure will enter it.

As for whatever touches the body and comes into direct contact with it, this too affects the body externally, just as impurities affect our bodies and the clothes in contact with them. Their effect, however, is less than that of something that mingles and blends with the body. Thus, if it is established that a thing may permissibly mingle and blend with the body, then the permissibility of

---

## Page 10947

its coming into contact with and directly touching the body is all the more firmly established. This is conclusive and admits of no doubt. It follows that whatever is forbidden to touch or come into contact with is also forbidden to mingle and blend with the body, but the converse does not hold. Thus, everything ritually impure is forbidden to eat, but not everything forbidden to eat is ritually impure. This is a thoroughly precise distinction.

Third:

All jurists agree that the default ruling concerning physical substances is ritual purity, that impure substances are exhaustively enumerated, and that whatever falls outside those defined limits is ritually pure. They say the same concerning what invalidates ablution, what necessitates a full ritual bath, whom one may not marry, and similar matters. For this is the ultimate distinction between opposing categories: you find one side precisely defined and delimited, while the other is unrestricted and open-ended. Allah Most High is the Guide to what is correct.

Chapter One

On the Ritual Purity of Dung and Urine from Animals and Birds Whose Consumption Is Not Forbidden

There are several proofs for this.

The First Proof:

The general principle is that all physical substances are ritually pure until their impurity becomes evident. Everything whose impurity has not been made clear to us is therefore ritually pure. The impurity of these substances has not been made clear to us; therefore, they are ritually pure. The first premise of this proof has already been established through manifest proofs and compelling arguments.

As for the second, we say:

Negative claims fall into

---

## Page 10948

two kinds:

The first consists of negations whose scope we can delimit and fully comprehend. Examples include our knowledge that there are not two suns or two moons aloft in the sky; that we have only one direction of prayer; and that no prophet will come after Muhammad. Indeed, we know that there is no god but Allah; that whatever is not between the two covers is not part of the Quran; and that no fasting has been prescribed except that of the month of Ramadan. Other examples include a person’s knowledge that there are no dirhams in … (1) before (2), that he has not changed, that he has not been fed, and that he did not sleep last night. The examples are too numerous to enumerate. All these are negations known with certainty, demonstrating the error of anyone who declares without qualification that testimony concerning a negative fact is inadmissible.

The second kind:

This concerns matters whose negation or nonexistence cannot be known with certainty. Some of these are nevertheless strongly believed and judged highly probable, while others are not. When we find a ruling contingent upon a negative claim of this second kind, what is required is that we judge the negation to hold and believe it highly probable. Reasoning from the presumption that an established state continues, from the absence of evidence restricting a general statement, and from the absence of any reason to interpret an expression figuratively all belongs to this category.

Thus, when we have searched and carefully examined the evidence indicating that these substances are ritually impure—a question people have discussed for hundreds of years—and have found only the familiar proofs, we can testify firmly, to the best of our knowledge, that there is no other evidence on this matter. We therefore say that the present argument can be fully established only by overturning the evidence adduced for ritual impurity

> (1) A blank in the original.

---

## Page 10949

and refuting it. Two approaches have been used to argue for this: one based on transmitted texts and the other on rational reasoning.

As for the approach based on transmitted texts, it relies on the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by two graves and said: ‘They are indeed being punished, yet they are not being punished for anything great. As for one of them, he did not shield himself from urine.’”

Another version reads: “did not keep himself free of it.”

The word al-bawl (urine) is a generic noun bearing the definite article, and therefore conveys generality. It is like al-insān (mankind) in Allah’s words:

“Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe.”

The preferred position is that generic nouns convey generality just as plural nouns do. I do not mean collective nouns whose individual unit is distinguished from the collective by the ending -ah, such as tamr (dates), burr (wheat), and shajar (trees), for these undoubtedly have the same status as plurals. Rather, I mean a singular generic noun denoting a thing and others like it, such as insān (human being), rajul (man), faras (horse), thawb (garment), and similar words.

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke of punishment on account of urine as a general category, one must guard against and keep oneself free of urine as a general category. This therefore encompasses the urine of all creatures, both humans and beasts, whether lawful to eat or not. The urine of livestock thus falls within this generality, which is the point intended.

This argument has been relied upon by some who claim to reason from revelation and a measure of independent opinion. It has also been endorsed by some who affect cleverness, making it their refuge and recourse.

---

## Page 10950

The Second Approach: Rational Reasoning

This proceeds along three lines.

First: Drawing an analogy with urine already deemed unlawful. We say: these are urine and dung, and are therefore impure, like all other urine. This analogy requires demonstrating that the basis of the ruling in the original case is precisely its being urine or dung. This is indicated by the revealed texts, such as his statement:

“Guard yourselves against urine.”

And his statement:

“When urine came into contact with the garment of one of the Children of Israel, he would cut out the affected portion with scissors.”

The suitability of this rationale also supports it: urine and dung are foul and filthy, repugnant to people to a degree that calls for keeping clear of them. This accords with prohibition, encouraging people to cultivate noble character and wholesome habits. Its legal relevance is further supported by the impurity of the dung of creatures deemed foul.

Second: We say that, when we examine and investigate the dividing line between impure and pure substances, we find that, of the food transformed within animals’ bodies, whatever becomes part of the body is the wholesome portion, while whatever remains over is the foul portion. Hence it is called rajīʿ (returned matter): it is as though it was taken in and then returned—that is, sent back out.

Whatever foul matter emerges from the lower part of the body—such as faeces, urine, semen, wadhy (seminal fluid), and wady (post-urinary discharge)—is impure.

Whatever emerges from the upper part—such as tears, saliva, spittle, nasal mucus, and phlegm from the head—is pure. Whatever falls between the two, such as phlegm from the stomach, is subject to uncertainty.

---

## Page 10951

This distinction between what emerges from the upper and lower parts of the body has been reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and others like him. It is a sound observation concerning this difficult issue, which has not been fully understood—so much so that some have claimed that it is purely a devotional requirement and a test distinguishing those who obey from those who disobey. In our view, this statement has no substance on its own unless other considerations are added to it. Some have distinguished between what undergoes transformation within an animal’s stomach, such as dung and vomit, and what is transformed from the contents of its stomach, such as milk.

Once this is established, these kinds of urine and dung belong to the matter transformed within an animal’s body: its wholesome portion is refined, while its foul portion emerges through its rear and lower parts and is impure.

If a distinction is drawn on the grounds that the flesh of animals lawful to eat is wholesome, whereas the flesh of forbidden animals is foul, the response is:

An animal’s wholesomeness, nobility, and dignity do not entail the purity of its dung. Human flesh is forbidden only out of respect for human dignity and nobility; nevertheless, human urine is the foulest of all urine.

Do you not yourselves say that death does not render a human being impure, and that whatever is severed from a person while alive is likewise pure, as stated in the transmitted report, even though human flesh may not be eaten? If the honour accorded to a creature entailed the purity of its dung, human beings would have the highest standing in this regard. This is the crux and essence of the issue.

Third: It occupies the lowest degree of foulness and the level

---

## Page 10952

of the most repulsive substances. People’s own feelings bear witness to this, as do their natural dispositions and temperaments: scarcely anyone places it on the same footing as an animal’s milk and offspring. We recognize only two categories: pure and impure. Once it falls outside the category of pure substances, it enters that of impurities. The treatment generally accorded to it—keeping it at a distance and avoiding it—is that accorded to impurities, so it cannot be pure. For when a substance resembles competing legal precedents, it is assigned to the one it most closely resembles. It stands between milk and other kinds of urine, and resembles the latter more closely.

This is reinforced by the words of Allah Most High:

“From between digested matter and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink it.”

It has been established that blood is impure; so too is digested matter, that His power and mercy may be manifest in bringing forth something wholesome from between two foul substances. All this is further clarified by the fact that it shares the physical characteristics, colour, smell, and taste of other urine. How, then, can a distinction be drawn between them despite these shared features, which almost make the essential nature of one identical to that of the other?

The first line of reasoning is analogy by comparison: attaching the ruling to the shared feature established by the evidence.

The second is causal analogy: refining the operative basis of the ruling and formulating a universal principle.

The third is to distinguish it from the category of pure substances, so that it cannot be included among them. These, then, are the forms of analogy: a foundation, a connection, and a distinction.

The first line of reasoning provides the foundation and links it with other impure substances.

---

## Page 10953

And the second is the underlying principle, general rule, and governing criterion under which it falls. The third distinguishes it from pure substances; this is inverse analogy.

We now turn to the answer to these arguments, seeking Allah’s help.

The first line of reasoning is very weak for two reasons. First, the lām in al-bawl (“urine”) marks definiteness, referring to what is already known to those addressed. If a particular referent is already known, that is what is intended. Where no particular referent is already known, the article denotes the genus: either the entire genus, according to the preferred view, or the genus without qualification, according to some—and it may sometimes have this latter sense.

Experts in the Arabic language and in the interpretation of discourse have expressly stated that the article is understood as designating a genus only when there is no previously known referent. When there is such a referent, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

The messenger is known through having been mentioned earlier. Likewise, in His words:

“Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you”

the Messenger is a particular individual, since he is already known and recognized. In such cases, the article does not designate the genus denoted by the noun, such that one would then consider whether it denotes the entire genus or the genus without qualification. Understand this well, for it is an excellent approach to interpretation.

Realities are of three kinds: universal, particular, and unqualified. Thus, when you say “the human being,” you may mean the entire genus, or you may mean the unqualified

---

## Page 10954

genus, or you may mean a particular member of that genus.

As for the universal genus, it exists in hearts and minds as knowledge, recognition, and conception. As for a particular member of the genus, such as Zayd or ʿAmr, it exists wherever that individual is located. This is what is called existence in concrete reality, outside the mind. It may also be conceived in the mind in this way, as a distinct particular.

As for the unqualified genus—such as the human being considered apart from universality and particularity, which is called the reality itself or the genus without qualification—just as it is unrestricted in itself, it is unrestricted as to its locus. However, it is apprehended only by the mind, which is therefore regarded as its locus in this respect. It is sometimes also regarded as existing in concrete individuals, on the grounds that every human being has a share in humanity without qualification. What exists in a particular individual of the species is that individual’s share and portion.

Once this is clear, his statement, “For he did not keep himself free of urine,” refers to the urine already understood in this context: the urine that would soil him, namely, his own urine.

This is further supported by seven considerations.

The first is the wording reported:

“For he did not ensure that he was clear of urine.”

Ensuring such clearance can only concern one’s own urine, for it means ascertaining that the penis is clear, just as one ascertains that the womb is free of a child.

---

## Page 10955

Second: The lām of the definite article can take the place of a possessive construction. Thus, “from urine” is equivalent to “from his urine.” This resembles the statement, “With the gates open to them,” meaning “their gates.”

Third: This hadith has been transmitted through authentic chains with the wording, “For he did not keep himself free of his own urine.” This explains the other version.

Furthermore, this variation in wording arose later than Mansūr; al-A‘mash narrated it from Mujāhid, from Ibn ‘Abbās. It is well known that a hadith transmitter does not combine these two wordings. The default assumption, and the apparent conclusion, is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not repeat this statement. It is therefore evident that they transmitted it by meaning, and it is unclear which wording was the original. Moreover, if the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did use both wordings, then although the meaning of one could either agree with or differ from that of the other, the apparent conclusion is that they agree. This is clarified by the fact that the hadith recounts what happened when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by two graves, and this was clearly a single incident.

Fourth: It reports that a particular individual would be soiled by urine and would not keep himself free of it. It is well known that what ordinarily occurs is that a person is soiled by his own urine.

Fifth: Al-Hasan said, “All urine is impure.” Yet he also said, “There is no harm in the urine of sheep and goats.” It is therefore evident that, in his usage, “urine” without qualification means human urine.

---

## Page 10956

Sixth: This is what a listener understands when his mind is free of obsessive misgivings and tamrīh. From the statement, “For he did not keep himself free of urine,” he understands only the man’s own urine. Indeed, it would be true to say that all kinds of urine—from camels, sheep, and bulls—never even occur to most people.

Seventh: It suffices to say that if the wording could mean either his own urine, as this is what is ordinarily understood, or urine of every kind, neither interpretation may be adopted without evidence. The argument would therefore be inconclusive. By my life, however, this is merely a concession for argument’s sake. What we have already explained is an established principle: the wording must be understood as referring to the familiar kind of urine—one particular kind—namely, a person’s own urine, which commonly soils him and splashes onto his thighs and lower legs. He may take its removal lightly and fail to cleanse himself thoroughly after urinating. As for another person’s urine, although it carries the same ruling as his own, this does not follow from the wording itself. Rather, it follows from their being identical in nature, and identity in nature entails identity in ruling.

Do you not see that a person is hardly ever soiled by someone else’s urine, and that if he were, he would find it distressing? In this hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was speaking only of something that actually and commonly occurs, saying:

“Guard yourselves against urine, for most of the punishment of the grave is due to it.”

How, then, could most of the punishment of the grave be due to something that hardly ever soils anyone? This is perfectly clear.

---

## Page 10957

The second argument:

Even if the wording encompassed all urine, we shall present specific evidence establishing the ritual purity of this kind, which requires excluding it from that general designation. It is a well-established principle of legal theory that when specific and general evidence conflict, the specific evidence takes precedence. Disregarding it would nullify it and deprive it of effect, whereas acting upon it merely excludes some cases covered by the general wording. Using general wording while intending a narrower scope is by no means unusual in speech; rather, it is exceedingly common.

Even if we conceded that the conflicting evidence carried equal weight in this respect, our evidence has other grounds for precedence and preference, including its greater number, its being acted upon, and other considerations that we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

One of the surprising arguments on which some have relied is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Most of the punishment of the grave is due to urine.”

The same response applies here as to the preceding evidence. Moreover, we know that a person is only rarely soiled by someone else’s urine; what commonly soils him is his own. Had the Prophet intended to include a person’s own urine within a broader category, one kind of which frequently occasions punishment, this would have been equivalent to saying, “Most of the punishment of the grave is due to impurities.”

This person also relied on the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“None of you should pray when food is present, nor while holding back the two foul things.”

This means urine and feces. He claimed that this entails describing every kind of urine and feces as “foul”

---

## Page 10958

and that what is foul is forbidden and ritually impure. This argument is utterly untenable, for the wording does not extend at all beyond what a person is holding back.

As for his statement, “The designation encompasses the entire category,” he may be asked: What is this encompassing category? All urine and feces, or human urine and feces? It is well known that what each person holds back belongs to the same category as what others hold back. Whatever is not held back at all has no place in the hadith. Such, then, is the opponent’s principal argument.

As for the rational line of argument, it may be answered in two ways: generally and in detail.

The detailed response to the first argument has two aspects:

First: We do not concede that the effective cause in the original case is simply that it is urine or dung. Their appeal to the indications of the scriptural texts has already been answered: what those texts mean is human urine.

As for their claim that this rationale is appropriate, we say: The ruling must be based either on the mere fact that people find something foul and repulsive, or on a specified degree of such revulsion and repugnance.

If the former is intended, everything considered foul and repulsive would have to be deemed ritually impure. Nasal mucus, saliva, and phlegm would therefore have to be ritually impure, as would semen, which the transmitted report mentions removing from clothing. Indeed, people may recoil from some of these things more strongly than from the dung of animals whose meat is lawful to eat—for example, mucus from a person with leprosy when it is mixed

---

## Page 10959

with food, or an elderly man’s phlegm when put into a drink. Such things may even cause some people to be overcome by vomiting.

If, however, the effective cause is a specified degree of revulsion, this may be valid, but the dividing line must be established between the degree of repugnance that entails ritual impurity and that which does not. He has not established this. Indeed, demonstrating the repulsiveness of these very substances may undermine the proposed threshold.

Moreover, the degrees of repulsiveness relevant to legal causes and rulings are generally known only through revelation. Thus we say: Whenever a category is ruled ritually impure, we know that its repulsiveness is severe; whenever a category is not ruled ritually impure, we know that its repulsiveness is not severe. We therefore end up inferring from the ruling which degree of the effective cause is legally relevant. Whenever we doubt the ruling, our doubt concerning the effective cause is even greater. This argument therefore fails. As for the evidence establishing its legal relevance, just as it supports repulsiveness in general, it also supports intense repugnance and extreme revulsion.

Second, we say:

Why may the effective cause in the original case not be that it is the urine of an animal whose meat is lawful to eat? This effective cause operates without exception, by the agreement of both ourselves and our opponents in this question. If the converse relationship is not required, our purpose has been achieved. If, however, it is a condition for effective causes, we say concerning it what they said concerning the consistent operation of the effective cause—and with greater justification, since they have been opposed on that point

---

## Page 10960

and failure of the converse relationship is less problematic than failure of consistent operation. If the two classes differ with respect to meat, bones, milk, and hair, why may they not differ with respect to dung and urine? This connection is clearer: each of these substances is either a part of the animal or something produced by it, and therefore follows the ruling governing the rest, by analogy between a part and the whole.

If it is said:

“This is contradicted by the human being: he is ritually pure, his milk is pure, and so too are his other bodily fluids and waste products. Yet his feces and urine are among the foulest impurities. Thus, in his case, a distinction exists between urine and other substances.”

We reply:

Know that human beings differ from other animals in this matter in both directions. What is required, therefore, is to draw analogies between animals, placing them in one category distinct from human beings, and to place human beings in a separate category. Do you not see that, according to the preferred view, a human being does not become ritually impure upon death, whereas animals do? Yet human urine is more severely impure than theirs.

Do you not see that the prohibition against consuming human beings differs from the prohibition against consuming other animals, owing to the dignity and inviolability of humankind? Thus, the prohibition includes disbelievers as well as others, and it is not even permissible to tan human skin, although human urine is more severely and gravely impure. These and other considerations show that human urine differs from other human waste products more markedly than animal urine differs from their other waste products, whether because of the prevalence of

---

## Page 10961

contact with it, lest it be treated lightly, or for some other reason best known to Allah. Moreover, human feces and urine possess a foulness, stench, and filth not generally found in other urine and dung. In short, making the purity or impurity of urine follow that of the flesh yields a more consistent rule than the alternatives. And Allah knows best.

As for the second argument, we say: That principle is conceded in the case of human beings. What has been transmitted from the early generations concerns only human beings: the transformation of substances within their bodies and their discharge from the upper or lower part. On what grounds, then, can the same be asserted of all other animals? The distinction has already been indicated. Furthermore, their opponents dispute most of the rulings they apply to animals, saying:

“It is established that an animal whose flesh is foul also has foul milk and semen, unlike the human being. Thus, this rule concerning transformation is invalid.”

Indeed, they may say that all moist bodily products of animals share the same ruling: an animal whose flesh is wholesome also has wholesome milk, urine, dung, semen, sweat, saliva, and tears. An animal whose flesh is foul also has foul milk, saliva, urine, dung, semen, sweat, and tears. This is Ahmad’s position according to the well-known report from him, and others have also held it.

In short, milk and semen provide conclusive evidence supporting their distinction between human beings and other animals, as well as some evidence that the bodily products of animals share the same ruling. On this basis, it may be said that, in the case of human beings, a distinction is drawn between what emerges from the upper and lower parts for reasons best known to Allah. For a human being stands upright, and all his impurities are in his upper parts. And his stomach, which is the site of the transformation of

---

## Page 10962

food and drink, lies in the lower part of the body. The breast and similar organs, however, are in the upper part. This is not so with an animal: its udder is toward its rear, yet contains wholesome milk. There is no hope of establishing rulings through conjectures such as these.

As for the third argument, it rests on distinguishing this substance from other pure substances. If the distinction is based on its being repugnant, it is invalidated by all the other repugnant substances, some of which may be even more repugnant. If it is based on a particular degree of repugnance, that degree must be precisely defined. This has already been explained.

The general response has three aspects:

First: This is an analogy set against explicit transmitted reports, and is therefore fundamentally unsound. Whoever treats as equivalent things that the Sunnah distinguishes echoes the statement of those who said:

“Trade is only like usury, whereas Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury.”

Thus, the Sunnah has declared one pure and the other impure.

Second: This is an analogy concerning a subject whose underlying causes and determining factors have not become apparent, and whose rationale has not become clear, and what … (1). Rather, people hold two positions on this:

One group says: This is purely a matter of submission and a test of obedience. There is therefore no room for analogy or extending rulings to other cases, nor for treating cases as equivalent or distinguishing between them.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 10963

and the other says:

“Its underlying causes and reasons are too subtle for us to grasp, and its workings and ways remain hidden from us. Allah has sent us a Messenger to purify us and teach us the Book and wisdom. He sent him to us when we knew nothing, so we simply do what we have seen him do. The Sunnah is not to be challenged with analogies or opposed with people’s opinions. Religion is not based on personal opinion; rather, opinion must be questioned when measured against religion. All people of understanding agree that analogy is inadmissible in matters of this kind.”

Third: It may be said that this entire argument rests on equating the urine of animals whose meat is lawful to eat with that of animals whose meat is unlawful to eat. Yet this treats two different things as equivalent. The urine of animals forbidden to eat has a foul smell, whereas some excrement from animals lawful to eat may even have a pleasant smell, such as the droppings of gazelles and other animals. Even when its smell is not pleasant, it does not smell like that of other animals. Its composition also generally differs, for it contains substances from what is lawful. This concerns the substance of the issue, to which we shall return, Allah willing, at the end of the discussion.

The second proof:

The widely transmitted hadith reported by the compilers of the Sahīh collections and others, narrated by Anas ibn Mālik:

“Some people from ʿUkl or ʿUraynah came to Medina and fell ill because its climate did not agree with them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered that they be provided with milk-producing she-camels and instructed them to drink their urine and milk. When they recovered, they killed the Messenger of Allah’s herdsman, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and drove away the camels.”

He then related the rest of the hadith. The point of evidence is that he permitted them to drink the urine, which would inevitably come into contact with their mouths, hands, clothes, and vessels. Thus, if it were

---

## Page 10964

impure, they would have been obliged to purify their mouths, hands, and clothes for prayer, and to purify their vessels. This would therefore have had to be explained to them, for clarification may not be delayed beyond the time it is needed. Yet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not explain to them that they were obliged to remove any of it that came into contact with them. This indicates that it is not impure. Clearly, had camel urine been like human urine, he would most likely have warned them very sternly about it.

Anyone who says that they knew it was impure and knew that purification from impurities was obligatory has gone far beyond what is plausible and advanced a claim whose falsity can be known with certainty, for several reasons:

(First: When the Sharia was first instituted, its rulings were less widely known. After Islam spread and knowledge was transmitted and disseminated, they became clearer and more evident. If, even to this day, its impurity has not become clear to us—rather, most people regard it as pure, and the Successors generally held this view; indeed, Abū Tālib and others said, “The early generations neither regarded it as impure nor took precautions against it.”

Abū Bakr ibn al-Mundhir—on whom most later scholars rely when reporting consensus and disagreement—mentioned that the early generations generally regarded urine as pure. He then said:

“Al-Shāfiʿī said: ‘All urine is impure.’”

He said:

“We know of no one before al-Shāfiʿī who said that the urine and droppings of livestock are impure.”

(I say: It has been reported that Ibn ʿUmar was asked about the urine of a she-camel, and he said:

---

## Page 10965

“Wash off any of it that gets on you.”

Al-Zuhrī, when asked about camel urine that gets on a shepherd, said, “It should be sprinkled with water.” Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān said concerning the urine of sheep and camels, “It should be washed off.” Abū Hanīfah’s school regards it as impure, subject to certain distinctions they make concerning it. Perhaps Ibn al-Mundhir meant the view that both small and large amounts of urine and dung must be avoided, for no such view has reached us from any of the early generations. Perhaps Ibn ʿUmar instructed that it be washed off just as mucus, saliva, semen, and similar substances are washed from clothing.

It is authentically reported that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī prayed on a spot containing animal dung, although open ground lay before him. He said, “Here and there are the same.” Anas ibn Mālik said, “There is nothing wrong with the urine of any ruminant.” I know of no Companion who held it to be impure; rather, their position was that it was pure—apart from what was reported from Ibn ʿUmar, if he intended impurity. How, then, could those people have known this?

Second: Even if it were impure, the obligation to purify oneself of impurity is not self-evident. A group of the Successors and others denied that this was obligatory with regard to clothing. How, then, could those people have known it?

Third: Even if this had been widely known among the Companions, it would not follow that those people knew it, for they had only recently left behind pre-Islamic ignorance and disbelief. Indeed, they were

---

## Page 10966

unaware of the different prayers, their prescribed numbers and times, and other manifest religious ordinances. They were therefore all the more likely to be unaware of an obscure condition concerning an obscure matter—especially since these people had not acquired even the slightest understanding of religion, which is why they apostatized. Nor had they associated with people of knowledge and wisdom. Rather, when they embraced Islam and became ill from the unwholesome conditions, he instructed them to live in the desert. How, then, I wonder, could they have known about this obscure matter?

Fourth: In his teaching and guidance, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not leave instruction to others. Rather, he explained to each person whatever they needed to know. This is well known to anyone thoroughly acquainted with the transmitted Sunnah.

Fifth: The impurity of this dung is no more obvious than the impurity of human urine, which was known even to maidens in their curtained chambers and secluded quarters. Yet he warned the Emigrants and Helpers about it, although they had been endowed with knowledge and faith. Thus, on this reasoning, rough Bedouins would have known more about obscure matters than the Emigrants and Helpers knew about obvious ones. You can see what this amounts to.

Sixth: He distinguished between the urine and the milk and treated them both in the same manner. Mentioning two things together, even if it does not establish their equal status, must at least give rise to uncertainty. Thus, even if clarification had not otherwise been obligatory, pairing it with something pure would have required distinguishing between the two, if such a distinction were valid.

---

## Page 10967

The hadith also supports another inference, though this is disputed: he permitted them to drink it, whereas, had it been forbidden and impure, he would not have permitted them to do so. I know of no one who disputes the permissibility of treating illness with camel urine, as established by the Sunnah. However, scholars have differed over the basis of this ruling. Some hold that it is permissible without restriction, whether for medicinal purposes or otherwise. Others hold that it is forbidden, and that he permitted it only for medicinal purposes. Still others hold that, besides being forbidden, it is also impure.

This line of argument requires another premise: that medicinal treatment with forbidden, impure substances is prohibited. There are several grounds for this.

First: The evidence establishing prohibition, such as the statements:

“Carrion has been forbidden to you,”

“Every fanged beast of prey is forbidden,”

and

“Intoxicants, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are an abomination,”

applies generally, whether these things are used medicinally or otherwise. Whoever distinguishes between the two cases thus separates what Allah has treated alike and restricts the scope of a general ruling; this is not permissible.

If it is said: “But He has permitted them in cases of necessity, and someone seeking treatment is compelled by necessity, so they become permissible for him. Alternatively, we may draw an analogy between permitting them to the sick and permitting them to the hungry, since both share a need for them. This is supported by the fact that illness waives such obligations as standing during prayer and fasting in Ramadan, and allows a transition from purification with water to purification with earth. Likewise, it permits otherwise prohibited things, since obligations and prohibitions are governed by the same principle. Further support for this concerns prohibited forms of adornment and clothing, such as gold and silk:

---

## Page 10968

the Sunnah has permitted using a gold prosthetic nose and securing teeth with gold. The Prophet also permitted al-Zubayr and ʿAbd al-Rahmān to wear silk because of an itch that afflicted them. These many precedents thus establish that prohibited things become permissible when there is a need for them.”

I reply:

It is indeed true that they become permissible in cases of necessity. However, medical treatment is not a necessity, for several reasons.

First: Many sick people—or most of them—recover without medical treatment, especially nomadic tent-dwellers, villagers, and those living in outlying regions. Allah heals them through the natural powers He has created within their bodies to overcome illness, or through what He makes available to them: some form of movement or work, an answered supplication, a beneficial ruqyah, strength of heart, sound reliance upon Him, or the many other means besides medicine. Eating, by contrast, is essential. Allah has made the bodies of living creatures dependent upon nourishment; without eating, a person would die. This establishes that medical treatment does not fall within the category of necessity at all.

Second: Eating in a case of necessity is obligatory. Masrūq said:

“Whoever is compelled by necessity to eat carrion, yet refuses to eat it and dies, will enter the Fire.”

Medical treatment, however, is not obligatory. Anyone who disputes this is refuted by the Sunnah account of the black woman whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave a choice between patiently bearing her affliction and entering Paradise, and having him supplicate

---

## Page 10969

for her recovery. She chose affliction and Paradise. Had removing illness been obligatory, there would have been no room for such a choice, just as there is none when it comes to warding off hunger. Further evidence is found in his supplication that Ubayy be afflicted with fever, his choosing fever for the people of Qubāʾ, his supplication that his community should perish through stabbing and plague, and his prohibition against fleeing from plague.

Anyone who disputes this is also refuted by the example of Allah’s prophets who were afflicted and patiently endured their afflictions without resorting to means of removing them, such as Job, peace be upon him, and others. He is likewise refuted by the example of the righteous predecessors. When Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked, “Shall we call a physician for you?” he replied, “He has already seen me.” They asked, “What did He say to you?” He replied, “He said, ‘I do whatever I will.’”

Similar accounts are related from al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, humble and ever turning to Allah, who was the finest of the people of Kufa, or equal to their finest; from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the upright caliph who guided others and was himself rightly guided; and from countless others.

I know of no predecessor who held medical treatment to be obligatory. Rather, many people of virtue and knowledge preferred to forgo it, considering this more virtuous and choosing what Allah had chosen, accepting it and submitting to Him. This is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position, although some of his followers hold treatment to be obligatory, while others consider it recommended and preferable. The latter approach was also followed by many of the predecessors, who adhered to the means Allah has created and made part of His established way with His servants.

---

## Page 10970

Third:
The ability of medicine to ward off illness is not certain; indeed, in many illnesses it is not even thought likely to do so. Were this invariably the case, no one would die. This differs from food’s ability to relieve hunger and starvation, which is certain according to Allah’s established way with His servants and His creation.

Fourth:
An illness may have various remedies. If it is not dispelled by a prohibited remedy, one turns to a lawful one. It is impossible that no cure or remedy for it should exist among lawful things. He who sent down disease sent down a remedy for every disease except death. It cannot be that the remedies for illnesses lie within the category of forbidden things, for He, glory be to Him, is Most Kind, Most Merciful.

This is what the reported hadith indicates:

“Allah has not placed the cure for my community in what He has forbidden them.”

Hunger is different. Although it may be relieved by whatever food happens to be available, prohibited food becomes permissible only when nothing else is available. If you envisage a comparable case involving medicine, that is a rare situation: illness is far less frequent than hunger, and it is rare for a particular medicine to be indispensable with no alternative available. Thus, this does not invalidate the argument. In any event, the preceding arguments suffice.

Fifth—and herein lies the essential understanding of this issue:
Allah Most High has made His creatures dependent upon food and nourishment. Their hunger and starvation can be relieved only by something belonging to the category of food. He has thus guided us to, and taught us about, the category of things that dispels hunger and relieves starvation.

As for illness, He removes it through many kinds of means: outward and inward, spiritual and bodily. Medicine is therefore not the sole means of removing it. Moreover, no particular kind of medicine is indispensable for a particular type of

---

## Page 10971

body in removing a particular disease. Moreover, identifying and knowing that particular kind of medicine eludes most people—indeed, people generally. Even an intelligent and discerning specialist who practises this art may devote much of his life to acquiring such knowledge, yet still fail to recognize the kind of illness and its true nature, or to identify its medicine and cure. The means of removing illness thus differ from the means of relieving starvation in these clear respects and others. Accordingly, their rulings also differ, as we have explained.

This makes clear the answer to the analogies mentioned above. A general account of what is waived and what is permitted on grounds of need and necessity, insofar as it occurs to me now, is as follows.

As for the waiving of such obligations as standing in prayer, fasting, and ritual bathing, the benefit of doing so is certain, unlike medical treatment. Moreover, omitting what is commanded is less serious than doing what is forbidden. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Consider how he required avoidance of everything forbidden, while distinguishing, with regard to what is commanded, between what one can and cannot do. This almost constitutes an independent proof concerning the issue.

Furthermore, obligations such as standing in prayer, attending Friday prayer, and performing Hajj are waived on account of kinds of hardship that do not justify permitting anything prohibited. This becomes clear upon reflection.

---

## Page 10972

As for adornment:

Gold was permitted for use in the nose and for securing teeth only because this is a matter of necessity and it certainly meets the need, just as eating does in severe hunger.

As for wearing silk to relieve itching and scabies:

Even if this is conceded, silk and gold are not absolutely forbidden. Both have been permitted to one of the two classes of people subject to religious obligations, and some use of them has been permitted to the other. Trading in them and giving them as gifts to polytheists have also been permitted. Thus, it is clear that they are permitted on grounds of need in general, and the need for medical treatment is greater than women’s need for adornment. This is unlike prohibited, ritually impure substances. Permission has also been granted because the intended benefit is generally achieved thereby.

Furthermore, the distinction between silk and food is that the rules governing food differ from those governing clothing, because food affects the body more profoundly than clothing does, as explained earlier. Prohibited food is therefore permitted only in cases of necessity, namely severe hunger and starvation, whereas prohibited clothing is permitted both for necessity and for need. This is what the Sunnah establishes, and we must not treat alike what Allah has distinguished. The distinction between necessities and needs is well known in many matters of religious law. This answers all the objections raised concerning this issue.

The second argument:

Muslim recorded in his Sahīh:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about wine: ‘May it be used as a remedy?’ He replied: ‘It is a disease, not a remedy.’”

---

## Page 10973

This is an explicit text prohibiting the medicinal use of wine, refuting those who permit it. Other prohibited substances fall under the same ruling by analogy, contrary to those who distinguish between them. Indeed, prohibited foods are more closely comparable to wine than one crow is to another. Moreover, wine was permissible during part of the early Islamic period, and some Muslims have permitted drinking beverages of its kind provided one does not become intoxicated. This is not the case with carrion and blood.

If it is said:

“The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stated that wine is a disease, not a remedy. It therefore cannot be called a remedy, unlike other substances. Furthermore, permitting its medicinal use would mean permitting its manufacture and the pressing of juice to make it, which would encourage drinking it. This is why, unlike other unwholesome foods, its consumption carries a prescribed punishment: people have such a strong desire for it.”

I reply:

Your statement that it cannot be called a remedy is correct. The same applies to all other prohibited substances, as indicated by the authentic hadith:

“Allah has not placed your cure in anything forbidden.”

But what do you mean by this? Do you mean that Allah has not endowed it with natural properties, such as heat and others? Experience among disbelievers and sinners has shown that it relieves certain cold ailments (1), like the other powers and properties He has placed in all medicinal substances. Or do you mean something else? For if

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A lacuna in the original.

---

## Page 10974

you mean the former, it is disproved by tested facts upon which nations agree and which many people regard as self-evident. Indeed, it denies what is directly observed and witnessed.

It has even been said that this contradicts the Quran, for the Most High says:

“Say, ‘In both there is great sin and benefits for people.’”

Perhaps this is clearer in the case of wine than any of the familiar claims concerning bodily health. If, on the other hand, you mean that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, declared it a disease of souls, hearts, and minds—and it is the mother of all evils—then bear in mind that the soul and heart constitute the sovereign whose soundness and perfection are sought. The body is merely its instrument, following and obeying it as the angels obey their Lord. When the heart is sound, the whole body is sound; when the heart is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Wine is thus a disease and sickness of the heart, corrupting it and undermining its finest qualities: reason and knowledge. When the heart is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, as the Sunnah teaches. In this respect, wine becomes a disease of the body because it is a disease of the heart. The same applies to all wealth seized unlawfully or stolen: the body may thrive, grow, and put on flesh through it, but the heart is corrupted by it, and the body is corrupted through the heart’s corruption.

As for the benefit wine contains, it benefits only the body, and that benefit is but a little enjoyment. Even if it improves some minor thing, that improvement amounts to nothing beside the corruption it causes. This is precisely the meaning of the Most High’s words:

“In both there is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.”

Such, by my life, is the case with all forbidden things, for they contain

---

## Page 10975

a corrupting power whose effects upon the heart, and then the body, in this world and the Hereafter far outweigh the slight benefit they may bring to the body alone, and only in this world. Moreover, even if we do not know precisely how forbidden things cause harm, we are certain that their harms outweigh whatever benefits we suppose they possess. Understand this well, for it reveals the legal reasoning behind this issue and its underlying wisdom.

As for the argument that this would lead to producing wine:

It carries no weight, since wine can be obtained from the People of the Book, while producing it remains forbidden. The discussion concerns only wine that already exists. This argument is also countered by using wine to extinguish a fire or relieve choking when nothing else is available.

As for wine alone being subject to a prescribed punishment:

Al-Hasan al-Basrī also holds that consuming carrion, blood, and pork incurs a prescribed punishment. The distinction, however, is that people have a natural inclination and an active desire for wine. A deterrent established by religious law, involving punishment in this world as well, was therefore instituted to counter that inclination and encourage less drinking. This is not the case with other forbidden things toward which people feel neither much inclination nor any strong desire.

The third argument:

Hassān ibn Mukhāriq narrated that Umm Salamah said: “A daughter of mine fell ill, so I prepared an infusion for her in a jug. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, came in while it was bubbling and said, ‘What is this?’

I replied, ‘My daughter fell ill, so we prepared this infusion for her.’ He said:

---

## Page 10976

‘Allah has not placed your healing in anything forbidden.’” Narrated by Abū Hātim ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh. Another version reads:

“Allah has not placed your healing in what He has forbidden you.”

Some hadith masters graded it authentic. This hadith explicitly addresses the issue.

The fourth argument:

Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan:

“A man was prescribed a frog to include in a medicine, but the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade killing frogs and said, ‘Their croaking glorifies Allah.’”

Here is a forbidden animal whose use was not permitted for medical treatment. This explicitly addresses the issue. The prohibition concerning frogs may even be less severe than that concerning other repugnant things, since the most that has been said about them is that their croaking glorifies Allah. What, then, of pork, carrion, and the like?

All this makes clear to you how little importance he attached to seeking medical treatment and insisting upon it, treating it as a matter of kindness to the sick and putting them at ease. Thus, when a man told the truthful and trusted Prophet, “I am a physician,” he replied:

“You are a caregiver; Allah is the Physician.”

The fifth argument:

It is also narrated in his Sunan that “the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade foul medicine.” This is a comprehensive and precise text, stating the very ruling at issue.

The sixth argument:

The hadith traced back to the Prophet:

“I would not care what I did—or what I committed—if I drank theriac, wore an amulet, or composed poetry of my own.”

Along with this, there is

---

## Page 10977

the reported disapproval of theriac by some of the early generations. Moreover, no opposing text, whether general or specific, reaches the degree of conclusiveness required in this matter. Had I not been writing this from memory, I would have discussed it exhaustively, covering every detail, great and small. Allah is the One who guides to the straight path.

The third proof—which is, in fact, the fourth:

The authentic hadith recorded by Muslim and others, on the authority of Jābir ibn Samurah and others:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about praying in sheep pens. He said, ‘Pray in them, for they are a blessing.’”

“He was also asked about praying in places where camels rest. He said, ‘Do not pray in them, for they were created from devils.’”

This provides evidence in two respects.

First, he gave unrestricted permission to pray there, without stipulating a barrier to prevent contact with them, although this was a situation requiring clarification. Had such a barrier been necessary, he would have explained it. This argument has already been established.

This resembles al-Shāfi‘ī’s statement:

“When an account of a situation admits of different possibilities, the omission of further inquiry has the force of a general statement.”

He did not ask the questioner for further details: “Is there a barrier between you and their droppings?” He gave unrestricted permission, even though this possibility was evident, not merely conceivable. Indeed, this is stronger evidence than the principle just cited, because the need for clarification here is more pressing and emphatic.

The second aspect is that, if these droppings were impure like human excrement, then

---

## Page 10978

praying in them would have been either forbidden, as in privies and latrines, or strongly disliked, since they would be places where filth and impurities were likely to be found. But to recommend praying in them and call them a blessing, while treating them as equivalent or nearly equivalent to privies, would be to combine two mutually contradictory positions. Far be it from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to do such a thing.

This is supported by the report that Abū Mūsā prayed where sheep rested, then pointed towards the open countryside and said:

“Here and there are alike.”

He was a Companion versed in religious law, knowledgeable about revelation and understanding its interpretation. He equated a place containing droppings with one free of them. How could this be reconciled with declaring those droppings impure? As for his prohibition of prayer where camels rest, this was not because of something peculiar to camels rather than cattle, sheep, gazelles, and horses. For if the reason were the impurity of urine, this would amount to distinguishing between things that are alike—which is certainly impossible.

The fourth proof—which is, in fact, the seventh:

The established and widely transmitted report:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, circumambulated on his mount and brought it into the Sacred Mosque,”

which Allah has favored above every other place on earth. He made it kneel there until he had completed seven circuits. Likewise, he permitted Umm Salamah to circumambulate while riding. It is well known that animals do not possess the understanding needed to refrain from soiling the mosque, which we are commanded to purify for those who circumambulate, those who remain there in worship, and those who bow and prostrate. Thus, if their urine were impure, this would have meant exposing

---

## Page 10979

the Sacred Mosque to ritual impurity, even though no necessity required this; there was merely a need for it. For this reason, some who regard their urine as impure have objected to bringing animals into the Sacred Mosque. His setting this view against the Sunnah that has been called into question is sufficient to demonstrate its invalidity.

The fifth proof—which is the eighth:

It is reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“As for animals whose meat may be eaten, there is nothing wrong with their urine.”

This states the very ruling under discussion. However, scholars have differed over whether to accept or reject the hadith. Abū Bakr Abd al-Azīz said that it is authentically established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while others said that it is attributed only to Jābir. If the former is correct, there is no doubt about it. If the latter is correct, it is the statement of a Companion, and similar statements have been reported from other Companions, including Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī. The argument then rests on the principle that the Companions’ statements take precedence over those of later generations and are more deserving of being followed. If it is known that this view became widespread among the other Companions without their objecting to it, it constitutes tacit consensus.

The sixth proof—which is the ninth:

The hadith reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was prostrating beside the Kaaba when Quraysh sent ‘Uqbah ibn Abī Mu‘ayt to some people who had slaughtered a camel of theirs. He brought its stomach contents and fetal membranes and placed them on the back of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, while he was prostrating. He did not leave until he had completed his prayer.”

This too clearly shows that

---

## Page 10980

those stomach contents and fetal membranes did not invalidate the prayer. As I see it, this can only be understood in one of three ways:

Either it is said that this ruling was abrogated. By abrogation, I mean that the ruling no longer applies, even if it had not been established by an explicit pronouncement, since this occurred in Mecca. This is a very weak interpretation, for abrogation may only be asserted with certainty; conjecture does not establish it.

Moreover, we have no knowledge that avoiding impurities was initially not obligatory and subsequently became obligatory. This is especially pertinent to those who argue that avoiding impurities is obligatory on the basis of Allah Most High’s words:

“And purify your garments.”

Surah al-Muddaththir was among the earliest revelations. According to their position, therefore, purification from impurities was among the earliest obligations. So much for that interpretation.

Or it is said that this proves the permissibility of carrying an impure substance while praying. Yet most of those who disagree on the issue under discussion do not hold this view, so their position requires them to set this hadith aside. Furthermore, this view is weak because it contradicts the authentic hadiths concerning menstrual blood and other hadiths. Nor do I know of any disagreement among them that this is disliked and that repeating a prayer performed in that condition is preferable. So much for that interpretation.

The only remaining explanation is that the stomach contents and fetal membranes are not impure but pure, since these are the stomach contents of an animal whose meat may be eaten. This is the conclusion that must be accepted, Allah Most High willing, given the many scholars who hold it and the clear evidence supporting it. The invalidity of the first two interpretations makes this the only remaining conclusion.

(If it is objected, “But the fetal membranes were among it, and they may contain blood,” we reply: It is possible that

---

## Page 10981

it was only a small amount of blood. Indeed, this is evidently the case, and carrying a small amount of blood during prayer is excused.

(If it is objected, “But the fetal membranes are flesh from an animal slaughtered by polytheists, and that is impure by agreement,” we reply:

We do not concede that animals slaughtered by polytheists had already been prohibited at that time. Rather, it is probable—or certain—that they had not yet been prohibited. There is no report that the Companions who embraced Islam regarded the animals slaughtered by their people as impure. Likewise, there is no report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, avoided anything other than what was slaughtered for idols. As for what his people slaughtered in their homes, he did not avoid it.

Had animals slaughtered by polytheists been prohibited in the earliest days of Islam, this would have imposed unbearable hardship on the few who embraced Islam. The overwhelming majority of the town’s inhabitants were polytheists, and those Muslims, being few, weak and poor, could only eat their food and bread and use their vessels for eating and drinking. Moreover, the presumption is that no prohibition existed at that time, so anyone claiming otherwise must provide evidence.

The seventh proof, which is the tenth:

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade using bones and dung to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself, saying:

“They are provisions for your brothers among the jinn.”

In another wording, he said:

“They asked me for food for themselves and their animals, so I said, ‘You may have every bone over which Allah’s name has been mentioned: it will be restored with the fullest covering of flesh. Every dropping will be fodder for your animals.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “So do not cleanse yourselves

---

## Page 10982

with either of them, for they are provisions for your brothers among the jinn.”

The point of evidence is that “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade cleansing oneself with bones and dung,” which are provisions for our brothers among the jinn and fodder for their animals. It is clear that he forbade this only so that we would not render these things impure for them. Hence, the jurists inferred that it is likewise impermissible to cleanse oneself with human food.

Moreover, numerous reports convey this prohibition and sternly warn against it, to the point that he said:

“Whoever wears a bowstring around his neck or cleanses himself with a bone or dung, Muhammad disavows him.”

It is clear that if dung were inherently impure, cleansing oneself with it would not render it impure. There would then be no distinction between dung used for cleansing and dung not used for that purpose. Yet this would erase a distinction made by the Sunnah.

Furthermore, if dung were impure, it would not be suitable as fodder for the animals of believing people, since their animals would thereby become filth-fed. If it were permissible for their animals to become filth-fed, it would also be permissible to feed them human excrement and animal dung, and there would then be no distinction.

Moreover, when he assigned them what human beings leave behind as provisions, and assigned their animals the dung left by human beings’ animals as fodder, he stipulated that their food should be every bone over which Allah’s name had been mentioned. A corresponding condition must therefore apply to their animals’ fodder: namely, purity. This makes clear to you that his words in the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, when the latter brought him two stones

---

## Page 10983

and a piece of dung, saying, “It is riks (rejected matter),” were due solely to its being human excrement or the like. Moreover, this was a particular incident: the dung could have come from an animal whose meat is eaten or from one whose meat is not eaten. The statement therefore does not apply generally to both categories, nor can one assert conclusively that it came from an animal whose meat is eaten. Furthermore, the word riks does not signify impurity, for riks means something cast back—that is, rejected—which is also the meaning of rajīʿ (excrement). It is well known that cleansing oneself with excrement is never permissible, either because it is impure or because it is fodder for the animals of our brothers among the jinn.

The eighth argument, which is the eleventh:

If these substances were impure, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have explained this. He did not explain it; therefore, they are not impure. This is because people frequently encounter these substances and come into direct contact with many of them, particularly the people among whom the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent. Camels and sheep constituted most of their wealth, and they constantly handled them and came into contact with the places where they stayed, both at home and on their journeys. Going barefoot was also common among them. Indeed, ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to enjoin this, saying: “Accustom yourselves to an austere life, embrace rugged living, and walk both barefoot and wearing sandals.”

The animals’ urine often falls into milking vessels, and their exposure to it is no less frequent than dogs’ lapping from their vessels. Thus, if these substances were impure, such that clothes, bodies, and vessels had to be washed clean of them, contact with them had to be avoided, prayer was prohibited while contaminated by them, ground containing any of them had to be purified before praying there—although they frequently prayed in such places on their journeys and in their sheepfolds—and it was forbidden to drink milk into which their droppings had fallen

---

## Page 10984

and one’s hand had to be washed if urine or moisture from their droppings touched it, along with the other rulings concerning impurity—then the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have been obliged to explain this clearly enough for the ruling to be known.
