## Page 11028

Chapter: Menstruation

Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

Is the following report attributed to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) authentic, and how is it interpreted according to the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad?

“Menstruation for a virgin girl lasts three days and their nights, and its maximum duration is fifteen days.”

He replied:

Attributing this report to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is false. Indeed, it is a fabricated lie, by agreement of the hadith scholars. It is, however, well known as a report transmitted by Abū al-Khuld from Anas, and Abū al-Khuld’s reliability has been questioned.

As for those who hold that the maximum duration of menstruation is fifteen days, as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad hold, and that its minimum is one day, as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad hold, or that it has no minimum limit, as Mālik holds, they say:

Nothing concerning this has been established from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) or his Companions. Rather, the matter is determined by usual menstrual patterns, as we have stated.

And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11029

He was asked:

Is intercourse with a menstruating woman permissible or not?

He replied:

Intercourse with a menstruating woman is forbidden by agreement of the imams, as Allah and His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) have prohibited it. If a man has intercourse with her while she is menstruating, there is a well-known disagreement over whether he must offer expiation. Scholars also disagree over her performing a ritual bath for the impurity resulting from intercourse separately from the bath for menstruation. Intercourse with a woman experiencing postnatal bleeding is likewise forbidden by agreement of the imams.

He may, however, take sexual pleasure with a menstruating woman or one experiencing postnatal bleeding in the area above the waist-wrapper, whether using his mouth, hand, or foot. Thus, if he rubs himself against her abdomen and ejaculates, that is permissible. Scholars disagree, however, over whether taking sexual pleasure between her thighs is permissible. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

If a woman’s menstruation ends and she cannot find water with which to bathe, may her husband have intercourse with her before she bathes, without any condition?

He replied:

When a woman’s menstrual bleeding ceases, her husband must not have intercourse with her until

---

## Page 11030

she performs a ritual bath, if she is able to do so; otherwise, she must perform dry ablution. This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Ahmad, and al-Shāfiʿī. This is also the meaning of the reports transmitted from the Companions. More than ten Companions—including the caliphs—are reported to have said concerning a woman observing her waiting period: “Her husband has the greater right to take her back so long as she has not bathed following her third menstrual period.”

The Quran supports this. Allah Most High says:

“Do not approach them until they become pure. Then, when they have purified themselves, approach them as Allah has commanded you.”

Mujāhid said that “until they become pure” means until the bleeding ceases, while “when they have purified themselves” means when they have bathed with water. It is exactly as Mujāhid explained.

Allah mentions two endpoints according to the majority reading because His words, “until they become pure,” mark the end of the prohibition arising from menstruation—a prohibition that cannot be lifted by bathing or by any other means. This prohibition ends when the bleeding ceases. Thereafter, intercourse is permissible on condition that she bathes; it does not remain unconditionally forbidden. Hence His words:

“Then, when they have purified themselves, approach them as Allah has commanded you.”

This is comparable to His words:

“If he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband.”

Marriage to the second husband marks the end of the prohibition arising from the three divorces. Once she marries the second husband, that prohibition ends. However, she is now married to the second husband and is therefore forbidden to the first because of the second husband’s marital right, not because of the three divorces. If the second husband divorces her, the first may marry her.

---

## Page 11031

Some adherents of the literalist school have said that His words, “Then, when they have purified themselves,” mean that they have washed their private parts. This interpretation is unfounded, for Allah has said:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

Thus, purification in the Book of Allah means bathing. As for His words:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who constantly repent and loves those who purify themselves,”

this includes those who bathe, perform ablution, or cleanse themselves after relieving themselves. However, purification mentioned in connection with menstruation is like purification mentioned in connection with major ritual impurity: what is meant is bathing.

Abū Hanīfah—may Allah have mercy on him—says that intercourse with her becomes permissible if she bathes, a prayer time has elapsed for her, or her bleeding ceases after ten days. This is based on her being deemed ritually pure in these circumstances. The majority’s view is correct, as explained above. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“What is the ruling on having intercourse with a menstruating woman before she bathes? And what is meant by Abū Hanīfah’s statement: ‘If her bleeding ceases before ten days, intercourse with her is not permissible until she bathes; but if her bleeding ceases after ten days, intercourse with her is permissible before she bathes’? Do the other imams agree with this?”

He replied:

“As for the position of the jurists, such as Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad, it is that it is not permissible

---

## Page 11032

to have intercourse with her until she bathes. As Allah Most High says:

“And do not approach them until they are pure. Then, when they have purified themselves, go in to them from where Allah has commanded you.”

As for Abū Hanīfah, he permits intercourse with her if her bleeding ceases at the maximum duration of menstruation, or if a prayer time has elapsed for her and she then bathes. The majority’s view is supported by the apparent meaning of the Quran and the transmitted reports.”

He was asked about the two hadiths recorded in both Sahīh collections:

The first is narrated from 'Ā'ishah—may Allah be pleased with her:

“Fātimah bint Abī Hubaysh asked the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—saying, ‘I suffer from persistent bleeding and never become pure. Should I stop praying?’ He replied, ‘That is bleeding from a vein. Rather, refrain from prayer for as many days as you used to menstruate, then bathe and pray.’”

Another version states:

“‘It is not menstruation. When your period begins, refrain from prayer; then, when its usual duration has passed, wash the blood off yourself and pray.’”

The second hadith is also narrated from 'Ā'ishah—may Allah be pleased with her:

“Umm Habībah suffered from non-menstrual bleeding for seven years. She asked the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—about this, and he instructed her to bathe for every prayer.”

Did she perform the full prescribed ritual bath, or did she wash away the blood and perform ablution? Furthermore,

---

## Page 11033

had she forgotten the days of her menstrual period, or was she experiencing menstruation for the first time? Did either hadith abrogate the other? If so, which one abrogated the other? If a woman suffers from the same condition as Umm Habībah, must she perform a full ritual bath? And if she is instructed to bathe, would this entail great hardship?

Allah Most High has said:

“He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion.”

Is there any disagreement among the imams on this matter?

He replied:

Neither hadith abrogates the other, nor is there any contradiction between them.

The first hadith concerns a woman who has an established menstrual pattern and knows its duration. If she then experiences non-menstrual bleeding, she refrains from prayer for the duration of her usual period. Hence he said:

“Refrain from prayer for as many days as you used to menstruate.”

He also said:

“When your period begins, refrain from prayer; then, when its usual duration has passed, wash the blood off yourself and pray.”

The majority of scholars have adopted this hadith as the basis for ruling that a woman with an established menstrual pattern who experiences non-menstrual bleeding should follow her usual pattern. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Imam Ahmad.

They disagree, however, about a woman who can distinguish black blood from red blood: should she give precedence to distinguishing between the types of blood over her usual menstrual pattern, or to her usual pattern over that distinction? Some give precedence to distinguishing between the types of blood. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him.

The second view is that she should give precedence to her usual menstrual pattern. This is the apparent meaning of the hadith, and it is the position of

---

## Page 11034

Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad, according to the stronger of the two reports from him. Indeed, Abū Hanīfah did not take the distinction between types of blood into account, just as Mālik did not take the usual menstrual pattern into account. Al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, however, consider both; the disagreement concerns which takes precedence.

As for the second hadith, it does not state that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed her to bathe for every prayer. Rather, he instructed her to bathe without specifying this, and she herself would bathe for every prayer. Bathing for every prayer is recommended, not obligatory, according to the four imams and others, provided that she refrains from prayer for the known days of her menstrual period, then bathes as a woman whose menstruation has ended would bathe, and thereafter prays and fasts despite this non-menstrual bleeding. What is obligatory, according to the majority—including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—is that she perform ablution for each of the five prayers.

Mālik, however, holds that neither ablution nor a full ritual bath is required of her on account of this bleeding, since, in his view, non-menstrual bleeding does not invalidate ablution, nor do other unusual discharges. The majority cite as evidence the report in al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed the woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to perform ablution for every prayer.”

The woman in the second hadith was not experiencing menstruation for the first time, although some people have supposed this, for she was an elderly woman. Rather, they understood her case as that of a woman who had forgotten her usual menstrual pattern. The Sunan collections state:

“She was instructed to treat six or seven days as her menstrual period.”

This also appears in the hadith of Salamah bint Sahl. It was on this that Imam

---

## Page 11035

Ahmad and others relied in arguing that a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding who can distinguish between the types of blood should refrain from prayer for six or seven days, the usual duration of menstruation.

Three teachings have been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning women experiencing non-menstrual bleeding: one concerns the usual menstrual pattern, as discussed above; another concerns a woman who can distinguish between the types of blood, namely his statement:

“Menstrual blood is black and recognizable.”

The third concerns the usual duration of menstruation, namely his statement:

“Treat six or seven days as your menstrual period, then bathe and pray for twenty-three or twenty-four days, just as women menstruate and become pure according to their regular times of menstruation and purity.”

Scholars disagree concerning non-menstrual bleeding, for it is a difficult matter: menstrual blood can be confused with non-menstrual blood, so there must be a criterion distinguishing the two.

Six indicators have been proposed:

One is the usual menstrual pattern, which is the strongest indicator, because the presumption is that menstruation, rather than other bleeding, persists during that period. Another is distinguishing between the types of blood, since black, thick, foul-smelling blood is more likely to be menstrual than red blood. Another is considering the usual menstrual pattern of most women, for the basic principle is to treat an individual case according to what is most general

---

## Page 11036

and prevalent. These three indicators are supported by the Sunnah and sound reasoning. Some jurists have her refrain from prayer for one night, the minimum duration of menstruation. Others have her refrain for its maximum duration, because the presumption is that the bleeding is normal, healthy bleeding. Still others have her follow the menstrual pattern of the women in her family. There is disagreement over whether this ruling applies only to a woman who has forgotten her menstrual pattern, or both to her and to a woman menstruating for the first time.

The soundest view is to consider the indicators established by the Sunnah and disregard all others. As for a woman who can distinguish between the types of blood, she should refrain from prayer for the usual duration of menstruation, as established by the Sunnah. Anyone who declines to classify any of her bleeding as menstruation, instead requiring her to take precautionary measures in every circumstance, has imposed an enormous burden upon her, the like of which the Sharia does not prescribe. This makes worshipping Allah hateful to those who follow His religion, whereas Allah has removed hardship from the Muslims. This is among the very weakest opinions.

The underlying principle is that blood, in terms of its legal ruling, falls into no more than five categories:

Blood that is certainly menstrual, such as regular menstrual blood unaccompanied by non-menstrual bleeding.

Blood that is certainly non-menstrual, such as the blood of a young girl.

Blood that could be either, but is more likely to be menstrual. This is the blood of a woman with an established menstrual pattern

---

## Page 11037

and of a woman who can distinguish between the types of blood, and similar women experiencing non-menstrual bleeding—blood that is ruled to be menstrual.

Blood that could be either, but is more likely to be abnormal bleeding. This is the blood of these women that is ruled to be non-menstrual.

Blood whose status is uncertain, with neither possibility outweighing the other. A group of scholars among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and others recognizes this category. They require a woman affected by it to fast and pray, and then make up the fasts. The correct view is that this opinion is invalid for several reasons:

First: Allah Most High says:

“Allah would never let a people go astray after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they must avoid.”

Allah Most High has explained to the Muslims what a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, or any other woman, must refrain from during menstruation: prayer and fasting. How, then, can it be said that the Sharia contains a state of perpetual uncertainty upon which the Messenger and his community base their rulings? Certainly, particular individuals may experience uncertainty, as when someone doubts whether he has invalidated his state of ritual purity, or concerning doubtful matters of which many people have no knowledge. But uncertainty and ambiguity inherent in the Sharia itself—this is untenable. Those who classify this blood as uncertain make that classification a ruling of the Sharia. They do not say, “We are uncertain.” Someone who is uncertain has no knowledge and therefore cannot make a categorical assertion. Yet these scholars categorically assert that fasting and repeating it are obligatory because of their uncertainty.

Second: The Sharia does not require prayer to be performed twice, nor

---

## Page 11038

fasting twice, except when the worshipper has been negligent. Where there has been no negligence, Allah has not required two months of fasting in a year or two noon prayers in a day. This demonstrates the weakness of the view that requires someone both to perform a prayer and to repeat it. This is a weak principle, as has been discussed at length elsewhere. It includes requiring someone to pray behind an openly sinful imam and then repeat the prayer; to pray despite rare impediments that do not persist and then repeat the prayer; or requiring a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to fast twice. Such rulings are found in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to one of the two views.

The correct position, held by the majority of Muslims, is that whoever performs an act of worship as commanded, to the best of their ability, need not repeat it. As Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

It has never been known that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded anyone to perform the same prayer twice. Rather, he would command someone to repeat it if they had failed to do what they were commanded despite being able to do so. Thus, he said to the man who prayed incorrectly:

“Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.”

Likewise, he commanded the man who prayed alone behind the row to repeat his prayer.

As for those with a valid excuse—such as someone who performs dry ablution because water is unavailable, or because using it could cause harm due to illness or cold; a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding; and others like them—the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is that they do whatever they can, according to their ability, while whatever lies beyond their ability is waived. Indeed, his Sunnah regarding someone who was unaware of an obligation is that there is no requirement to make it up

---

## Page 11039

on their part, because religious obligation is conditional upon the ability to acquire knowledge and to perform the act. This is why he did not command ʿUmar and ʿAmmār to repeat their prayers when they were in a state of major ritual impurity. ʿUmar did not pray, while ʿAmmār rolled in the dust as an animal does, thinking that the dust should reach wherever water would reach. Likewise, he did not command those Companions who continued eating until they could distinguish black cords from white ones to make up their fasts.

Similarly, he did not command those who prayed in a direction other than the Kaaba before news of the change in ruling reached them to repeat their prayers. Some were in Abyssinia, some in Mecca, and others elsewhere. Indeed, even some of those in Medina performed part of their prayer facing the Kaaba and part facing the Rock, yet he did not command them to repeat it. There are numerous similar examples.

Anyone who thoroughly examines what the Quran and Sunnah have brought will see that religious obligation is conditional upon the ability to know and to act. Whoever is incapable of either is relieved of whatever lies beyond their ability:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

This is why someone who errs in exercising independent judgment is excused: they were unable to ascertain the truth in that particular matter. This is unlike someone who is negligent despite being able to do what they were commanded; that is the person who deserves punishment.

This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

This is a major principle that requires an extensive discussion, for which this is not the place.

---

## Page 11040

The questioner’s concern is with a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding. We have explained that the correct view is that under no circumstances is she required both to fast and to make up that fast, as some followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and others require in certain cases. Nor is she required to perform the ritual bath for every prayer, by agreement of the four imams and others. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Regarding a woman with postnatal bleeding who has not performed the ritual bath: is intercourse with her permissible before she bathes?

He answered:

Intercourse with a menstruating woman or a woman with postnatal bleeding is not permissible until she has performed the ritual bath. If she cannot find water, or fears harm from using it because of illness or severe cold, she should perform dry ablution, after which intercourse with her is permissible. This is the position of the great majority of the imams, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The Quran indicates this in the words of the Most High:

“Do not approach them until they are pure,”

meaning until the bleeding stops;

“Then, when they have purified themselves,”

meaning when they have bathed with water. Likewise, He says:

“If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves.”

Reports supporting this have been transmitted from leading Companions, including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Mūsā and others. They held that the husband had the greater claim to her so long as she had not bathed after her third menstrual period.

As for Abū Hanīfah, his position is that if the bleeding stops after ten days or more, and a prayer time has elapsed for her or she has performed the ritual bath, he may have intercourse with her; otherwise, he may not. Allah knows best.

---

## Page 11041

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Regarding a woman experiencing postnatal bleeding: may she recite the Quran during this bleeding? Is intercourse with her permissible before forty days have elapsed? If forty days have elapsed but she has not performed the ritual bath, is intercourse with her permissible without her bathing?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Intercourse with her before the bleeding stops is forbidden by agreement of the imams. If the bleeding stops before forty days have elapsed, she must perform the ritual bath and pray. Her husband, however, should refrain from intercourse with her until the forty days are complete.

As for reciting the Quran, if she does not fear forgetting it, she should not recite it. If she fears forgetting it, she may recite it according to one of the two scholarly views. Once the bleeding has stopped and she has performed the ritual bath, she may recite the Quran and pray, by scholarly agreement. If she is unable to bathe because water is unavailable, or because she fears harm due to illness or the like, she should perform dry ablution. She may then do whatever the ritual bath would permit her to do. Allah knows best.
